_readme: The Learn tab: required reading for H1 2026-27. Books, chapters, levels, skills, deal files, badges, rules and the question bank. Every question is written in our own words from the books (never paste text from them). Calculation questions carry ranges for their inputs (vars) and the formulas that give the answer (let, ans), so members get new figures on every try. Rand amounts in applied questions are illustrative and companies in deal files are fictional; historical figures from the books stay in dollars. See README.md, section Learn.

books.title: The Intelligent Investor
sections: Graham’s chapter
Zweig’s commentary

units.label: Introduction
units.title: What This Book Expects to Accomplish
ideas: The book teaches investment policy and the investor’s attitude, not the techniques of security analysis. It is written for investors, not speculators.
The defensive investor puts avoiding serious mistakes first and freedom from effort second; the enterprising investor gives time and care to find sound securities that are better than average.
Always ask “How much?” The price you pay decides your result, and obvious growth in an industry does not mean obvious profits for its shareholders.

units.label: Chapter 1
units.title: Investment versus Speculation
ideas: An investment, after thorough analysis, promises safety of principal and an adequate return. Anything that fails those tests is speculation, whatever it is called.

The defensive investor keeps between 25% and 75% in high-grade bonds (50/50 is the simple choice), rebalances when the mix drifts about 5%, and buys only important companies with long profitable records.
To beat the average, the enterprising investor needs policies that are sound and unpopular. Speculation belongs in a small, separate account that never mixes with investing.

units.label: Chapter 2
units.title: The Investor and Inflation
ideas: Inflation hurts anyone living on a fixed income, but shares are not an automatic hedge: Graham finds no close link in time between inflation and share earnings or prices.
Corporate returns on capital did not rise with inflation. Earnings grew from reinvested profits and much more debt, so neither an all-bond nor an all-share portfolio is safe.
Judge returns after inflation, not before (the “money illusion”). Shares beat inflation most of the time but not always; very high inflation and deflation both hurt them.

units.label: Chapter 3
units.title: A Century of Stock-Market History
ideas: Over a century, shares rose through many booms and busts, and the price the public paid for each rand of earnings swung widely with its mood.

Judge the market’s level by comparing share earnings and dividend yields with high-grade bond yields, not by the P/E ratio alone. On that test, Graham found early 1972 unattractive for conservative investors.
Never forecast by extending the past. Higher prices mean higher risk, and expected returns come from earnings growth, inflation and dividends, pushed up or down for a while by sentiment.

units.label: Chapter 4
units.title: General Portfolio Policy: The Defensive Investor
ideas: The return to aim for depends on how much intelligent effort you can bring, not on how much risk you are willing to run.
The defensive investor keeps shares between 25% and 75%, with 50/50 as the default, and rebalances mechanically. This is simple, but hard, because it goes against human nature.
In bonds, choose taxable or tax-free by arithmetic, avoid low-grade high-yield issues, prefer protection against early calls, and treat preference shares as an inherently weak form.

units.label: Chapter 5
units.title: The Defensive Investor and Common Stocks
ideas: Graham’s four rules for the defensive investor’s shares: hold 10 to 30 companies; choose large, prominent, conservatively financed ones; require a long record of unbroken dividends; and cap the price at 25 times average earnings (20 times the latest year’s).

Growth shares are too uncertain for the defensive investor. Large, unpopular companies at reasonable multiples are a sound, if unspectacular, choice, and regular monthly buying is a dependable method.

True risk is a permanent loss of value from selling low, a business getting worse, or overpaying. A temporary fall in price is not, and what you buy should depend on your knowledge and temperament, not your wealth.

units.label: Chapter 6
units.title: Portfolio Policy for the Enterprising Investor: Negative Approach
ideas: Graham’s don’ts for the enterprising investor: leave high-grade preference shares to companies; avoid inferior bonds and preference shares unless they are real bargains (at least 30% below par for high-coupon issues); skip foreign government bonds; be wary of new issues.
Accepting a possible loss of capital for 1% or 2% more income is bad business. Take risk only where a substantial capital gain is possible if things go well.
New issues come with a hard sell and are timed to suit the seller. A flood of small, poor-quality listings signals a late bull market. Zweig adds: the more you trade, the less you keep.

units.label: Chapter 7
units.title: Portfolio Policy for the Enterprising Investor: The Positive Side
ideas: Graham recommends three fields to the enterprising investor: relatively unpopular large companies, bargain issues worth at least 50% more than their price, and special situations. The usual growth-share approach brings no outstanding rewards.
Better-than-average results need a policy that is sound and different from the crowd’s. There is no safe middle ground: “you cannot soundly become half a businessman.”

Secondary companies, foreign bonds and ordinary preference shares are for bargain prices only, at no more than two-thirds of appraised value. Zweig adds that market timing fails, growth shares above 25 to 30 times earnings carry ugly odds, and some money belongs offshore.

units.label: Chapter 8
units.title: The Investor and Market Fluctuations
ideas: There are two ways to profit from market swings. Timing means forecasting the market; pricing means buying below fair value and selling above it. Pricing works; emphasising timing turns you into a speculator.

Mr Market is a moody partner who quotes a price every day. Deal with him only when his price suits you; otherwise judge value from the company’s results. A price fall is not a loss unless the value has fallen or you are forced to sell.

Expect large swings, even in excellent companies: the more successful the company, the more speculative its share price can become. Prefer shares near tangible asset value, keep a mechanical plan, and control what you can: costs, risk, taxes and your own behaviour.

units.label: Chapter 9
units.title: Investing in Investment Funds
ideas: Funds as a whole have served investors well, encouraging saving and preventing costly mistakes, but they earn roughly the market’s return, because professionals largely are the market.

“Performance” funds chasing spectacular gains with large sums take on risks that come home to roost. Lasting outperformance is rare, and usually comes from small, specialised funds that are not heavily sold.

Graham prefers buying closed-end funds at a discount to paying a premium for load funds, and owning bonds directly. Zweig adds: judge a fund on costs first, distrust past performance, favour low-cost index funds, and be patient.

units.label: Chapter 10
units.title: The Investor and His Advisers
ideas: Asking someone to tell you how to make money is an odd request. A good adviser protects you from mistakes and secures the normal return your money is entitled to; be wary of anyone promising more.
If you rely on advice, either keep to standard, conservative investments or know your adviser intimately. Take unconventional advice only once you can judge it yourself.

Brokers earn commissions, so they lean towards speculation; make clear you are an investor. Zweig adds: verify an adviser’s record, expect total fees near 1% a year at most, and use a written plan so the adviser helps manage you.

units.label: Chapter 11
units.title: Security Analysis for the Lay Investor: General Approach
ideas: A bond’s safety rests mainly on how many times earnings have covered its fixed charges over several years. Earning power, not asset values, is the main protection.

Value a share by estimating average future earnings and applying a multiplier shaped by long-term prospects, management, financial strength, dividend record and the current dividend. For growth shares, Graham’s shortcut is value = normal earnings × (8.5 + 2 × expected growth rate).

The more a valuation rests on the distant future, the less reliable it is. Distrust elaborate maths, prefer group estimates, and start from a past-performance value before adjusting. Zweig adds checks on moats, steady growth, honest managers, owner earnings and debt.

units.label: Chapter 12
units.title: Things to Consider About Per-Share Earnings
ideas: Don’t take a single year’s earnings seriously. If you do, watch for traps: special charges, tax credits from past losses, dilution from convertibles and warrants, and changes in depreciation or inventory methods.
Use average earnings over seven to ten years, including the special charges, and measure growth by comparing the last three years’ average with the same average ten years earlier.

Zweig: ignore “pro forma” earnings, and watch for aggressive revenue recognition, costs capitalised as assets, “one-off” charges that keep recurring, and income from pension plans. Read the annual report backwards, notes first.

units.label: Chapter 13
units.title: A Comparison of Four Listed Companies
ideas: Compare companies on profitability, stability, growth, financial position, dividend record and price history, then ask whether their price differences really match their performance differences.
High multiples price in years of future growth: even if it comes, the buyer may not profit. Modestly priced companies with solid records offer protected, value-type investments.

Graham’s seven tests for the defensive investor: adequate size, strong finances, 20 years of dividends, no loss in ten years, ten-year EPS growth of at least a third, price at most 1.5 times net assets, and price at most 15 times three-year average earnings.

units.label: Chapter 14
units.title: Stock Selection for the Defensive Investor
ideas: The defensive investor can simply own a cross-section of leading companies, or screen each share for a minimum of quality (record and finances) and a minimum of quantity (earnings and assets per rand of price).

Graham’s seven tests in full: size; a 2-to-1 current ratio with long-term debt no larger than working capital; earnings in each of ten years; 20 years of dividends; a third more EPS over ten years; at most 15 times three-year earnings; at most 1.5 times book, or P/E × P/B no more than 22.5.

There are two ways to face the future: prediction and protection. Graham chose protection, a margin of present value above the price, and tells the defensive investor to emphasise diversification over picking “the best”.

units.label: Chapter 15
units.title: Stock Selection for the Enterprising Investor
ideas: Beating the market is extremely hard, even for well-resourced funds: prices already reflect much of what is knowable, and analysts often buy “the best” companies at any price. The opening lies in parts of the market that are neglected.

Graham’s own methods were narrow and unpopular: arbitrage, liquidations, related hedges and diversified groups of shares bought below net current asset value. He dropped anything that wasn’t dependable and “headache proof”.

The enterprising investor can screen for low multiples, sound finances and prices near tangible assets, with more flexibility than the defensive investor. Zweig: practise on paper for a year, keep picks to 10% at most, and judge returns on capital and management.

units.label: Chapter 16
units.title: Convertible Issues and Warrants
ideas: A conversion privilege cannot make a deal much better for both sides: the buyer usually gives up quality, yield or both. Convertibles issued late in a bull market do badly as a group, and their soundness shows only in a falling market.

Even a winning convertible brings a dilemma (sell early or hold), and the old rule is “never convert a convertible bond”. Convertibles and warrants also dilute the ordinary shares, so adjust earnings and prices for them.

Graham calls large warrant issues a near fraud that conjures market value from thin air. Zweig: convertibles behave like shares, work like options and are best owned through a low-cost fund; covered calls cap your gains.

units.label: Chapter 17
units.title: Four Extremely Instructive Case Histories
ideas: Elementary analysis is often enough. Penn Central’s thin interest cover, absent tax payments and poor operating ratio were all visible long before it failed; professionals simply didn’t do the basic work.

Empire building on borrowed money (LTV) and tiny companies swallowing big ones (NVF) leave top-heavy debt, dilution and accounting puzzles. Lenders and shareholders who ignore the ratios share the blame.
Hot new issues (AAA Enterprises) sell hope at many times book value. Zweig’s modern cases (Lucent, Tyco, AOL Time Warner, eToys) show the same four extremes repeating: watch with both eyes.

units.label: Chapter 18
units.title: A Comparison of Eight Pairs of Companies
ideas: Side-by-side comparisons expose how far market prices can stray from performance: popular companies with growth and glamour often sell at many times the price of steadier ones with larger sales, earnings and assets.

Growth and profitability justify a higher multiple, but not any multiple. When the price contains “too much promise and not enough performance”, even an excellent company is too rich for the conservative investor.
Graham would have analysts hunt for the minority of cases where the price is clearly below value. Zweig’s modern pairs repeat the lesson: there are no good stocks, only good stock prices.

units.label: Chapter 19
units.title: Shareholders and Managements: Dividend Policy
ideas: Shareholders own the business and should question management when results are poor in themselves, poorer than comparable companies’ and reflected in a long-lasting poor share price. In practice, takeovers have done more than shareholder votes to fix bad managements.

Retained earnings must earn their keep: shareholders should expect a normal payout (about two-thirds) or clear proof that reinvestment has lifted per-share earnings. Mediocre companies holding back dividends “to expand” need a convincing defence.

Zweig: be an intelligent owner. Read the proxy statement, vote, and watch for conflicts of interest, hoarded or wasted cash, buybacks that buy high to cover options sold low, and option grants that reward managers without superior results.

units.label: Chapter 20
units.title: “Margin of Safety” as the Central Concept of Investment
ideas: The secret of sound investment in three words: margin of safety. For bonds it is earnings well above interest, or value well above debt; for shares, an earnings yield well above the bond rate, or a price well below appraised value.

The margin makes an accurate forecast unnecessary, depends entirely on the price paid, and works with diversification: it gives a better chance of profit than loss, so many such holdings together should come out ahead.

A true margin of safety can be shown by figures, reasoning and experience; that is what separates investment from speculation. Run investing like a business: know it, supervise it, rely on arithmetic, and have the courage of your conclusions.

units.label: Postscript
units.title: Postscript
ideas: There are several ways to make and keep money. One shrewd or lucky decision can outweigh a lifetime of careful work, but it usually rests on preparation, a disciplined capacity and the courage to act.
The partners bought because the price was moderate against earnings and assets, not because Wall Street liked the industry: value first, popularity irrelevant.

Zweig: Graham took little financial risk but a large psychological one. Most of us should diversify; uncertainty is the permanent condition of investing, and investing requires faith in a better tomorrow.

units.label: Chapter 1
units.title: Comparable Companies Analysis
sections: Step I: Select the universe of comparable companies
Step II: Locate the necessary financial information
Step III: Spread key statistics, ratios and trading multiples
Step IV: Benchmark the comparable companies
Step V: Determine valuation
ideas: Trading comps value a target against listed peers that share its business and financial profile: select the universe, locate the data, spread statistics, ratios and multiples, benchmark, then apply the closest comparables’ multiples to the target.

Measure consistently. Equity value is fully diluted (treasury stock method for options; if-converted or net share settlement for convertibles); enterprise value adds debt, preferred and noncontrolling interest and subtracts cash. Pair enterprise value with sales, EBITDA or EBIT, and equity value with net income or EPS.

Clean the numbers first: use LTM figures, calendarise different year-ends, scrub non-recurring items (tax-effecting them for net income) and reflect recent events. Comps are current and market-based, so use them alongside the other methods.

units.label: Chapter 2
units.title: Precedent Transactions Analysis
sections: Step I: Select the universe of comparable acquisitions
Step II: Locate the necessary deal-related and financial information
Step III: Spread key statistics, ratios and transaction multiples
Step IV: Benchmark the comparable acquisitions
Step V: Determine valuation
ideas: Precedent transactions value a target on the multiples paid in comparable past acquisitions, ideally recent ones (two to three years) involving fundamentally similar companies. Read each deal’s story: market conditions, buyer type, motivations, sale process and consideration.

Transaction multiples usually exceed trading multiples because buyers pay for control and synergies. They are built on actual LTM figures at announcement, with equity value from the offer price times fully diluted shares (all in-the-money options, vested or not).

How the price is paid matters: cash gives certainty, a fixed exchange ratio shares the risk of the acquirer’s share price, a floating ratio fixes the value. Measure premiums against the unaffected price, and test the result against trading comps.

units.label: Chapter 3
units.title: Discounted Cash Flow Analysis
sections: Step I: Study the target and determine key performance drivers
Step II: Project free cash flow
Step III: Calculate WACC
Step IV: Determine terminal value
Step V: Calculate present value and determine valuation
ideas: A DCF values a business as the present value of its projected unlevered free cash flow plus a terminal value, discounted at WACC. It gives intrinsic rather than market value, so it checks the market-based methods and helps where no pure-play peers exist.

Free cash flow = EBIT × (1 − tax rate) + D&A − capex − increase in net working capital. Project it, usually for five years, to a steady state; drive working capital with DSO, DIH and DPO; keep the terminal year normalised, with capex close to depreciation.

WACC blends the after-tax cost of debt and the CAPM cost of equity at a target capital structure (unlever and relever peer betas for private companies). Terminal value comes from an exit multiple or perpetuity growth, each checking the other. It is often three-quarters of the value, so sensitise the inputs and compare with other methods.

units.label: Chapter 4
units.title: Leveraged Buyouts
ideas: An LBO buys a company largely with debt (traditionally 60–70% of the price) and a sponsor’s equity (30–40%). The target’s cash flow and assets carry the debt; sponsors have aimed for 20%+ IRRs and an exit within about five years.

Strong candidates have predictable cash flow, defensible market positions, growth and efficiency opportunities, low capex, a solid asset base and proven management. Returns come from repaying debt and growing enterprise value; leverage magnifies them, and the risk.

The financing stack runs from bank debt (secured, floating, prepayable, maintenance covenants) through high yield bonds (unsecured, fixed, bullet, incurrence covenants, call protection) to mezzanine (PIK, equity kickers) and then equity. The structure must balance sponsor, lenders, company and management.

units.label: Chapter 5
units.title: LBO Analysis
sections: Step I: Locate and analyse the necessary information
Step II: Build the pre-LBO model
Step III: Input the transaction structure
Step IV: Complete the post-LBO model
Step V: Perform the LBO analysis
ideas: LBO analysis builds a model to test a financing structure: can the target service and repay the debt, how do its credit statistics evolve, and what returns does the sponsor earn? It also frames valuation, including what a rival sponsor could afford to pay.

Build it in order: a stand-alone three-statement model with several cases; the purchase price and a balanced sources and uses table; adjustments to the opening balance sheet (new debt, goodwill created, capitalised financing fees, equity net of deal fees); then a debt schedule that applies free cash flow to mandatory and optional repayments.

Then analyse: deleveraging and coverage; returns from an exit, usually after five years at or below the entry multiple; sensitivity of IRR to entry and exit multiples and exit year. LBO values usually sit at the lower end of the football field.

units.label: Chapter 6
units.title: Sell-Side M&A
ideas: The sell-side advisor balances value, speed and certainty for the seller, choosing a broad auction, a targeted auction or a negotiated sale to suit the seller’s priorities on confidentiality, disruption and fit.

The classic two-round auction runs three to six months to signing: preparation (diligence, valuation from each buyer’s view, buyer list, teaser, CIM, confidentiality agreement); a first round of non-binding bids; a second round of management meetings, site visits and the data room; then final binding bids, negotiation, fairness opinion and signing.

Value is price and terms together. The definitive agreement allocates risk through representations, covenants, closing conditions, termination rights and break-up fees, and indemnities in private deals. Closing needs regulatory and shareholder approvals and financing.

units.label: Chapter 7
units.title: Buy-Side M&A
ideas: Companies buy to grow faster, more cheaply and with less risk than building from scratch. Synergies, with cost savings more reliable than revenue gains, let strategic buyers pay more. The main strategies are horizontal integration, vertical integration (backward or forward) and conglomeration.

Financing and structure change value. Cash and debt are cheaper than equity; equity is more flexible but issues shares. A stock sale is cleanest for the seller, but asset write-ups are not tax-deductible (hence a deferred tax liability). An asset sale gives the buyer a tax step-up, but risks double tax for the seller; a 338(h)(10) election suits subsidiary sales.

Buy-side valuation combines the football field (including the value of synergies), analysis at various prices and contribution analysis. Merger consequences analysis then tests goodwill, credit statistics and EPS accretion or dilution across price, financing mix and synergies.

cases.title: JacarandaCo
cases.lead: JacarandaCo is a fictional JSE-listed retailer. Value it against its listed peers.
facts: EBITDA, six months to December 2025; same period 2024

items.q: Fully diluted shares, using the treasury stock method?

errs.why: The exercise cash buys back shares; only the net new shares count.
The options are in the money, so they dilute.

items.why: Options in the money add their net new shares.

items.q: Enterprise value, using {dil|1m} fully diluted shares?

errs.why: That uses basic shares. Use the fully diluted count.
Non-controlling interest is added, not subtracted.
Cash is subtracted.

items.why: Equity value plus debt and non-controlling interest, less cash.

items.q: LTM EBITDA to December 2025?

errs.why: Take off the same six months of the previous year.
Doubling one half ignores seasonality; LTM uses reported figures.

items.why: The last full year, plus the latest half, less the same half a year before.

items.q: EV/LTM EBITDA, using {ev|R0m} and {ltm|R0m}?

errs.why: Use enterprise value, not equity value, over EBITDA.

items.why: Enterprise value over LTM EBITDA.

items.q: The implied share price at the peer median of {pm|1x}, using {dil|1m} shares?

errs.why: Take the debt, cash and non-controlling interest out before dividing by shares.

items.why: Multiple to enterprise value, then back through the bridge to equity, then per share.

items.q: JacarandaCo trades at {mult|1x} against peers at {pm|1x}. Which fact would best justify part of the premium?
options: Faster expected EBITDA growth and higher returns on capital than its peers
More shares in issue than its peers, which makes the shares easier to trade
A share price that has risen sharply this year, ahead of its peers
items.why: Multiples price in growth and returns. Share count and past price moves don’t justify paying more for each rand of EBITDA.
items.src: Step IV: Benchmark the comparable companies
miss: Share count is already in equity value; it says nothing about the value of each rand of EBITDA.
A rising price may explain the multiple, but it doesn’t justify it: it could just as well be a sign of exuberance.

cases.title: ProteaCo
cases.lead: ProteaCo, a fictional JSE-listed consumer brands company, has agreed to be bought by a larger listed rival for cash and shares.
facts: {op|1m} at an average {k|R}; all in the money, some unvested

items.q: What is the offer worth per ProteaCo share?

errs.why: Add the cash part.
Value the shares at the buyer’s price.

items.why: Cash plus the share part valued at the buyer’s price.

items.q: What premium does the offer pay over the unaffected price?

errs.why: Divide by the unaffected price, not the offer.

items.why: Premium over the unaffected price.

items.q: Fully diluted shares at the offer price, counting all options?

errs.why: The exercise cash buys back shares at the offer price.
The options are in the money, so they count.

items.why: Treasury stock method at the offer price; unvested options count because vesting accelerates.

items.q: The equity purchase price, using {dilr|2m} fully diluted shares?

errs.why: Use the fully diluted count, not basic shares.

items.why: Fully diluted shares times the offer price.

items.q: The transaction’s EV/LTM EBITDA, using an equity purchase price of {eqp|R0m}?

errs.why: Add net debt to reach enterprise value.
Cash is subtracted.

items.why: Equity purchase price plus net debt, over LTM EBITDA.

items.q: Before closing, the buyer’s shares fall 10%. The exchange ratio is fixed and there is no collar. What happens to the offer?
options: The cash part is unchanged; the share part, and so the total per share, is worth less
The buyer must issue more shares so that the total stays at {off|R2} per share
Nothing: the offer price was fixed in rand when the deal was announced
items.why: A fixed ratio fixes the number of shares, not their value, so ProteaCo’s holders carry that risk.
miss: That is how a floating ratio works.
Only the cash part and the number of shares are fixed.

cases.title: BaobabCo
cases.lead: BaobabCo is a fictional JSE-listed food producer. Build the key pieces of its DCF.
facts: D&A; capex; increase in NWC, year 1
Present value of FCF, years 1 to 5

items.q: Unlevered free cash flow in year 1?

errs.why: An increase in working capital is subtracted.
Tax on EBIT comes off first.

items.why: EBIT after tax, plus D&A, less capex and the increase in working capital.

items.q: Relever the peer beta at BaobabCo’s target structure ({wd|0%} debt to total capital). What is the levered beta?

errs.why: The formula needs debt to equity, not debt to total capital.
Use the after-tax debt to equity.

items.why: Convert the weight to debt to equity first, then relever after tax.

items.q: WACC, using a levered beta of {blr|2}?

errs.why: Use the after-tax cost of debt.
The weights are swapped.

items.why: CAPM for equity, the after-tax cost for debt, weighted by the target structure.

items.q: Terminal value at year 5 by the perpetuity growth method, using a WACC of {wr|1%}?

errs.why: Grow the year-5 flow by one year first.
Divide by WACC less growth.

items.why: Grow the year-5 flow by one year, then divide by WACC less growth.

items.q: Enterprise value, using a terminal value of {tv|R0m} (discount it at year-end over five years at {wr|1%})?
work: Present value of the terminal value = {tv|R0m} ÷ (1 + {wr|1%})^5 = {pvtv|R0m}

errs.why: Discount the terminal value to today first.
Add the present value of the projected cash flows.

items.why: Bring the terminal value back five years, then add the present value of the projected cash flows.

items.q: The terminal value makes up {share|0%} of BaobabCo’s enterprise value. What is the right reading?
options: Normal for a DCF, which is why the growth rate and WACC need sensitivity tables
A sign the projections are wrong and should run for fifteen years
Proof that WACC is too low and must be raised until the terminal value falls below half
items.why: Most of a DCF’s value usually sits beyond the forecast. The answer isn’t to distrust it but to test it: show how value moves with WACC and growth.
miss: Longer projections don’t remove the issue; they move it. Sensitivity analysis shows how much the assumptions matter.
A large terminal share is normal at any sensible WACC.

cases.title: MopaneCo
cases.lead: MopaneCo is a fictional South African packaging business. A private equity sponsor is weighing a buyout.
facts: End of year 5, at the entry multiple

items.q: Purchase enterprise value?

errs.why: That is the debt raised, not the price.

items.why: LTM EBITDA times the entry multiple.

items.q: How much equity must the sponsor put in, with fees of {fees|R0m}?

errs.why: Fees are a use of funds too: equity has to cover them.
Take off the debt raised.

items.why: Sources must equal uses: equity fills the gap between the price plus fees and the debt raised.

items.q: Equity value at exit, at the entry multiple?

errs.why: Take off only the debt still outstanding, after repayments.
Lenders are repaid before equity.

items.why: Exit value less the debt still outstanding.

items.q: The sponsor’s cash return, using exit equity of {ex|R0m} and equity invested of {eq|R0m}?

errs.why: Measure the sponsor’s return on its equity, not the company’s value growth.

items.why: Equity out over equity in.

items.q: The IRR over five years, using a cash return of {mor|2x}?

errs.why: That ignores compounding; take the fifth root.

items.why: The yearly rate that compounds the equity to the exit proceeds.

items.q: The fund’s hurdle is a 20% IRR. Which change to the plan would most reliably lift MopaneCo’s returns?
options: Negotiating a lower entry price
Assuming a higher exit multiple than the entry multiple
Holding the business for ten years instead of five
items.why: Price discipline is in the sponsor’s control today. Multiple expansion is a bet on the market, and a longer hold usually lowers the IRR even as the cash return rises.
miss: That raises the modelled return but relies on the market; prudent models exit at or below the entry multiple.
A longer hold raises the cash return but usually lowers the IRR.

cases.title: AloeCo
cases.lead: AloeCo is a fictional South African healthcare products business. A sponsor is modelling a buyout from its owners.
facts: Existing debt (refinanced); cash on balance sheet (used)
Year-5 EBITDA; term loan repaid by year 5
End of year 5 at {m|1x}; no cash left

items.q: The equity purchase price for AloeCo’s shares?

errs.why: Cash in the business goes to the sellers: add it.
Take off the existing net debt.

items.why: Enterprise value less the existing debt, plus the cash.

items.q: The sponsor’s equity, using an equity purchase price of {eqp|R0m}?

errs.why: Fees are a use too.
The cash on hand is a source.

items.why: Equity balances sources and uses.

items.q: Year-1 interest on the term loan, using the average balance?

errs.why: Use the average balance, not the opening one.

items.why: Average of opening and closing balances, times the rate.

items.q: Total leverage at exit (all debt ÷ year-5 EBITDA)?

errs.why: Take off the term loan repaid by year 5.
The notes are still outstanding: include them.

items.why: Remaining term loan plus the notes, over exit EBITDA.

items.q: The sponsor’s IRR, using debt at exit of {d5|R0m} and equity invested of {sp|R0m}?

errs.why: Take the fifth root: IRR compounds.
Take the debt off the exit value first.

items.why: Exit equity over equity in, then the fifth root.

items.q: AloeCo’s total leverage falls from {(tl+nt)/e|1x} at close to {lev|1x} by exit. What drives that?
options: Debt repaid from free cash flow, with EBITDA growing too
Rising interest rates over the period, which shrink the debt
The sponsor’s management fees, charged each year to the fund’s investors
items.why: Deleveraging comes from both sides: less debt on top and more EBITDA beneath.
miss: Higher rates raise interest costs; they don’t reduce debt.
Fees are paid to the sponsor by its investors; they don’t touch the company’s debt.

cases.title: FynbosCo
cases.lead: FynbosCo is a fictional family-owned South African beverage company. You advise the family on a sale by auction.
facts: {lv|2x} EBITDA of debt; at least {ep|0%} equity
{ba|R0m}, subject to financing and further diligence

items.q: What price does the staple imply a sponsor could pay?

errs.why: Gross the debt up for the equity.
Divide by the debt share of the price, not the equity share.

items.why: The staple’s debt grossed up by the minimum equity: a floor for strategic bids.

items.q: Which bid should you recommend the family takes forward?
options: Bid B: committed financing and a near-final contract can outweigh a {1-bb/ba|0%} lower price
Bid A, because its headline price is higher and price is what the family asked for
Neither: restart the auction, hoping to draw out a higher bid that is fully financed
items.why: Value is price and terms together. Bid A’s conditions are risks the family would carry.
miss: The headline price is only part of value: Bid A could fall away or be renegotiated.
Restarting loses momentum and signals weakness; Bid B is a strong, certain offer.

items.q: What does Bid B pay the family for the shares?

errs.why: The debt is repaid out of the proceeds.
The family keeps the cash: add it.

items.why: Cash-free, debt-free: the bid less the debt repaid, plus the cash kept.

items.q: What EV/EBITDA multiple does Bid B represent?

errs.why: Use the enterprise value bid, not the equity proceeds.

items.why: The bid, a cash-free, debt-free enterprise value, over EBITDA.

items.q: After your {fp|2%} success fee on Bid B’s price, what do the family receive for the shares?

errs.why: Take off the success fee.
Start from the proceeds for the shares, after debt and cash.

items.why: Proceeds for the shares, less the adviser’s fee.

items.q: A year after closing, a {L|R0m} tax liability the family warranted against emerges. How much can the buyer recover under the indemnity?

errs.why: The deductible and cap both apply.
The cap limits the claim.

items.why: The deductible comes off first; the cap limits the total.

cases.title: MarulaCo
cases.lead: AcaciaCo, a fictional JSE-listed food group, plans to buy MarulaCo, a fictional listed snacks maker, for cash and shares.
facts: AcaciaCo net income; shares; share price
MarulaCo net income; shares; share price
Paid in cash (new debt); in AcaciaCo shares
Interest rate on the new debt

items.q: The equity value of the offer for MarulaCo?

errs.why: Add the premium.
Use MarulaCo’s shares, not AcaciaCo’s.

items.why: Premium on the share price, times the shares.

items.q: New AcaciaCo shares issued, using an equity value of {eqvr|R0m}?

errs.why: Only {1-cs|0%} is paid in shares.
New shares are issued at AcaciaCo’s price.

items.why: Only the share part is paid in new shares, at AcaciaCo’s price.

items.q: After-tax interest on the debt that funds the cash part?

errs.why: Take off the tax saved.

items.why: Debt at the rate, less the tax it saves.

items.q: Pro forma net income, using after-tax interest of {intr|R1m}?

errs.why: Synergies are taxed: use the after-tax amount.
Take off the new interest.

items.why: Both companies’ earnings, plus synergies after tax, less the new after-tax interest.

items.q: Is the deal accretive (+) or dilutive (−), and by how much? Use pro forma net income of {pfr|R1m} and {nwr|1m} new shares.

errs.why: Count the new shares issued.
Measure against the stand-alone EPS.

items.why: Pro forma EPS over stand-alone EPS, less one.
items.hint: As a percentage to 1 decimal place; use − for dilution.

items.q: AcaciaCo’s board is weighing the deal. Which is the soundest basis for its decision?
options: Strategic fit and value created, using EPS impact over several years as one test among others
Only whether year-one EPS rises, since that is the figure the market reacts to first
Only the size of the premium paid, compared with recent deals in the sector
items.why: Accretion/dilution is a test, not the goal. A deal that dilutes EPS at first can still create value, and an accretive one can destroy it.
miss: Year-one EPS ignores growth, synergies that take time and whether the price is fair for the value bought.
The premium matters only against the value and synergies the buyer gets.

cases.title: SpekboomCo
cases.lead: SpekboomCo, a fictional JSE-listed clothing retailer, reports under IFRS 16. YellowwoodCo, a fictional JSE-listed retail group, plans to buy a controlling stake from the founders.
facts: SpekboomCo share price; shares in issue
EBITDA before rent; lease payments in the year
Buy {s|0%} from the founders at a {pr|0%} premium: {off|R2} a share

tomb.line: offer value for all the shares

items.q: SpekboomCo’s enterprise value, including its lease liabilities?

errs.why: Include the lease liabilities.

items.why: Equity value, plus debt and lease liabilities, less cash.

items.q: EV/EBITDA on a consistent basis, using an enterprise value of {ev|R0m}?

errs.why: EBITDA after rent doesn’t match an enterprise value that includes the leases.
The leases belong in enterprise value.

items.why: Enterprise value including leases over EBITDA before rent.

items.q: The implied share price at the peer median of {m|1x}?

errs.why: The peer EV includes leases, so subtract the lease liabilities too.

items.why: The peer multiple includes leases, so take the lease liabilities off on the way back to equity.

items.q: YellowwoodCo buys {s|0%} of SpekboomCo from the founders. What must it then do?
options: Offer to buy out the other shareholders: it has crossed 35%
Nothing more: a mandatory offer only applies once a buyer passes 50%
Sell part of the stake back to the market to get under 35% again
items.why: Going from below 35% to {s|0%} triggers a mandatory offer to every other shareholder; YellowwoodCo can’t stop at buying the founders out.
items.src: South African takeover rules (beyond the book)
miss: The South African trigger is 35%, not 50%.
Crossing 35% requires an offer, not a sale.

items.q: If every shareholder accepts at {off|R2} a share, what percentage of YellowwoodCo’s market capitalisation is the total consideration?

errs.why: That is the founders’ stake only; with a mandatory offer, every holder may accept.

items.why: Below 30% this is a Category 2 deal for YellowwoodCo (an announcement); at 30% or more, Category 1 (a circular and a shareholder vote). A mandatory offer means planning for every holder accepting.

That uses the company tax rate.

facts.text: Buffett read the first edition early in 1950, aged 19, and thought it by far the best book about investing ever written. He still does.
In his preface, Buffett singles out Chapters 8 and 20 as the ones to study most closely.
Graham was born Benjamin Grossbaum in London on 9 May 1894. The family changed its name to Graham during the First World War.
Before he graduated from Columbia in 1914, second in his class, three departments (English, philosophy and mathematics) asked Graham to join their faculty. He was 20.
From 1936 until Graham retired in 1956, Graham-Newman gained at least 14.7% a year, against 12.2% for the market as a whole.
Near the age of 80, Graham said he hoped every day to do “something foolish, something creative and something generous”.
Graham taught his compare-and-contrast method in lectures at Columbia Business School and the New York Institute of Finance.
The authors wrote the book they wished had existed when they were students trying to break into Wall Street, building on their own interview preparation notes.
The first edition was published in 2009. The second edition, in 2013, added a full chapter on buy-side M&A analysis.
Comps, precedent transactions, DCF and LBO analysis each follow a five-step method in the book, all applied to the same illustrative company, ValueCo.
EBITDA is not a reported accounting measure, so bankers usually build it from operating income plus depreciation and amortisation.
In 1929 a General Motors financier promised that $15 a month in good shares would grow to $80,000 in 20 years. Graham worked out that the plan would actually have produced about $8,500.
Isaac Newton doubled his money in South Sea Company shares in 1720, bought back in at a much higher price and lost £20,000. Afterwards he banned the words “South Sea” in his presence.
Graham started on Wall Street in June 1914. Two months later the First World War closed the New York Stock Exchange.
In a 1948 survey, over 90% of Americans said they were against buying shares. The decade that followed was one of the best in market history, at about 18.7% a year.
In 1998, traders mistook a tiny building-maintenance company’s ticker, TMCO, for Ticketmaster’s new listing, TMCS. The wrong share nearly tripled in minutes.
In 1973 a typical New York Stock Exchange share was held for about five years. By 2002 it was held for under a year.
Asked what the market would do next, the financier J. P. Morgan always gave the same short and accurate answer: “It will fluctuate.”
Over the 35 years to early 1972, gold rose only from $35 to $48 an ounce, paying no income and costing money to store.
It took 25 years for General Electric, and the Dow itself, to recover what they lost in the 1929–1932 crash.
Some of the earliest US share indexes held as few as seven companies and left out the hundreds that went bust, which makes early returns look better than investors really got.
In June 1949 the S&P index sold at only 6.3 times earnings; by March 1961 it was 22.9 times. Graham calls it the most remarkable turnabout in the public’s attitude in market history.
Graham quotes Aristotle: an educated mind expects only as much exactness as the subject allows. He places the financial analyst between the mathematician and the orator.
Yale’s endowment once followed a formula built around holding 35% in shares. It dropped the formula in the long bull market and held 61% in shares by 1969.

A utility sold 100-year 5% bonds at 101 in 1928. They fell to 62½ in the 1932 panic, and when rates later fell the company called them back at just 106. Graham calls such call terms “heads I win, tails you lose”.
Zweig notes that a popular 1999 book told anyone under 30 to hold 95% in shares, even with only a moderate tolerance for risk.
Texas Instruments rose from 5 to 256 in six years without paying a dividend. Two years later its earnings had nearly halved and its price had fallen by four-fifths.
One dollar in US shares in 1900 grew to about $198 by 2000 if you spent the dividends, and to about $16,797 if you reinvested them.
Graham notes that doctors were “notoriously unsuccessful” investors: confident in their intelligence, keen on a good return, but short of time and of a professional approach.
Czechoslovakia’s 8% bonds were sold in 1922 at 96½, collapsed to 6 in 1939, recovered to 117 in 1946 and were down to 8 by 1970.
VA Linux was priced at $30 for its 1999 listing, first traded at $299 and closed day one at $239.25. Three years later it was $1.19.
In America’s first IPO boom, in 1825, a man was reportedly crushed to death in the rush to buy shares in the new Bank of Southwark.
A study found that $10,000 in the cheapest Dow shares from 1936, switched each year, grew to $66,900 by 1962. The most popular shares grew it to only $25,300.
In 1957, 85 shares selling below their net working capital were bought and held for two years. Together they gained 75% against 50% for the index, and not one showed a significant loss.
Of the 400 richest Americans listed in 1982, only 64 were still on the list in 2002. Most had kept everything in the one basket that had made them rich.
In 1938 the market valued A&P, America’s largest retailer, at less than its working capital. A year later the shares had tripled.
Warren Buffett’s preface calls Chapters 8 and 20 the most valuable advice in the book. Zweig calls Graham’s paragraph about the true investor’s “basic advantage” perhaps the most important in it.
Research by Kahneman and Tversky found that the pain of a loss is more than twice as intense as the pleasure of an equal gain.
The mutual fund was invented in 1924 by a former salesman of aluminium pots and pans.
Two of the largest holdings of the famous “performance” fund Manhattan Fund went bankrupt within six months of the end of 1969, while its founder sold his management company for over $20 million.
The Sequoia Fund trailed the S&P 500 in 12 of its first 29 years, yet gained more than 12,500% against about 4,900% for the index.
Graham was the main force behind the Chartered Financial Analyst (CFA) qualification, which he championed for nearly two decades before it became a reality.

In 1969–70 several New York brokerage firms nearly failed, partly because their partners had held the firms’ capital in speculative shares. One was saved only by a loan of over $50 million from a Texas entrepreneur.
Zweig quotes a planner who says you hire an adviser “not to manage money but to manage you”.
Graham said that in 44 years he never saw dependable share valuations that used more than simple arithmetic or elementary algebra. Calculus, to him, was a warning sign.
In 1963 the market priced Xerox for about 32% yearly growth and General Motors for under 3%. Xerox and IBM went on to grow close to the rates the market had implied.
Sycamore Networks listed in 1999 with one customer providing all of its revenue, and was valued at $15 billion. That customer went bankrupt about two years later, and the shares fell 97%.
ALCOA’s 1970 report gave four different figures for earnings per share. Depending on which you used, the share looked like 10 times earnings or 22.
Graham compares companies that count only their profitable operations to King Edward VII’s sundial, which marked only the sunny hours.
In 2002 a record 330 US listed companies restated their past financial statements.
Emery Air Freight’s share price rose from ⅛ to 66 between 1936 and 1968, a 528-to-1 increase.
Emhart had paid a dividend every year since 1902.
Exodus Communications split its shares 2-for-1 three times in 1999, rose over 1,000% that year, and was bankrupt by September 2001.
At the end of 1970 only five of the 30 Dow Jones industrials passed all seven of Graham’s tests: American Can, AT&T, Anaconda, Swift and Woolworth.
Penn Central, then America’s most important railroad, went bankrupt in 1970 after paying dividends continuously for more than 120 years.
MicroStrategy fell from $3,130 a share in March 2000 to $15.10 at the end of 2002, a loss of 99.5%.
Graham-Newman bought “bargain” issues at two-thirds or less of their net current asset value, typically holding at least 100 at a time.
A Burton-Dixie buyer at 20 in March 1964 was offered 53¾ in August 1967: a 165% profit in 3½ years.
Graham likens Wall Street analysts to master bridge players at a duplicate tournament, looking over each other’s shoulders and arguing out each hand.
American & Foreign Power warrants were worth over $1 billion in 1929, $8 million by 1932, and were wiped out in 1952, though the company stayed solvent.
Tri-Continental warrants rose from 1/32 of a dollar in the Depression to 75¾ in 1969, a gain of about 242,000%.
AT&T sold at least nine convertible bond issues between 1913 and 1957, paying interest at less than half the dividend yield on its shares.
Penn Central’s share fell from 86½ in 1968 to 5½ in 1970. Its railroad bonds ended 1970 at 18½ while a comparable utility bond stood at 66½.
AAA Enterprises came to market at $13 in March 1969, doubled to 28, and filed for bankruptcy in January 1971.
eToys raised $166.4 million at $20 a share in 1999, closed its first day at $76.56, and was bankrupt by March 2001.
Real Estate Investment Trust had paid dividends continuously since 1889, while its near-namesake Realty Equities blew its assets up from $6.2 million to $154 million in eight years.
At the end of 1969 International Flavors & Fragrances was worth more on the market than International Harvester, a Dow giant with 27 times its sales.
In March 2000 the market valued 3Com’s businesses, apart from its stake in Palm, at about minus $22 billion.
Texas Instruments’ share rose from 5 in 1953 to 256 in 1960 without paying any dividend at all.
In the 1949 edition Graham wrote that Jesus seemed to have been a more practical businessman than American shareholders, citing “Give an account of thy stewardship”.
Between mid-1999 and mid-2000, Oracle issued shares to insiders at an average of $3.53 and bought shares back at an average of $18.26.
Many 1920s real-estate bonds sold at par as “safe” and later fell below 10 cents on the dollar; at that price, Graham says, their true values were four or five times the market quotation.
Asked to sum up how to get rich, the financier J. K. Klingenstein answered simply: “Don’t lose.”
Bought at its March 2000 peak, JDS Uniphase would need more than 43 years at 10% a year just to get back to the purchase price from its 2002 level.
The two unnamed partners in the Postscript were Graham himself and Jerome Newman; the company was GEICO, bought in 1948.
A holder of 100 Graham-Newman shares in 1948, worth $11,413, who kept the GEICO distribution had about $1.66 million by 1972.
Warren Buffett made a huge bet of his own on GEICO in 1976, when it was near bankruptcy, and it became one of his best investments.
The book’s worked example values ValueCo, a private chemicals company, against three tiers of listed peers: specialty, commodity or diversified, and small-cap chemicals.
Some sectors use their own multiples: EBITDAR for casinos, restaurants and retail; EBITDAX for oil and gas; reserves for metals and mining; funds from operations for real estate.
Moody’s rates on an alphanumeric scale (Aaa at the top), while S&P and Fitch use letters with pluses and minuses (AAA at the top).
Under NYSE and Nasdaq rules, an acquirer issuing more than 20% of its pre-deal shares to pay for a deal needs its own shareholders’ vote.
In a tender offer, the target’s board must give its recommendation in a Schedule 14D-9 within ten business days.

In the book’s example, Pearl’s $20 cash offer for Rosenbaum was only 15% above the previous day’s price, but about 35% above the price before Rosenbaum announced it was exploring strategic alternatives.
The terminal value often makes up three-quarters or more of a DCF valuation; in the book’s ValueCo example it was 73%.
Ibbotson’s market risk premium for 1926 to 2011, measured as an arithmetic mean, was 6.62%.
At a 10% discount rate, R1 received at the end of year one is worth about R0.91 today, but about R0.95 if received evenly through the year (the mid-year convention).
Limited partners typically pay a sponsor 1–2% a year in management fees, and the sponsor takes about 20% of profits as carried interest once required returns are met.
Average LBO leverage fell from 6.2× EBITDA in 2007 to 4.0× in 2009, while sponsors’ contributed equity rose from 31% to 46% of the price.
A common asset-based borrowing base is 85% of eligible receivables plus about 60% of eligible inventory.

In the book’s example, ValueCo is bought for 8.0× LTM EBITDA of $700 million ($5.6 billion), with total leverage of 5.2× and about 35% equity, for an IRR of about 20% and a 2.5× cash return after five years.
LBO models are typically projected for seven to ten years to match the longest-dated debt, though a sponsor may use five years to match its holding period.
Deal fees such as M&A advisory are expensed, but debt financing fees are capitalised and amortised over the life of the debt.
A teaser is usually one or two pages; the confidential information memorandum often runs to 50+ pages, and each copy carries a control number.
Under the US Hart-Scott-Rodino Act, deals without antitrust concerns can close after a 30-day waiting period, or 15 days for a cash tender offer.
In a two-step tender offer, reaching the threshold (typically 90%) lets the buyer squeeze out remaining holders without a vote; the whole deal can take as little as five weeks.
In the book’s example, BuyerCo pays a 35% premium for ValueCo, 8.5× LTM EBITDA, but only 7.4× once $100 million of annual synergies are counted.
The same deal is 23.2% accretive to EPS if paid all in cash, 7.0% with half cash and half shares, and 1.5% dilutive if paid all in shares.
Commercial paper is short-term (usually under 270 days), unsecured debt issued by investment-grade companies at a discount to face value.

questions.q: Graham’s main aim in the book is to teach detailed techniques for analysing individual securities and their accounts.
options: True
False
He says little about analysis technique; the book is about principles and attitude
He covers analysis in full, but only for bonds, and leaves shares to the professionals
He teaches technique first, because sound principles follow from reading accounts well

questions.why: He says little will be said about analysis technique. The focus is investment principles and the investor’s attitude.

questions.q: The defensive investor’s first aim is to avoid serious mistakes or losses; the second is freedom from effort and frequent decisions.
questions.why: That is exactly how Graham defines the defensive, or passive, investor.

questions.q: In 50 years on Wall Street, Graham had met many people who made lasting money by following the market’s trends.
options: True
False
He had not known anyone who consistently made money by following the market
He says trend-followers did make money, but only during the long bull markets
He says most of them made money, but then lost it by speculating in later years

questions.why: The trap is the word “many”. He says he had not known a single person who consistently made money by “following the market”.

questions.q: When Graham first wrote the book in 1949, high-grade bonds offered investors a higher yield than shares did.
questions.why: In 1949 it was the other way round: bonds yielded about 2.7% and shares about 6.8%. By early 1972 bonds paid far more than shares.

questions.q: Graham says a lay investor can get a creditable result with little effort, but beating that result takes much more work and wisdom.
questions.why: He warns that bringing just a little extra cleverness can leave you doing worse than the simple, defensive result.

questions.q: From the airline and computer examples, Graham concludes that clear growth prospects for a business translate directly into profits for its shareholders.
options: True
False
Air traffic boomed while airlines lost money: obvious growth isn’t obvious profit
Airlines made fortunes, which shows that growth always reaches shareholders in time
Computer makers grew slowly, so he drew no lesson about growth from the period at all

questions.why: His moral is the reverse. Airline traffic boomed while the industry lost money, so obvious growth does not mean obvious profits for investors.

questions.q: Graham told readers to buy shares “as they bought their groceries, not as they bought their perfume”. What did he mean?
options: Judge what you get for the price you pay, every time
Buy consumer-staples companies rather than luxury brands
Buy small amounts regularly rather than all at once
Avoid companies that spend heavily on marketing
questions.why: Groceries are bought with an eye on value; perfume is bought on emotion and image. The losses he describes came when buyers forgot to ask “How much?”

questions.q: According to Graham, what single principle sits behind nearly all “technical” approaches to trading?
options: Buy because a share has risen, sell because it has fallen
Buy below intrinsic value and sell above it
Buy after earnings upgrades and sell after downgrades
Buy when interest rates fall and sell when they rise
questions.why: He calls this the exact opposite of sound business sense everywhere else, and unlikely to bring lasting success.

questions.q: Why does Graham suggest limiting purchases to shares selling not far above their tangible-asset value?
options: The investor owns a sound business at a rational price and depends less on the market’s moods
Asset-backed companies grow faster than others, so buying near book value captures that growth
Tangible assets can be sold for at least book value if the company fails, so nothing can be lost
Regulators cap how much of a portfolio may sit in growth shares, and the rule keeps within that limit
questions.why: His reason is practical and psychological: a buyer of shares priced at several times net assets is too dependent on market fluctuations.

questions.q: In Graham’s sense, what makes an investor “intelligent”?
options: Patience, discipline, eagerness to learn and control of emotions
A high IQ, strong mathematics and a good grasp of statistics
A finance degree, professional training and access to research
Speed in reacting to news and the confidence to act on it
questions.why: Graham calls it a trait more of character than of the brain. Zweig points to Long-Term Capital Management’s Nobel laureates as proof that brains alone are not enough.

questions.q: Isaac Newton made a profit on South Sea shares, bought back in higher and lost heavily. What is Zweig’s lesson?
options: Even a brilliant mind fails at investing when the crowd overrides its judgment
Scientists should leave shares to professionals, who have more market experience
Taking profits early is a mistake, because a rising share usually keeps rising
Bubbles can be timed safely if you study the crowd’s behaviour carefully enough
questions.why: Newton was a genius by any measure, but by letting the crowd’s excitement override his own judgment he acted unintelligently as an investor.

questions.q: Raskob promised $80,000 from $15 a month over 20 years; Graham’s estimate was about $8,500. Which further point does Graham draw from the same example?
options: Steady monthly buying through good times and bad still earned over 8% a year
Shares are unsuitable for monthly savers, who should keep their money in bonds
The Dow was too narrow an index, so a broader list would have saved the plan
Reinvesting dividends made no real difference to what the monthly saver earned
questions.why: Even starting at the 1929 peak, regular buying compounded at better than 8% a year. Graham calls this a persuasive case for dollar-cost averaging.

questions.q: A share falls 95% from your purchase price. What gain from its new price would you need just to break even?
questions.why: R100 becomes R5. Getting back to R100 means rising by R95 on a base of R5, which is a 1,900% gain. This is why Graham stresses avoiding big losses.

questions.q: A friend says: “Electric-vehicle sales will obviously triple this decade, so EV shares are a sure thing.” Which reply is closest to Graham?
options: Industry growth doesn’t guarantee profits for shareholders, especially once prices already reflect it
Then buy the largest EV maker, since market leaders capture most of an industry’s growth
Then buy every EV maker, so that you are sure to own the eventual winner of the industry
Wait for EV share prices to break out on the charts, then buy to ride the trend upwards for longer
questions.why: Airline traffic grew spectacularly while airline shareholders lost money. Zweig adds that once everyone expects an industry to win, its prices are already bid up.

questions.q: The JSE falls 30% while the businesses you own are unchanged. You invest monthly, have years ahead and enough cash for living costs. How would Zweig see it?
options: Shares are now cheaper and less risky to buy; welcome it
A warning to sell before prices fall further
Proof that the businesses have become worse
A reason to stop monthly investing until prices recover
questions.why: Zweig argues that shares become riskier as prices rise and less risky as they fall. The intelligent investor welcomes a bear market as a sale.

questions.q: A Member has little spare time, wants above all to avoid serious mistakes, and does not want to make frequent decisions. Which of Graham’s investor types fits?
options: Defensive
Enterprising
Speculative
Aggressive
questions.why: Avoiding serious losses and freedom from effort are the defining aims of Graham’s defensive investor.

questions.q: Sort each trait: does it describe Graham’s defensive investor or his enterprising (active) investor?

items.t: Wants freedom from effort, annoyance and frequent decisions
Puts safety and avoiding serious mistakes first
Will give time and care to choosing securities
Aims for a better-than-average return, and does the work for it
Is content with a simple, largely automatic portfolio
Hunts for bargains the market has overlooked

questions.why: Graham’s two kinds of investor differ in effort, not intelligence: the defensive one keeps it simple, the enterprising one does the extra work.

questions.q: After a year in which the JSE rose 30%, a friend wants to move all their savings into the shares that rose most. What would Graham say?
options: Be wary: a strong year says little about the next one, and chasing it invites serious losses
Go ahead: shares that led a strong year usually keep leading for several more years
Go ahead, but spread the money across all of the top risers so that no single fall hurts too much
The investor’s worst enemy is often himself: excitement after a rise leads to the worst mistakes
Momentum is the most reliable force in markets, so last year’s leaders tend to keep on leading for years
Spreading money across several winners removes the risk that any one of them falls

questions.why: Graham’s aim is to help readers avoid serious mistakes. Enthusiasm after a rise is when people take risks they don’t see.
miss: Recent performance is a poor guide; buying after a boom is when investors get hurt.
Spreading the bet across last year’s winners is still chasing prices, not judging value.

questions.q: Graham defines an investment operation as one that, on thorough analysis, promises safety of principal and an adequate return.
questions.why: This is the definition from Security Analysis (1934), which Graham kept for decades. Anything that fails it is speculative.

questions.q: Under Graham’s definition, holding a share for at least a year is enough to make it an investment rather than a speculation.
options: True
False
Holding period plays no part: his tests are analysis, safety and an adequate return
The dividing line is two years, not one, under the definition he sets out in the book
Holding period is the main test, but it applies only to shares and never to bonds

questions.why: Holding period plays no part in the definition. The tests are thorough analysis, safety of principal and an adequate return.

questions.q: Graham says a non-professional who buys shares on margin is speculating by that very fact.
options: True
False
Buying on margin is speculation in itself, and brokers should tell clients so
Margin is fine for amateurs and professionals alike, provided the shares are sound
Margin buying counts as speculation only when the shares are of small companies

questions.why: Borrowing to buy shares is speculation in itself, he says, and it is the broker’s duty to tell the client so.

questions.q: Graham lets the defensive investor hold anywhere from 10% to 90% of the portfolio in bonds, depending on the outlook.
questions.why: The range is 25% to 75%, with the rest in leading shares. A 50/50 split is the simplest choice.

questions.q: Graham calls outright speculation illegal and immoral, and says no investor should ever take part in it.
options: True
False
He says it is neither illegal nor immoral, just unprofitable for most people
He says some kinds of speculation are illegal, and the rest are merely unwise
He says speculation is moral only for professionals who have better information

questions.why: He says it is neither illegal nor immoral, just not fattening to most pockets. Some speculation is even necessary; the danger is speculating unintelligently.

questions.q: Graham suggests restoring a 50/50 split once market moves have disturbed it by about 5%.
questions.why: He recommends adjusting back to equality when the mix has drifted by as much as, say, 5%.

questions.q: Zweig suggests putting up to a quarter of your wealth in a speculative “mad money” account.
questions.why: His limit is 10% at most, kept strictly apart from your investment accounts.

questions.q: From 1949 to 1969 the Dow rose more than fivefold while its earnings and dividends only about doubled.
options: True
False
So most of the rise came from changed attitudes, not from higher business values
Earnings also rose about fivefold, so share prices simply kept pace with them
Prices and earnings both doubled; the fivefold figure is a misreading of the index

questions.why: So most of that bull market came from changed attitudes, not higher business values. Graham calls it a “bootstrap operation”.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of Graham’s three forms of unintelligent speculation?
options: Keeping a small speculative fund apart from your investments
Speculating when you think you are investing
Speculating seriously without the knowledge and skill for it
Risking more money than you can afford to lose
questions.why: A small, separate speculative fund is what Graham recommends for anyone who wants to try their luck. The other three are his named dangers.

questions.q: For a reasonable chance of continued better-than-average results, Graham says the enterprising investor’s policies must be:
options: Inherently sound, and not popular on Wall Street
Popular, so the market will reward them quickly
Focused on companies with the best growth records
Based on next year’s expected earnings
questions.why: If a policy is popular, others are already doing it and the price reflects it. Sound and unpopular is his “logical if disconcerting” conclusion.

questions.q: Why, according to Graham and Zweig, do published market-beating formulas tend to stop working?
options: Publicity brings in copycats who erase the edge, and some “patterns” were only luck
Regulators ban strategies once they become known, to keep the market fair for all
Markets have become too efficient for any kind of analysis to beat them any longer
The formulas only work for professionals, whose trading costs are far lower than ours
questions.why: Graham calls it a self-destructive process, like diminishing returns. A real anomaly gets traded away once known; a statistical fluke simply stops.

questions.q: What does Graham say the defensive investor can expect from buying new offerings and “hot” issues?
options: Not better than average results; worse is almost certain in the long run
Better than average results, because new companies tend to grow the fastest
Average results, as with any other diversified list of common shares
Good results, provided he sells his allotment on the first day of trading
questions.why: He repeats the warning “without apology”: hot issues are not for the investor, and the long-run result is likely worse than average.

questions.q: Which question did Graham suggest asking before buying a share?
options: If there were no market for these shares, would I still want to own this company on these terms?
Has the share risen more than the market this year, showing that other investors can see its value too?
Do analysts expect the company’s next earnings to beat the consensus forecast for the year?
Would I be happy to sell these shares at a profit within the next few months if they rise?
questions.why: Investors judge price by value; speculators judge value by price. Graham’s test is whether you would be content to own the business without a daily quote.

questions.q: Why does dollar-cost averaging (investing the same amount every month) tend to give a satisfactory average price?
options: The fixed amount buys more shares when prices are low than when they are high
It ensures you buy at or near the market’s lowest point in each year, whatever happens
It avoids brokerage costs, which take most of a small investor’s return
It guarantees a profit to anyone who keeps it up for twenty years
questions.why: A fixed rand amount automatically buys more units when the market is cheap, so the average cost per share lands below the average price.

questions.q: A R200,000 portfolio starts 50/50. A year later shares are worth R130,000 and bonds R100,000. Following Graham’s simple policy, what should the investor do?
options: Sell R15,000 of shares and buy bonds
Sell R30,000 of shares and buy bonds
Buy R15,000 more shares
Nothing: let the winners run
questions.why: Shares are now about 56.5% of R230,000, beyond the 5% drift. Half of R230,000 is R115,000, so moving R15,000 from shares to bonds restores 50/50.

questions.q: A student buys R10,000 of a blue-chip share using R5,000 of savings and R5,000 borrowed from the broker. How would Graham classify this?
options: Speculation, because a non-professional is buying on margin
Investment, because the company is a blue chip with a record
Investment, provided the share is held for several years
Arbitrage, because the loan is repaid from the share’s return
questions.why: For Graham, buying on margin makes a non-professional a speculator whatever the quality of the share.

questions.q: A Member wants to try short-term trading in tech shares “for the fun of it”. Which plan follows Graham and Zweig?
options: A small, separate account (no more than 10% of wealth), never topped up after gains
A trading section inside the main portfolio, so that profits can be reinvested there
Borrow the money to trade, so that savings stay untouched whatever happens
Trade with all savings for a year, then decide whether to carry on trading
questions.why: Keep speculation small and separate, and never add to it because it has been winning. That is the time to take money out.

questions.q: A share market has a 4% dividend yield and earnings are expected to grow about 6% a year. Using the approach Graham sums up (dividend yield plus growth), what return might you roughly expect?
options: About 10% a year
About 6% a year
About 4% a year
About 24% a year
questions.why: Expected return ≈ dividend yield + growth = 4% + 6% = 10%. Zweig notes this is the “Gordon equation” behind Graham’s 7.5% estimate (3.5% + 4%).

questions.q: A website’s formula picks four shares, puts 40% in one of them, and “beat the market for 25 years” in back-tests. Why does it fail Graham’s test of an investment?
options: No analysis of the businesses, too little diversification for safety, and the pattern may be pure luck
It holds too many shares to beat the market, and 25 years of back-tests is far too short a record to judge
Back-tests can’t legally be published, so investors have no way of checking the claimed record
It ignores technical charts, which Graham saw as the main test of when to buy any share
questions.why: Zweig uses this “Foolish Four” case: a back-tested pattern says nothing about the businesses, and 40% in one share is not safety of principal.

questions.q: Sort each action: is it investment or speculation, in Graham’s sense?

items.t: Buying a share after analysis that promises safety of principal and an adequate return
Buying because the price has risen five days running
Day-trading with borrowed money
Holding a low-cost, diversified index fund for decades
Buying a hot new listing on its first day because everyone is talking about it
Buying a high-grade bond after checking that interest is well covered

questions.why: Graham’s test: thorough analysis, safety of principal and an adequate return. Anything else is speculation.

questions.q: You have R50,000 to invest and want to try picking a few exciting shares as well. What does Zweig suggest?
options: Keep it in a separate “mad money” account of 10% at most, and never top it up from the rest
Put a third into exciting shares while you are young and have time to recover from any losses
Mix the exciting shares into your main portfolio so their swings are diluted
Walled off and small, speculation can’t creep into the money you are investing
Speculation always loses money, so the amount should be as small as possible
Losses in a separate account can be set off against tax on your other gains

questions.why: Speculation isn’t forbidden; mixing it with investing is the danger. A walled-off, small account keeps the two apart.
miss: A third is far more than Zweig allows, and youth doesn’t make speculation investing.
Mixing the two is exactly the danger: speculation then creeps into the whole portfolio.

questions.q: Graham says high-quality shares are a better buy than bonds under all conditions.
options: True
False
He calls that as absurd as saying any bond is safer than any share: price decides
He says bonds always beat shares for the defensive investor, whatever the yields
He says shares beat bonds only in the years when inflation runs above about 3%

questions.why: He calls that as absurd as the old claim that any bond is safer than any share. It depends on price and the yields on offer.

questions.q: Graham found a close year-to-year link between inflation and the movement of share earnings and prices.
options: True
False
He found no close link: in 1966–70 living costs rose 22% while earnings fell
He found a close link, but only for companies with the power to raise their prices
He found the link so close that shares work as a near-perfect hedge against inflation

questions.why: He is categorical that there is no close time connection. From 1966 to 1970 the cost of living rose 22% while share earnings and prices fell.

questions.q: Graham suggested basing decisions on a probable, but uncertain, future inflation rate of about 3% a year.
questions.why: That was his working assumption in 1971. Zweig notes it proved one of his rare misjudgments: 1973–1982 was the most inflationary decade in modern US history.

questions.q: Graham’s figures show that US companies earned a rising rate of return on their capital as inflation rose from 1950 to 1970.
options: True
False
The rate earned on capital actually fell over those twenty years, despite inflation
It rose sharply over the period, which is why he recommended holding mostly shares
It stayed the same throughout, which showed him that inflation was irrelevant

questions.why: The rate earned on capital actually fell over those twenty years, despite inflation.

questions.q: Between 1950 and 1969, US corporate debt grew nearly fivefold while pre-tax profits only a little more than doubled.
questions.why: Graham highlights this as a striking and under-noticed development: part of the return on equity came from extra borrowing.

questions.q: Zweig shows that US shares beat inflation in every five-year period since 1926.
questions.why: They beat inflation in 50 of 64 five-year periods, about 78%. That means they fell short roughly one time in five.

questions.q: In years when US inflation ran above 6%, shares tended to do poorly.
options: True
False
High inflation hurts customers and the economy: shares lost in 8 of 14 such years
Shares always rise with inflation, so those years were among the best on record
Inflation above 6% only came in wartime, when the stock exchanges were closed anyway

questions.why: The market lost money in eight of the 14 such years, averaging only 2.6%. High inflation squeezes customers and the whole economy.

questions.q: Which of these is an example of the “money illusion”?
options: Feeling better about a 2% raise with 4% inflation than a 2% cut with no inflation
Believing that shares always beat inflation over any period of five years or more
Preferring cash because its rand value never changes, whatever happens to prices
Thinking a high share price means a good company, whatever its earnings are
questions.why: Both leave you about 2% poorer after inflation, but the positive nominal number feels better. Measure what you keep after inflation.

questions.q: According to Graham, inflation can add to the value of shares only if it:
options: Raises the rate of earnings on companies’ capital
Raises consumer prices faster than wholesale prices
Pushes interest rates down
Encourages more people to buy shares
questions.why: That is the only route he accepts, and the 1950–1970 record showed it had not happened.

questions.q: How does Graham judge gold as an inflation hedge for the 35 years to 1972?
options: A near-complete failure: a small price rise, no income and storage costs
An excellent hedge that beat shares, with low costs and steady price gains
Adequate: its price roughly kept pace with the rise in the cost of living
Ideal for the bond portion, since it held its value better than bonds did
questions.why: Money at interest in a savings bank would have done much better. Zweig notes that others later disagreed, and suggests at most a small allocation.

questions.q: Given the uncertainty about inflation, what is Graham’s conclusion for the defensive investor?
options: Hold a significant part in bonds and a significant part in shares
Go entirely into shares, since only shares can keep up with inflation
Go entirely into bonds while their yields are higher than share yields
Hold gold and property instead of securities until inflation settles
questions.why: Because the future is uncertain, he will not put everything in one basket: not bonds despite record yields, and not shares despite inflation.

questions.q: Why does Graham think an investor whose case rests on inflation is dangerous in a bull market?
options: He reads the rise as proof of his theory and keeps buying however high prices go
He sells too early because he expects inflation to fall, and misses the gains
He moves everything into gold as soon as share prices start to look high
He ignores dividends entirely and buys only the shares that have risen most
questions.why: Instead of treating a big rise as a danger signal or a chance to take profits, he sees vindication. “That way lies sorrow.”

questions.q: What is Graham’s view of rare coins, stamps and old-master paintings as inflation hedges?
options: The prices often seem artificial or precarious, and he admits he is out of his depth
They are the best hedge of all, because their supply is fixed and demand keeps rising
