They suit the defensive investor in small amounts, held alongside bonds and shares
They count as investments as long as they are insured and properly valued each year
questions.why: He finds it hard to call paying a fortune for one coin an “investment operation”, and warns that few readers will find the swimming safe.

questions.q: What makes inflation-protected government bonds (TIPS in the US) attractive, according to Zweig?
options: They are government-backed and their value rises with inflation
They pay the highest yield of any government bond, year after year
They can’t fall in price in the short run, whatever happens to rates
Their inflation gains are free of tax in every country that issues them
questions.why: They protect against both default and inflation. Zweig warns that they can be volatile in the short run and that the inflation uplift may be taxed. South Africa issues inflation-linked bonds too.

questions.q: A savings account pays 8% for a year in which inflation is 9%. What happened to your purchasing power?
options: It fell by about 1%
It rose by about 8%
It rose by about 17%
It stayed the same
questions.why: The real return is roughly 8% − 9% = −1%. The nominal 8% feels good, but inflation quietly took more.

questions.q: You get a 5% raise in a year of 7% inflation. A friend gets no raise in a year of 2% inflation. Who is better off in real terms?
options: Neither: both are about 2% worse off
You, because your salary rose
Your friend, because their salary is stable
You, by about 5%
questions.why: 5% − 7% and 0% − 2% both leave about 2% less purchasing power. Feeling better about the raise is the money illusion at work.

questions.q: Your bonds earn 6% after tax and inflation is 3%. Following Graham’s arithmetic, how much of the interest can you spend each year and still keep your purchasing power intact?
options: About half
All of it
None of it
About a quarter
questions.why: Reinvesting the other 3% grows the capital by as much as prices rise. Graham makes this point for 3% inflation against roughly 6% income.

questions.q: A group of shares earns 10% on its book value and trades at 1.6 times book. What earnings yield does a buyer get on the market price?
questions.why: Earnings yield = 10% ÷ 1.6 = 6.25%. Graham gets the same result for the Dow in 1971: 10% on a book value of 560, at a market level of 900.

questions.q: A Member wants some protection from a spike in inflation through gold. Which approach matches Zweig’s advice?
options: A low-cost, diversified fund of precious-metal shares, kept to about 2% of assets
Physical gold bars, kept in a safe at home and making up a quarter of the portfolio
A single gold-mining share, bought on margin to make the most of a price spike
Selling all bonds to buy gold coins, since bonds suffer most when inflation rises
questions.why: Zweig avoids gold bullion because of storage and insurance costs, and keeps the stake small: about 2%, or perhaps 5% for investors over 65.

questions.q: A bond yields {n|1%} while inflation runs at {i|1%}. What is the real return, using (1 + yield) ÷ (1 + inflation) − 1?

errs.why: That is the nominal yield, before inflation.

questions.why: What matters is what your money will buy. The simple difference ({n-i|1%}) slightly overstates it.

questions.q: Which investment gives the most direct protection against inflation, as Zweig suggests?
options: Inflation-linked government bonds, whose capital rises with inflation
Gold bullion, held for decades as a store of value against rising prices
Long-dated fixed-rate government bonds, locked in at today’s high yields
questions.why: Zweig points to inflation-protected government bonds: their principal rises with inflation. South Africa’s inflation-linked government bonds work the same way.
miss: Graham notes that gold rose only from $35 to $48 an ounce over 35 years, paying nothing.
A fixed rate loses real value if inflation rises further.

questions.q: Inflation jumps to 9%. A defensive investor considers moving everything into shares as a hedge. What would Graham advise?
options: Keep a balance: shares are only a partial and unreliable hedge against inflation
Move everything into shares, since companies pass rising costs on to customers
Move everything into bonds, since higher rates soon bring inflation back down
He found no reliable year-to-year link between inflation and share prices
Over every ten-year period he studied, shares beat inflation by a wide margin
Rising interest rates push share and bond prices up together

questions.why: Graham’s evidence: over long periods shares did better than bonds against inflation, but not reliably in the short run. Hence the balanced portfolio.
miss: Shares can fall while inflation rises; putting everything in them is speculation.
Bonds alone give no protection if inflation persists.

questions.q: Graham’s useful data on US share prices, earnings and dividends went back about 100 years, to 1871.
questions.why: He notes the early half is less complete, but it is enough to show how prices, earnings and dividends moved over a century.

questions.q: Between 1949 and 1961 the S&P’s P/E ratio rose from about 6 to about 23, while its dividend yield fell from over 7% to about 3%.
questions.why: Over the same years high-grade bond yields rose. Graham calls this the most remarkable turnabout in public attitude in market history.

questions.q: Graham judged the early-1972 market attractive for conservative buyers, because its three-year P/E was lower than in 1963.
options: True
False
The lower P/E was outweighed by how much better bonds now yielded than shares
He did find it attractive, but only for enterprising investors willing to do the work
He judged it attractive because dividends had just reached a record high

questions.why: The lower P/E was fully offset by how much better bonds now yielded than shares. He called the level unattractive for conservative investment.

questions.q: Graham admits that his cautious advice about the 1953 market was “not a particularly brilliant counsel”.
questions.why: The market went on to double in the next five years. He adds that professional forecasters did no better.

questions.q: Zweig argues that the market becomes less risky as prices rise, because rising prices show investors’ confidence.
options: True
False
Higher prices make the market riskier: it always has been and always will be
Rising prices reduce risk, because more and more investors stand behind the market
Price levels have no bearing on risk, only on how fast earnings grow in future

questions.why: The opposite. Asked whether the market is riskier just because prices are higher, his answer is yes: it always has been and always will be.

questions.q: Survivorship bias makes historical index returns look better than what real investors earned.
options: True
False
Indexes drop companies that went bust, so the record overstates investors’ returns
Indexes count only the survivors’ dividends, which makes the returns look too low
Survivorship bias makes index returns look worse than investors’ actual results

questions.why: Indexes drop companies that went bust. Early US returns may be overstated by two percentage points a year or more.

questions.q: In 1964 Graham’s most urgent advice was to borrow so as to buy more shares before prices rose further.
options: True
False
His first and most urgent point was not to borrow to buy or hold securities
He did urge borrowing, but only against bonds and never against ordinary shares
He urged buying quickly before prices rose any further, though without borrowing

questions.why: His first point, in order of urgency, was no borrowing to buy or hold securities at all.

questions.q: What did Graham find offset the better P/E ratio of the market in late 1971?
options: Earnings and dividend yields on shares had fallen far behind high-grade bond yields
Company earnings were falling fast, so the low P/E would soon rise again
Inflation was about to fall, which would make bonds less attractive than shares
Too many new issues were being sold, diluting existing shareholders’ earnings
questions.why: In 1948 shares yielded about twice as much as bonds; by 1972 bonds yielded more than twice as much as shares.

questions.q: Looking back at his own judgments of the market level in 1948, 1953, 1959 and 1964, what did Graham conclude?
options: A consistent, controlled share policy was more useful than trying to call the market
His forecasts were accurate enough to time the market, so investors should follow them
Market levels can’t be judged at all, so investors should ignore them completely
Bonds should be preferred whenever the market is high, and shares only when it is low
questions.why: His judgments could be defended, but his more pedestrian counsel against beating the market or picking winners proved more useful.

questions.q: Graham says that by 1949 the public had no enthusiasm for shares, so “by the rule of opposites” the time was ripe for a great bull market. What does the rule of opposites suggest?
options: The best opportunities often come when the public is most pessimistic
Shares and bonds tend to move in opposite directions over a cycle
Bear markets last about as long as the bull markets before them
Prices that have risen fastest are the ones most likely to keep rising
questions.why: Low enthusiasm meant low prices, so the stage was set for the greatest advance in US history.

questions.q: Zweig splits the market’s long-run return into three sources. Which list matches his?
options: Real earnings growth, inflation and shifts in investor sentiment, plus the dividend yield
Interest rates, exchange rates and oil prices, plus the net money flowing into equity funds
Share buybacks, mergers and new listings, plus the dividend yield each year
GDP growth, population growth and tax cuts, plus the country’s export earnings
questions.why: Real growth plus inflationary growth plus the dividend yield gives the base estimate. Speculative growth or decline moves returns around it for a while.

questions.q: Robert Shiller’s Graham-inspired measure compares today’s index price with what?
options: Average inflation-adjusted earnings over the past 10 years
Analysts’ forecast earnings for the next twelve months
The current dividend, adjusted for the rate of inflation
The 200-day moving average of the index price itself
questions.why: When that ratio has been well above 20, the following decade has usually been poor; well below 10, usually good.

questions.q: In 1964, what did Graham advise about starting a new monthly dollar-cost averaging plan?
options: Rather strongly against starting one at such high levels, though existing plans could go on
Start one immediately, since with monthly buying the timing of the start never really matters at all
Start one only with borrowed money, so that the full amount is invested at once
Start one in bonds instead of shares, and switch to shares after the next big fall
questions.why: He feared that new savers would lack the stamina to continue if the early results looked bad.

questions.q: Why did Graham use the S&P 500 rather than the Dow for his 1971 market analysis?
options: It is more comprehensive and representative of the whole market
It had risen less than the Dow, which made the market look cheaper
The Dow had stopped publishing the earnings data he needed
The S&P included bonds as well as shares, giving a fuller picture
questions.why: The Dow holds only 30 companies. The S&P’s 500 give a better picture of the general market.

questions.q: A market’s dividend yield is 3%, real earnings grow about 2% a year and inflation is 5%. Using Zweig’s method, and ignoring changes in sentiment, what yearly return is reasonable?
options: About 10% before inflation, or about 5% after
About 5% before inflation, or about 0% after
About 15% before inflation, or about 10% after
About 3%, the dividend yield, before inflation
questions.why: 2% real growth + 5% inflation + 3% dividend yield ≈ 10% nominal. After inflation that is roughly 5%.

questions.q: An index trades at 18 times earnings, while high-grade government bonds yield 9%. By Graham’s yield comparison, how do shares look?
options: Earnings yield about 5.6%, well below the bond yield: unfavourable
Earnings yield 18%, double the bond yield: very favourable
Earnings yield 9%, equal to the bond yield: neutral for shares
The P/E of 18 alone shows that shares are cheap: favourable
questions.why: The earnings yield is 1 ÷ 18 ≈ 5.6%. Being well below the bond yield is the warning sign Graham found in 1972.

questions.q: A market trades at 30 times its 10-year average inflation-adjusted earnings. What does the historical evidence Zweig cites suggest?
options: Below-average returns over the following decade are likely
Above-average returns, because the momentum is strong
Returns over the next decade are unrelated to valuation
A crash within the next month is all but certain
questions.why: Shiller’s data show that ratios well above 20 have usually been followed by poor returns. Nothing about the timing is certain, though.

questions.q: A manager shows that today’s 40 largest JSE shares returned 18% a year over the past 30 years. Why might this overstate what investors actually earned?
options: It ignores companies that failed or dropped out over the period
Dividends weren’t counted, so the true return was even higher
The JSE didn’t exist in its current form 30 years ago
Inflation makes every past return look lower than it was
questions.why: Picking today’s survivors and looking back is survivorship bias. An investor 30 years ago could not have known which companies would last.

questions.q: An excellent company with superb prospects trades at 80 times earnings. What would Graham and Zweig say?
options: Whether it is a good investment depends on the price; great businesses can be overpriced
Great companies are worth almost any price, because their earnings compound for decades
A high P/E proves the market expects even more growth, so the share is a buy
Only the dividend matters to a long-term holder, so the P/E is irrelevant
questions.why: Profits are finite, so the price worth paying is finite. Zweig’s analogy: Michael Jordan was worth $34 million a season, not $34 billion.

questions.q: After a long rise, you hold 65% in shares and believe the market may be too high. In what order did Graham put his 1964 advice?
options: No borrowing; no increase in shares; reduce shares to at most 50%
Sell all shares; buy gold; wait for the market to fall by half
Borrow to rebalance; increase bonds; hold the rest in cash
Increase shares to 75% to ride the momentum; then reassess
questions.why: In order of urgency: no borrowing, no increase in shares, then cut shares to a 50% maximum, paying any capital gains tax with good grace.

questions.q: The market trades on a P/E of {pe|1x}. Government bonds yield {y|1%}. What is the market’s earnings yield?
work: Earnings yield = 1 ÷ {pe|1} = {ey|2%}, against a bond yield of {y|1%}

errs.why: Invert the P/E: earnings over price.

questions.why: Graham compared the earnings yield on shares with bond yields: shares earning less than bonds pay leave little room for error.
questions.src: Chapter 3: A century of stock-market history

questions.q: After a decade of 15% yearly returns, a colleague projects 15% a year for the next decade too. What would Zweig say?
options: Expect less: part of the past return came from rising valuations, which can’t rise for ever
Expect about the same: long-run returns tend to repeat themselves from one decade to the next
Expect more: a decade of strong returns shows the economy has entered a new era
Future returns come from today’s dividends, earnings growth and any change in valuation
Share returns settle at roughly the same long-run average in every decade
New technologies have made companies permanently more profitable than they were in the past

questions.why: Zweig splits returns into real earnings growth, inflation, dividends and sentiment. Sentiment can’t rise for ever, so high-valuation starts mean lower returns.
miss: Trends don’t guarantee anything; high starting valuations usually mean lower future returns.
The past decade’s returns depended on where valuations started and ended.

questions.q: Graham says the return an investor aims for should depend on the intelligent effort he brings, not on the risk he accepts.
options: True
False
He breaks with the usual view: the alert, skilful investor can earn more
He follows the usual view that taking more risk always brings a higher return
He says returns depend only on luck, and never on the effort an investor puts in

questions.why: This is where he departs from the usual view. The passive investor earns the minimum; the alert, skilful investor can earn the maximum.

questions.q: Graham sets the share portion of a defensive portfolio by the investor’s age, using the rule of “100 minus your age”.
options: True
False
Graham never uses age; Zweig points to your circumstances and need for cash
He uses “110 minus your age”, not 100, to give a more aggressive mix of shares
He does use age, but only for investors who have already reached retirement

questions.why: Graham never mentions age. Zweig criticises the age rule and suggests looking at your life circumstances and need for cash instead.

questions.q: Under Graham’s 50/50 formula, if shares grow to 55% of the portfolio, you sell one-eleventh of them and buy bonds.
questions.why: Selling one-eleventh of a 55% holding removes 5 points and restores 50/50. The reverse applies at 45%.

questions.q: Graham suggests the defensive investor boost the income from his portfolio by buying lower-grade, higher-yielding bonds.
options: True
False
Ordinary investors are wiser to avoid them: the bargains there need special skill
He recommends them, provided they are bought at par and held until they mature
He recommends them for extra income, as long as they stay under 10% of the portfolio

questions.why: He says experience shows the ordinary investor is wiser to keep away from them. Bargains exist, but they need special study and skill.

questions.q: Graham calls the preference share an inherently bad form: no creditor’s legal claim and no share in profits beyond its dividend.
options: True
False
Good ones are good in spite of their form: buy them as bargains or not at all
They give both a creditor’s claim and a share in profits, which makes them ideal
He likes the form itself, but dislikes the companies that usually issue them

questions.why: Good preference shares exist, he says, but they are good in spite of their form. Buy them on a bargain basis or not at all.

questions.q: In Graham’s day, a company buying preference shares got a better tax deal on the dividends than a private individual did.
questions.why: Companies were taxed on only a small part of dividends received, but in full on interest. In strict logic, Graham says, companies should own investment-grade preference shares.

questions.q: Zweig recommends rebalancing whenever you sense that the market is about to turn, rather than on fixed dates.
questions.why: He recommends a fixed, patient schedule, every six months on easy-to-remember dates, so that discipline replaces guesswork.

questions.q: Why does Graham say the maxim “sell shares when prices are high, buy when they are low” is easy to state but hard to follow?
options: It goes against the very human nature that drives bull and bear markets to extremes
Trading costs wipe out most of the benefit for anyone who follows it
No one, including the most experienced professionals, can ever tell when prices are high or low
Fund managers trade against individuals and stop them from profiting this way
questions.why: The average person acts the opposite way, which is why markets swing so far. The mechanical formula is meant to protect the investor from himself.

questions.q: According to Graham, what is the most important benefit of the 50/50 formula?
options: It stops the investor being drawn further into shares as the market rises to dangerous heights
It produces the best returns of any formula, in rising and falling markets alike, over every decade
It removes the need to choose good bonds, since half the money stays in shares
It lets the investor time the market precisely, selling at peaks and buying at lows
questions.why: He admits it may not give the best results. Its virtues are simplicity, the right direction and restraint at market peaks.

questions.q: Why does Graham describe easy call provisions on bonds as “heads I win, tails you lose”?
options: The investor bears the loss when rates rise, but the issuer calls the bond when rates fall, capping the gain
The issuer can stop paying interest whenever it chooses, and the investor has no claim for missed payments
The investor must sell the bond back to the issuer at a loss whenever the issuer asks
Callable bonds pay no interest in their first years, so the investor waits for any return
questions.why: When rates fall, a bond’s price should rise, but the issuer calls it at a small premium. He advises giving up a little yield for 20 to 25 years of call protection.

questions.q: When does Graham say preference shares should be bought?
options: Only at bargain prices, when temporary adversity has unduly depressed them
Whenever their yield is higher than that of the company’s own bonds of a similar term
When the company has just raised the dividend on its ordinary shares
Never, because preference shares have no place in any portfolio
questions.why: They should be bought on a bargain basis or not at all, and even then they suit the aggressive investor more than the defensive one.

questions.q: Why does Graham think companies should use income bonds more often in place of preference shares?
options: Interest is tax-deductible, roughly halving the cost, and investors get better protection
Income bonds never have to pay any interest, so the company keeps all its cash in bad years
Investors prefer them because they rank behind ordinary shares in a liquidation
They avoid the need for a credit rating and the costs of a formal bond issue
questions.why: He sees the weaker preference-share form persisting through habit and prejudice, not logic.

questions.q: Why does Zweig say even a young investor should keep at least 25% in bonds and cash?
options: The cushion gives the courage to hold shares through a fall and covers unexpected needs
Bonds beat shares over most 30-year periods, so holding them lifts the long-run return
Regulations require it for anyone saving for retirement through a fund
Young investors can’t buy shares directly, so bonds and cash fill the gap
questions.why: Most people cannot predict how they will feel in a crash, and a job loss or emergency can strike at any age.

questions.q: Zweig suggests intermediate-term bonds (five to ten years) for most investors. Why?
options: They neither soar nor crash much when interest rates move, so you avoid guessing rates
They pay the highest yields of any bonds, because investors dislike the middle range
They can’t lose value, because they mature before interest rates can change much
They are free of tax, unlike the long bonds that most pension funds hold
questions.why: Long bonds swing most with rates and short bonds least. The middle of the range takes interest-rate guessing out of the decision.

questions.q: Shares have grown to R60,500 and bonds are R49,500 (55/45). Using Graham’s one-eleventh rule, how much do you move from shares to bonds?
questions.why: One-eleventh of R60,500 is R5,500. That leaves R55,000 in each, which is 50/50.

questions.q: A taxable bond yields 10% and an equally safe tax-free bond yields 7%. Your marginal tax rate is 36%. Which pays you more after tax?
options: The tax-free bond: 7% against 6.4%
The taxable bond: 10% against 7%
They are equal
It depends on how long you hold them
questions.why: 10% × (1 − 0.36) = 6.4% after tax. The break-even tax rate is 30%; above it, tax-free wins. Graham calls this mainly a matter of arithmetic.

questions.q: Your R100,000 target is 70% shares and 30% bonds. Shares rise 25% and bonds stay flat. Where are you now, and what should you do?
options: About 74.5% shares; sell about R5,250 of shares
About 75% shares; sell about R5,000 of shares
About 87.5% shares; sell about R17,500 of shares
Still about 70% shares; no need to sell anything
questions.why: Shares are R87,500 of R117,500, about 74.5%. A 70% target is R82,250, so sell about R5,250 of shares and buy bonds.

questions.q: You can buy a 10% bond at par that is callable in three years, or a 6% bond trading at a discount with a similar yield to maturity. Which does Graham’s reasoning favour?
options: The low-coupon bond at a discount, because it is protected against an unfavourable call
The callable 10% bond, because its higher coupon pays more income every single year until it is called
Either one, since their yields to maturity are the same and so is their risk
Neither: avoid bonds completely and hold cash until interest rates fall
questions.why: A bond far below par is unlikely to be called, so you keep the upside if rates fall. The 10% bond would be called just when it became valuable.

questions.q: A 24-year-old Member is saving for a deposit on a flat needed in two years. What does Zweig’s approach suggest for that money?
options: Keep it mostly in bonds and cash, because it will be needed soon, whatever your age
Put it all in shares, because a 24-year-old has decades in which to recover from any fall
Follow the 100-minus-age rule: 76% in shares and 24% in bonds and cash
Borrow to invest more in shares, since time is on a young investor’s side
questions.why: Zweig argues risk should follow your circumstances and need for cash, not age. A near-term need cannot ride out a crash.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of Zweig’s tests for whether someone might hold 100% in shares?
options: Being under 30
Having at least a year’s living costs set aside in cash
Investing steadily for at least 20 more years
Having bought more shares during the last bear market
questions.why: Age is not on his list. The tests are about cash reserves, time horizon and proven behaviour in a bear market.

questions.q: A company issues new preference shares with an unusually high dividend instead of borrowing. What should make you suspicious, according to Zweig?
options: A healthy company would borrow and deduct the interest from tax, so this one may not be healthy
High preference dividends show high profits, so the new issue is a sign of the company’s real strength
Preference shares rank ahead of bonds, so the high yield is a free bonus
Nothing: a higher yield is simply better for the investor, whatever the reason
questions.why: Zweig calls preference shares a worst-of-both-worlds investment, and says to ask why the company is not borrowing more cheaply instead.

questions.q: A {v|R0} portfolio starts 50% in shares and 50% in bonds. Shares then rise {g|0%} and bonds are flat. How much must move from shares to bonds to get back to 50/50?

errs.why: That moves the whole gain; move half of the gap so both sides end equal.

questions.why: Rebalancing back to 50/50 makes you trim what has risen and add to what has lagged, without forecasting anything.

questions.q: After three strong years, shares have grown to 80% of your portfolio. What does Graham’s 25–75 rule say?
options: Sell shares back towards 50%, and never hold more than 75%
Hold: rebalance only once shares pass 90% of the portfolio
Sell shares down to 25% now, to lock in all of the gains
Rebalancing makes you sell after rises and buy after falls, against your instincts
Bonds usually beat shares in the years that follow a strong three-year run in the market
The rule keeps your dividend income steady from one year to the next

questions.why: Graham’s formula keeps the investor from being drawn further into shares as prices rise to dangerous heights.
miss: Graham’s ceiling is 75%; letting it run means more risk exactly when prices are highest.
25% is the floor, for when shares look very expensive, not a reaction to one strong run.

questions.q: Graham suggests the defensive investor hold between about 10 and 30 different shares.
questions.why: That is “adequate though not excessive” diversification. Zweig adds a warning about being overexposed to one industry.

questions.q: Graham’s price limit for the defensive investor is 25 times the latest year’s earnings, with no other earnings test.
options: True
False
It is 25 times average earnings over about seven years, and 20 times the last year
It is 15 times the latest year’s earnings, with no long-term average involved
It is 25 times next year’s forecast earnings, which allows properly for growth

questions.why: The trap: it is 25 times average earnings over about seven years, and no more than 20 times the last twelve months.

questions.q: Graham asks for unbroken dividend payments going back at least to 1950, about 20 years before he wrote.
questions.why: A long dividend record is his third rule. Zweig suggests at least ten years today, and notes that twenty is not too restrictive.

questions.q: Graham’s test of conservative financing is equity at book value of at least half of total capitalisation, bank debt included.
questions.why: This is his specific test. For railways and utilities he accepts 30%.

questions.q: Graham thinks growth shares, with their high prices relative to earnings, are well suited to the defensive investor.
options: True
False
Their high prices carry too much speculation for the defensive investor
He thinks them ideal, because their growth protects the investor against inflation
He thinks them suitable, provided the investor holds at least 30 different ones

questions.why: He calls them too uncertain and risky for the defensive investor, because their high prices carry a large speculative element.

questions.q: Graham argues that a temporary fall in market price is not a true risk of loss for a genuine investor.
options: True
False
Real risk is a realised loss, a weaker business or overpaying, not a price dip
Any fall in price is a real loss, whether or not the investor goes on to sell
A fall in price is a real risk for bonds, but it never is for ordinary shares

questions.why: Otherwise a sound holding would have to be called risky and safe at once. True risk is a realised loss, a business getting worse, or overpaying.

questions.q: Graham says the securities you buy and the return you seek should depend mainly on how much money you have.
options: True
False
They depend on knowledge, experience and temperament, not on how much you have
They depend mainly on your age and how many years remain until you retire
They depend on how high the market stands in the year you begin to invest

questions.why: They depend on your financial equipment: knowledge, experience and temperament, not your resources.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of Graham’s four rules for the defensive investor’s shares?
options: Prefer companies growing earnings much faster than average
Hold 10 to 30 different shares
Choose large, prominent, conservatively financed companies
Require a long record of continuous dividends
questions.why: His fourth rule is a price limit, which in fact excludes most growth shares.

questions.q: Why does Graham exclude growth shares from the defensive portfolio?
options: Their high prices relative to earnings add a heavy speculative element, and they can fall very hard
Their earnings rarely grow as forecast, so analysts’ estimates for them are of little use to an investor
They seldom pay dividends, and the defensive investor relies on dividend income alone
Regulators restrict them for private investors, who may hold them only through funds
questions.why: Even IBM, “the best of common stocks”, lost about half its price twice in a decade. Picking and timing them well is beyond the average investor.

questions.q: Which of these does Graham count as a true risk of loss?
options: Paying a price well above the share’s intrinsic value
A temporary fall in the share’s price on the market
The share falling out of fashion with investors
Day-to-day swings in the share’s quoted price
questions.why: Real risk comes from a realised loss, serious deterioration in the business, or overpaying. Fluctuations alone are not risk to a holder who need not sell.

questions.q: What does Graham advise a young beginner with modest savings who wants to be an enterprising investor?
options: Study values and test your judgment of price against value with the smallest possible sums
Try to beat the market quickly, while you are still young enough to afford some heavy losses
Avoid shares completely until your savings are large enough to diversify widely
Copy the trades of successful professionals until you have learnt their methods
questions.why: Starting early is a real advantage and youth can absorb mistakes, but he urges beginners not to waste effort and money trying to beat the market.

questions.q: Zweig accepts Peter Lynch’s “buy what you know” only with a condition. What is it?
options: You must still research the financial statements and estimate the business’s value
You must work in the industry, so that your knowledge is first-hand and current
You must buy only companies whose products you use every day and understand well
You must hold the share for at least ten years, whatever happens to the business
questions.why: Familiarity breeds overconfidence (“home bias”). Enron employees who loaded up on their own company’s shares had only the illusion of knowledge.

questions.q: What did Lucile Tomlinson’s study of dollar-cost averaging in the Dow shares find?
options: Every ten-year buying period from 1929 to 1952 showed a profit at its end or within five years
It lost money in about half of the ten-year periods tested, mostly those starting near peaks
It worked only in rising markets, and lost money whenever buying began before a crash
It beat every other formula by a wide margin in each year, including the worst of the slump
questions.why: She concluded that no other formula could be used with so much confidence of ultimate success, whatever happened to prices.

questions.q: A widow needs more income than her conservative portfolio produces. What does Graham say she must not do?
options: Take speculative chances to make some extra income
Draw a modest amount from her capital each year
Keep about half of her money in government bonds
Ask a reputable investment adviser to review her plan
questions.why: He says it is far better to draw a modest amount from principal than to risk half of it in poorly grounded ventures.

questions.q: A share trades at R150. Its average earnings per share over seven years are R5.50 and its last twelve months’ EPS is R8.00. Does it meet Graham’s price limit for the defensive investor?
options: No: about 27 times the seven-year average, above the 25 limit
Yes: under 20 times the last twelve months’ earnings of R8.00
Yes: both of Graham’s price tests are met comfortably here
No: above 20 times the last twelve months’ earnings per share
questions.why: R150 ÷ R5.50 ≈ 27.3, which fails the 25-times test, even though R150 ÷ R8.00 = 18.75 passes the 20-times test. Both must be met.

questions.q: A company grows its earnings at 9% a year. Using the Rule of 72, roughly how long until its earnings double?
options: About 8 years
About 12 years
About 6 years
About 15 years
questions.why: 72 ÷ 9 = 8 years. Graham’s growth-share yardstick of doubling in ten years needs about 7.1% a year.

questions.q: An industrial company has R400m of shareholders’ equity at book value, R300m of long-term debt and R200m of bank debt. Does it pass Graham’s test of conservative financing?
options: No: equity is about 44% of capitalisation, below 50%
Yes: equity is larger than the long-term debt alone
Yes: equity is 57% if you leave out the bank debt
No: any debt at all fails Graham’s financing test
questions.why: Capitalisation including bank debt is R900m, and R400m ÷ R900m ≈ 44%. Leaving out bank debt is the trap: Graham says to include it.

questions.q: A share’s price rose from R5 to R256 while its earnings per share rose from R0.40 to R3.91. What happened to its P/E ratio?
options: It rose from 12.5 to about 65
It stayed roughly the same at 12.5
It fell from 65 to about 12.5
It rose from 5 to about 256
questions.why: R5 ÷ R0.40 = 12.5 and R256 ÷ R3.91 ≈ 65. As in Graham’s Texas Instruments example, the price ran five times as fast as profits, which is typical of popular shares and dangerous.

questions.q: A Member works at a JSE-listed bank and wants 60% of their savings in its shares, because “I know it best”. What would Zweig say?
options: Dangerous: their job and savings would hang on one company, and familiarity breeds overconfidence
Sensible: as an insider, the Member knows far more about the bank than any of the outside analysts do
Fine, as long as the bank keeps paying dividends and its share price holds up well
Fine, but only if the shares are bought through the bank’s employee share scheme
questions.why: Enron and WorldCom staff were wiped out this way. Knowing a company well often reduces the scrutiny you give it.

questions.q: A Member can invest R1,000 a month and wants a low-effort defensive plan. Which best matches Zweig’s autopilot approach?
options: A monthly debit order split across local and global share index funds and a bond fund
Each month, buy whichever JSE share has risen most, and hold it for the long term
Save in cash until the market looks cheap, then invest the whole amount at once
Buy one blue-chip share each month and sell it as soon as it shows a gain
questions.why: Automatic buying into index funds removes the need to forecast, and buys more units when prices are low. That lets you answer market questions with “I don’t know and I don’t care.”

questions.q: In September 1929, $12,000 put into the US market in one go was worth $7,223 ten years later. Someone who started with $100 and added $100 every month ended with $15,571. Why the difference?
options: Monthly buying kept purchasing at the much lower prices after the crash
The monthly investor paid much lower fees on each of the small purchases
The lump-sum investor happened to buy the wrong shares in 1929
Dividends were paid only to investors who bought every month
questions.why: Regular buying through the Depression bought far more shares at low prices. Zweig uses this to show the power of disciplined, automatic buying.

questions.q: Sort each portfolio feature: does it fit Graham’s four rules for the defensive investor’s shares?

items.t: Ten to thirty shares, not too many or too few
Large, prominent, conservatively financed companies
A long record of continuous dividends
Price within 25 times average earnings over seven years
Three fast-growing technology shares
A share bought after a 200% rise on exciting news

questions.why: Diversified, large, financially sound dividend payers, bought at reasonable prices: the defensive investor’s shares.
questions.src: Chapter 5: Rules for the common-stock component

questions.q: A share’s average earnings over seven years are {a|R2} and its last twelve months’ earnings {l|R2}. What is the highest price Graham’s two limits allow?

errs.why: Both limits must be met, so take the lower one.

questions.why: Both limits apply, so the stricter one sets the maximum price.
questions.src: Chapter 5: Rules for the common-stock component

questions.q: A Member wants to invest R2,000 a month in an index fund, but worries the market looks high. What does Graham’s approach suggest?
options: Invest the same amount every month (rand-cost averaging), whatever the level
Hold the cash until the market falls 20%, then invest it all at once
Invest only in the months after the market has fallen, and skip the rest
Fixed sums buy more units when prices are low and fewer when high, with no forecasting
Index funds are built to avoid falls, so the market level doesn’t affect them
Buying only after a fall guarantees a lower average cost than buying on a fixed schedule

questions.why: Regular, fixed investing gives a satisfactory average price without forecasting, which no one does well.
miss: Waiting for a crash is market timing, and it can mean years on the sidelines.
Investing only after falls is still trying to time the market.

questions.q: Graham tells the enterprising investor to leave high-grade preference shares to corporate buyers.
questions.why: Companies get a tax advantage on dividends that individuals do not, so the logic of the form favours corporate owners.

questions.q: Graham recommends buying second-grade bonds at par, since their extra 1% to 2% of yield more than covers the risk.
options: True
False
He calls it a fallacy: risking capital for a little more income is bad business
He agrees, provided the bonds are bought at par and held all the way to maturity
He agrees, but only for railway bonds, which he trusted more than industrial ones

questions.why: He calls that a popular fallacy. Risking principal for a little more income is bad business; buy only at a big discount, if at all.

questions.q: Graham says inferior high-coupon bonds and preference shares should normally be bought only at prices at least 30% under par.
options: True
False
Only a deep discount gives enough chance of capital gain to justify the risk
A discount of 30% or more guarantees that the issuer will repay in full
The discount makes up for the fact that such issues pay no interest at all

questions.why: Only a deep discount offers enough chance of capital gain to justify the risk. For lower coupons the discount needed is smaller.

questions.q: Railway income bonds bought near par in 1946 lost about a third of their value within a year, though railway earnings rose.
questions.why: Second-grade issues sink with the general market whatever the business is doing. The fall was steeper than that of the Dow shares.

questions.q: Graham considers sound foreign government bonds safe because a holder can enforce his claim in court if needed.
options: True
False
If trouble comes, the holder has no legal or other way to enforce the claim
Foreign bonds are safe because their governments can always print more money
Foreign bonds are safe as long as they are bought through a large international bank

questions.why: His point is the opposite: if trouble comes, the holder of foreign bonds has no legal or other means of enforcing his claim.

questions.q: A dependable sign of a bull market nearing its end is new shares of small, nondescript companies priced above established ones.
options: True
False
As a bull market runs on, issues get more frequent, poorer and more overpriced
Small new companies are priced high because they grow faster than older ones
High prices for new issues are a sign that the market is only beginning to rise

questions.why: As a bull market runs on, flotations become more frequent, the companies poorer and the prices more exorbitant.

questions.q: In a study of 66,000 brokerage accounts, the most active traders beat the market after costs by a wide margin.
questions.why: Before costs they were slightly ahead. After costs the most hyperactive traders trailed the market by about 6.4 percentage points a year.

questions.q: Buying the average IPO at its first-day close in 1980–2001 and holding for three years trailed the market by over 23 points a year.
questions.why: Big first-day gains go mostly to insiders and institutions at the offer price. Ordinary buyers come in afterwards, at inflated prices.

questions.q: What are Graham’s two reasons for being wary of new issues?
options: They carry special salesmanship, and they are sold when conditions favour the seller
They are restricted for private investors, and new companies often default early
They pay no dividends at first, and they come with limited voting rights
They are priced above value by the underwriting fee, which buyers end up paying
questions.why: Special selling effort calls for special sales resistance, and favourable timing for the issuer means poor timing for the buyer.

questions.q: What does Graham call the “businessman’s investment” fallacy?
options: Buying a higher-yield, riskier security at full price for a little extra income
Putting savings into your own business instead of into listed securities
Buying only shares of companies whose business you understand from your work
Holding a large cash reserve in case your business has an emergency
questions.why: Accepting a real chance of losing principal for 1% or 2% more a year makes no sense unless a large capital gain is also possible.

questions.q: Graham says second-grade bonds and preference shares have two contradictory traits. What are they?
options: They sink badly in weak markets, yet many recover fully when conditions improve
They pay high yields, yet their prices hardly move at all when markets fall
They hold up well in recessions, yet swing wildly whenever markets start to boom
They rise with inflation, yet fall sharply whenever interest rates go up
questions.why: This is why patient buyers who pick them up when “friendless” can do well, while buyers at full prices suffer.

questions.q: Even if second-grade issues bought at full price might match first-grade ones on average, why does Graham still advise against them?
options: He can’t diversify enough to earn the average, will fret in declines, and can usually buy at 70 in a weak market
They are banned for individual investors in most markets, and brokers usually refuse to sell such issues to him
Their interest is taxed more heavily than that on first-grade bonds, which cancels the extra yield
Credit ratings on them are usually wrong, so he can’t tell which ones will default and which won’t
questions.why: In theory the higher yields may cover the losses; in practice an individual cannot hold enough of them to collect the average.

questions.q: What is “market impact”, as Zweig describes it?
options: The hidden cost of moving the price against yourself when you are eager to buy or sell
The effect that changes in interest rates have on the prices of shares and bonds over time
The commission printed on your statement each time a broker carries out a trade
The influence that large index funds have on the weights of shares in an index
questions.why: Push the price up 5 cents on 1,000 shares and you have paid an extra R50 that never appears on your statement. Panic selling below the last price costs you the same way.

questions.q: Of hot new-issue profits, Graham says: “For every dollar you make in this way you will be lucky if you end up by losing only two.” What is he warning?
options: Easy early gains draw you into a game that ends in bigger losses
Commissions take about two-thirds of the profit on new issues
New issues pay out only about a third of their earnings as dividends
You should invest twice as much in new issues to make them worthwhile
questions.why: Early issues may rise, but the quality falls and prices become exorbitant. Collapses of 75% or more follow.

questions.q: How does Zweig update Graham’s objection to high-yield (“junk”) bonds?
options: Funds now spread the default risk, but fees are often high, so they are a minor option at most
Junk bonds are now safer than government bonds, because defaults have become rare events
Graham’s objection still applies with full force, so investors should never own any at all
They now suit every investor as a core holding, since funds remove almost all of the risk
questions.why: Graham’s main complaint was that individuals could not diversify. Funds solve that, but Zweig still calls them “an option, not an obligation”.

questions.q: A second-grade bond pays 6% on a R1,000 face value. Graham would rather buy it at 70 than at par. At 70, what is its current yield, and what gain would you make if it recovered to par?
options: About 8.6% yield and about a 43% gain
About 6% yield and about a 30% gain
About 8.6% yield and about a 30% gain
About 4.2% yield and about a 43% gain
questions.why: R60 ÷ R700 ≈ 8.6%. Recovering from R700 to R1,000 is a R300 gain on R700, about 43%. That is the real upside that justifies the risk.

questions.q: A railway’s earnings available for interest are R30m and its interest charges R20m. How well is the interest covered, against Graham’s standard for a well-protected railway bond?
options: 1.5 times, far below his requirement of 5 times
1.5 times, which meets his standard for railways
0.67 times, slightly below his required standard
3 times, just below his requirement of 4 times
questions.why: R30m ÷ R20m = 1.5. Graham gives exactly this kind of example: a 7.35% yield on a bond covered only 1.5 times, against his 5-times test.

questions.q: Buying a small share costs about 3% and selling another 3% (commission, spread and market impact). Before tax, roughly what gain do you need just to break even?
options: About 6%
About 3%
Nothing: costs are refunded on sale
About 12%
questions.why: Costs on the way in and the way out compound to just over 6%. Zweig adds that tax on short-term gains pushes the hurdle to about 10%.

questions.q: On its first trading day a company is valued at R12 billion. It has made R44m of sales in its life, lost money every year, and its accumulated losses exceed R30m. What does Zweig’s “neighbour over the fence” test suggest?
options: No private buyer would pay anything near that; the price reflects popularity, not value
The market price proves the value is right, since thousands of buyers have agreed on it
Buy now, before the price rises further as more investors discover the company
Value doesn’t matter as long as someone else will pay more for the shares later
questions.why: This is VA Linux in 1999. Asked privately, you would never pay R12 billion for a loss-maker already R30m in the hole. In public, price becomes a popularity contest.

questions.q: A company’s pre-tax income fell short of its interest charges in two of the last five years. It now issues a record amount of new bonds yielding 8%. What would Graham and Zweig advise?
options: Avoid: no yield compensates for interest that earnings cannot cover
Buy: 8% is well above what government bonds pay at the moment
Buy, because issues of record size are snapped up by professionals
Buy, as long as the bonds are still rated investment grade
questions.why: This was WorldCom in 2001. Its bonds defaulted within about a year and lost over 80% of their value. Buying a bond only for its yield invites disaster.

questions.q: A Member wants some emerging-market government bonds for diversification. What is Zweig’s limit?
options: No more than 10% of the bond portfolio, through a low-cost fund
Up to half the bond portfolio, since they move apart from shares
Any amount, but only through individual bonds, never through funds
None at all: emerging-market debt is never suitable for investors
questions.why: He sees some value because they seldom move with the share market, but says no sane investor would put more than 10% of a bond portfolio there.

questions.q: Sort each purchase: does Graham tell the enterprising investor to avoid it, or is it acceptable?

items.t: Second-grade bonds or preference shares bought at full price
New issues in a buoyant market
Foreign government bonds
High-grade bonds at fair prices
Second-grade issues at bargain levels, about 30% below par
Shares of large, sound companies at reasonable prices

questions.why: The negative approach: lower-quality issues only at bargain prices, and steer clear of new issues and foreign bonds.

questions.q: A popular JSE consumer brand is listing, and the offer is many times oversubscribed. A friend says you must get in on day one. What would Graham and Zweig say?
options: Pass: in hot markets new issues are priced to favour the sellers
Buy on day one: heavy demand shows the shares are priced too low
Buy a week later, once the first-day rush has settled the price
Sellers choose when to list and at what price, and hype often fades after listing
Oversubscription proves that professional investors value the shares well above the price
Listing rules require new shares to be priced below their fair value

questions.why: Zweig’s summary: IPO can stand for “It’s Probably Overpriced”. Graham warned that new issues sell easily only in bull markets.
miss: Demand in a hot market shows enthusiasm, not value; first-day prices are least tied to value.
A week later the price still reflects the excitement, not the business.

questions.q: Graham says an issue is not a true bargain unless its indicated value is at least 50% more than its price.
options: True
False
A value at least 50% above the price is his concrete test of a bargain
A gap of 10% is enough, provided the company also pays a regular dividend
He measures bargains by their dividend yield alone, rather than by value

questions.why: That margin is his concrete test for a bargain issue, whether a bond, a preference share or an ordinary share.

questions.q: Graham’s study of growth funds from 1961 to 1970 found that they far outperformed the market.
questions.why: They gained about 108% against 105% for the S&P, and most did worse in 1969–70. No outstanding rewards came from growth investing as such.

questions.q: Graham sees no sound middle ground between the defensive and the enterprising investor.
options: True
False
A halfway position tends to disappoint; most should choose the defensive role
He recommends a middle path for most people, half defensive and half enterprising
He sees no real difference between the two roles, so there is no middle to find

questions.why: Trying to be in between is a compromise more likely to bring disappointment. Most investors should choose the defensive role.

questions.q: Graham tells the enterprising investor to concentrate on small, unpopular companies.
options: True
False
He prefers large ones: they have the resources to recover and are quickly noticed
He says small unpopular companies rebound fastest, so they are the best hunting ground
He tells enterprising investors to avoid unpopular companies of every size

questions.why: He stresses large unpopular companies. They have the resources to recover, and the market responds quickly to their improvement.

questions.q: In one-year tests from 1937 to 1969, the low-P/E Dow shares beat the average far more often than they lagged it.
questions.why: They clearly did better in 25 of 34 years, about the same in six, and clearly worse in only three.

questions.q: Following the best 10% of market-timing newsletters from 1991 to 1995 beat simply holding an index fund.
questions.why: The best timers earned about 12.6% a year against 16.4% for an index fund, before their subscription fees and extra costs.

questions.q: Zweig suggests putting up to a third of your share money in funds that hold foreign shares.
options: True
False
Living, working and earning in one country is already a big bet on it
Foreign shares always grow faster than shares at home over the long run
Foreign shares are always less volatile, because they are priced in dollars

questions.why: Living, working and earning in one country is already a large bet on that economy. Offshore holdings insure against home not always being the best place to invest.

questions.q: Graham recommends that most investors become enterprising investors in order to raise their returns.
options: True
False
Most should be defensive, accept its return and resist the urge to stray
He wants everyone to be enterprising, because the defensive return is too low
He wants most to be enterprising, provided they have a good adviser to help

questions.why: He says most should choose the defensive role, be satisfied with its return, and resist temptations to stray from it.

questions.q: What are the two catches Graham sees in simply buying the shares with the best growth records?
options: Their prices already reflect the good prospects, and the growth may not last
They pay no dividends, and their shares are hard to buy and sell in size
They are usually too small, and their accounts are often unreliable
They are taxed more heavily, and their managers keep selling their shares
questions.why: You can be right about the company and still do poorly by overpaying. And size itself makes rapid growth harder to repeat.

questions.q: Why does Graham prefer unpopular large companies to unpopular small ones?
options: They have the capital and talent to ride out adversity, and the market reacts quickly to their recovery
They pay higher dividends than small companies do, so investors are paid well while they wait for a recovery
They are hardly affected by recessions, so their earnings recover within a year
Their shares are cheaper per share, so a small investor can buy a meaningful holding
questions.why: Small companies risk a permanent loss of profitability, or long neglect by the market even after they improve.

questions.q: Graham gives two tests for spotting a bargain share. What are they?
options: An appraisal based on future earnings, and the value of the business to a private owner
A rising share price, and upgrades to the analysts’ earnings forecasts for the company
A high dividend yield, and a share price that is low in rands compared with its peers
Buying by the directors, and trading volume well above the share’s usual level
questions.why: The private-owner test pays special attention to realisable assets, especially net current assets (working capital).

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of Graham’s causes of a share selling at an unduly low price?
options: Unusually strong earnings growth
Currently disappointing results
Long neglect or unpopularity
The market missing the true earnings picture
questions.why: Strong growth tends to make the market overvalue a share, not undervalue it.

questions.q: Earnings and price have both fallen. What else does Graham require before treating the share as a buy?
options: Reasonably stable earnings over ten years or more with no loss year, plus size and financial strength
A new management team with a clear plan to restore earnings to their former level
A dividend increase within the last year, showing the board’s confidence that earnings will soon recover
A recommendation from the company’s bankers, who have the best view of its finances
questions.why: A falling price alone is no guide: some shares, like Anaconda Wire and Cable, never recovered.

questions.q: Why have shares of secondary (non-leading) companies usually sold at low prices relative to earnings and assets?
options: Since the 1931–32 depression, investors have strongly preferred industry leaders
Secondary companies may not pay dividends until they reach a minimum size
Their accounts are not audited to the same standard as those of the leaders
Funds are not allowed to buy them, which leaves only private investors as buyers
questions.why: Investors acted as if such companies were headed for extinction, just as in 1929 they thought no price was too high for blue chips. Both views were exaggerations.

questions.q: The old Wall Street motto says “never buy into a lawsuit”. Why does Graham see opportunity there?
options: The public’s aversion holds prices of affected securities unduly low
Lawsuits usually end in the company’s favour, which lifts the share price
Court cases make share prices more stable while they are being heard
Legal settlements are added to reported earnings once a case is won
questions.why: Prejudice against complicated legal situations creates bargains for those who analyse them. Zweig adds that some lawsuits really do destroy companies, so the rule still protects most investors.

questions.q: How can a buyer of undervalued secondary shares profit even if they stay below fair value for a while?
options: High dividends, reinvested earnings, bull markets lifting cheap shares, and takeovers at generous prices
By borrowing to buy more as they fall, which lowers the average cost of the whole holding
By selling them short while they are cheap, then buying them back once the market has lifted them to fair value
By waiting for them to join a major index, which forces the index funds to buy them
questions.why: Over five to seven years these advantages can add up, even before the market corrects the price.

questions.q: A company has R2.4bn of current assets and R1.0bn of total liabilities (including long-term debt and preference shares). It has 190m shares trading at R7. Is it a Graham “net-net”?
options: Yes: net working capital is about R7.37 a share, above the R7 price
No: current assets per share are R12.63, well above the price
No: only current liabilities should be deducted, so the test fails
Yes, but only if it has no long-term debt or preference shares
questions.why: R2.4bn − R1.0bn = R1.4bn, and R1.4bn ÷ 190m ≈ R7.37. At R7 the market values the ongoing business at nothing. Zweig’s real case was Comverse in 2002.

questions.q: You appraise a share at R60. Under Graham’s definition, at what price or lower is it a true bargain?
questions.why: Value must be at least 50% more than price: R60 ÷ 1.5 = R40. At R45 the value is only a third more than the price.

questions.q: A secondary company is appraised at R90 a share. What is the most an enterprising investor should pay, by Graham’s rule for secondary issues?
questions.why: Bargain prices for these categories are no more than two-thirds of appraisal value: ⅔ × R90 = R60.

questions.q: A company earned R3.00 a share last year but averaged only R0.50 over the six years before. Using 25 times average seven-year earnings, what price does Graham’s approach allow?
options: About R21.43
R75.00, at 25 times last year
questions.why: Seven-year earnings total R6.00, an average of about R0.857. 25 × R0.857 ≈ R21.43. Using last year alone (25 × R3 = R75) would value a one-off spike as if it were permanent.

questions.q: A study claims that avoiding the five worst days each year would have turned $1 into $987 instead of $11.71. Why is this no guide for investors?
options: No one can identify the worst days before they happen
The figures ignore dividends, but the idea still works
It only applies to US shares
Trading costs would be too low to matter
questions.why: Hindsight is 20/20, but foresight is legally blind. Even the future Fed chairman was unqualifiedly bullish just before the 1973–74 crash.

questions.q: A Member has 80% of their savings in one JSE company they admire but do not work for or control. What would Graham say?
options: One-share fortunes mostly come from insiders; an outsider is under constant strain and should diversify
Concentration is how great fortunes are made, so hold on and add to it on any dip
Fine, as long as the company keeps paying dividends and its earnings keep growing
Fine, if the share has risen strongly since they bought it, because that shows the market agrees with their view
questions.why: Insiders can justify holding through every setback. Outsiders will keep wondering whether too much is in one place. Zweig adds that concentration also produces most of the great failures.

questions.q: A South African lives, works and is paid in rands, and owns only JSE shares. What does Zweig’s “Japan in 1989” story suggest?
options: Put part of the share portfolio offshore, because you are already heavily exposed to your home economy
Stay fully invested at home, since you understand the local economy and companies best
Move everything offshore, since home markets in emerging economies tend to lag the rest of the world over time
Wait for the rand to strengthen before deciding, so that offshore assets cost less
questions.why: Japanese investors who kept everything at home after a great decade lost about two-thirds over the next ten years. No one knows which market will lead.

questions.q: A cyclical company trades at only 7 times earnings in a record-profit year, and at a very high multiple in a loss year. Why can the low P/E in the boom year mislead?
options: The market doubts that peak profits will last, so a low multiple of peak earnings is not necessarily cheap
A low P/E is a bargain whatever the cycle, so the boom year is the best time to buy
P/E ratios mean nothing for cyclical firms, so only the dividend yield should be used to judge whether they are cheap
The high P/E in loss years shows the share is cheapest then, so buy in the bad years
questions.why: Graham’s Chrysler table shows this. He suggests also requiring a low price relative to past average earnings, to filter out such roller coasters.

questions.q: A company has current assets of {ca|R0m} and total liabilities of {tl|R0m}, with {n|0m} shares trading at {p|R2}. What is the price as a percentage of net current asset value per share?
work: Net current asset value = ({ca|R0m} − {tl|R0m}) ÷ {n|0m} = {ncav|R2} a share

errs.why: Take all liabilities off the current assets first.

questions.why: Graham’s bargain test: shares bought at two-thirds or less of net current asset value, with nothing paid for the fixed assets.

questions.q: A large, well-financed JSE company is out of favour after a poor year, and its P/E has fallen to half the market’s. Its long record is sound. What does Graham’s positive approach suggest?
options: Consider it: large, temporarily unpopular companies are a good hunting ground
Avoid it: a falling P/E usually signals a decline the market can already see
Wait until the P/E is back at the market’s, to confirm the recovery is real
A large company has the resources to recover, and the market overreacts to a bad spell
Low P/E shares double within a few years in most of the cases that Graham studied over decades
Large companies are protected by their size from ever going out of business

questions.why: Graham favoured large companies selling at low prices because of temporary unpopularity: their size gives them staying power.
questions.src: Chapter 7: The relatively unpopular large company
miss: With a sound record and strong finances, a bad spell is more often temporary than not.
By then the price will reflect the recovery.

questions.q: Graham says the intelligent investor can do well by pricing, but an emphasis on timing (forecasting) makes him a speculator.
options: True
False
Pricing means buying below fair value; timing means forecasting the next move
Timing is the safer of the two, because prices always follow good forecasts
He sees no difference between them: pricing and timing are both speculation

questions.why: Pricing means buying below fair value and selling above it, or at least not overpaying. Timing means predicting the market’s next move.

questions.q: Once the Dow theory became widely followed, it kept working just as well as it had in the decades before.
questions.why: After 1938 it mostly took followers out at a good price and put them back in higher. For nearly 30 years, simply holding the Dow did better.

questions.q: Graham argues a trading formula grows less reliable as it spreads, partly because its popularity changes the market.
options: True
False
Conditions change, and its followers’ own buying and selling erodes its profits
Formulas become more reliable as more people use them and prove them in practice
Formulas never lose their edge; only the investors who use them lose their nerve

questions.why: New conditions arise that the formula no longer fits, and its followers’ own actions erode its profits. Anything easily described and followed by many is too simple to last.

questions.q: Graham tells investors to expect most shares to swing 50% up from lows, and a third down from highs, within five years.
questions.why: He calls it a probability, not a mere possibility. Zweig adds that anyone who can’t live with this is not yet entitled to call himself an investor.

questions.q: Graham says that the better a company’s record and prospects, the more stable its share price tends to be.
options: True
False
The bigger the premium over book value, the more the price swings with moods
He agrees with it: strong records and good prospects always bring steady prices
He says record and prospects have no link at all to how the share price behaves

questions.why: His paradox runs the other way. The bigger the premium over book value, the more the price depends on market moods, so the best companies can be the most speculative shares.

questions.q: For a conservative investor, Graham suggests favouring shares priced no more than about one-third above their tangible asset value.
questions.why: A price near asset value has support independent of the market. The small premium can be seen as a fee for the benefit of a stock-exchange listing.

questions.q: Graham says you must accept Mr Market’s daily price as the true value of your holding, whatever you think of it.
options: True
False
You can ignore him, use his price when it suits you, and judge value yourself
He says to accept it, because the market is always proved right in the end
He says to accept it, but only for the shares you happen to hold through a fund

questions.why: You are free to ignore him. Use his price only when it suits you, by buying when he is gloomy and selling when he is euphoric, and otherwise form your own view from the company’s reports.

questions.q: Graham’s summary motto is: never buy a share immediately after a substantial drop, since falls tend to continue.
options: True
False
His motto: never buy right after a big rise, or sell right after a big drop
He says falls tend to continue, so selling quickly is the safest course to take
He says to buy right after a big rise, while the market’s momentum still lasts

questions.why: The trap reverses it. His motto is never buy a share immediately after a substantial rise, or sell one immediately after a substantial drop.

questions.q: Even the highest-grade bonds can swing widely in price when interest rates change.
questions.why: Prime tax-free bond yields more than doubled between 1965 and 1970 and their price index fell by about 40%, though their safety was never in doubt.

questions.q: According to Graham, what is the only significant meaning of price fluctuations for the true investor?
options: They give him the chance to buy wisely after sharp falls and sell wisely after big rises
They tell him whether the business itself is improving or getting worse
They show him what other experts and insiders think the company is worth
They signal when to follow the market’s trend and when to step aside from it until the trend turns
questions.why: Price signals mislead at least as often as they help. The rest of the time he does better to watch dividends and operating results.

questions.q: Why does Graham say timing is of no real value to the investor unless it coincides with pricing?
options: Waiting on the sidelines costs dividends, so it pays only if he buys back substantially lower
Brokers charge more for trades timed around market turns, and the extra costs eat up most of the gain
Acting on timing signals is restricted for investors who hold shares for income
The market seldom falls far, so waiting for lower prices is usually pointless
questions.why: The speculator hates waiting, but waiting itself costs the investor nothing. Getting out pays only if he repurchases at a much lower price.

questions.q: Why does Graham think the general public can never make money from market forecasts?
options: If everyone sells on the same signal, who buys? The average investor can’t beat the public he is part of
Forecasts are only published after the moves have happened, so they always come too late
Brokers deliberately publish wrong forecasts so that they can trade against the public
Good forecasting services are too expensive for individuals, so only the large institutions benefit from them
questions.why: There is no basis in logic or experience for thinking the typical investor can anticipate the market better than everyone else trying to do the same.

questions.q: Besides a price close to asset value, what else does Graham require before a share counts as a sound investment?
options: A satisfactory earnings yield, a strong financial position, and earnings likely to be maintained
A rising share price, strong trading volume and a place in one of the main indices that funds must track
Better-than-average expected growth and a management team with a strong record
A recent dividend increase, analyst upgrades and buying by the company’s directors
questions.why: A share does not become sound just because it is cheap relative to assets. Giving up brilliant prospects makes these criteria easy to meet.

questions.q: What are the two morals Graham draws from the A&P story?
options: The market can go badly wrong, and businesses change in quality, so review your holdings from time to time
Retail shares are riskier than most, and dividends matter little to a company that is still growing fast
Large companies seldom fail, and their shares nearly always recover in the end if you hold on long enough
Buy after a share has tripled, since momentum lasts, and sell once it has halved
questions.why: In 1938 A&P was being given away; in 1961 the public clamoured for it at 30 times earnings. Meanwhile the company itself declined from outstanding to mediocre.

questions.q: What does Graham see as the chief advantage of a mechanical formula for shifting between shares and bonds?
options: It gives the investor something to do, against the crowd, instead of following bull-market enthusiasm
It guarantees the highest long-run returns of any approach to dividing a portfolio between shares and bonds
It removes the effect of price fluctuations from the portfolio almost entirely
It lets him predict the start of the next bear market from the market’s level
questions.why: His reasons are human nature more than arithmetic: the formula channels pent-up energy into selling as prices rise and buying as they fall.

questions.q: In 1931–33, owners of unquoted mortgages told themselves their investments had kept their full value, while listed bonds showed big price falls. What was Graham’s verdict?
options: It was self-deception; the listed bonds were better, because owners could sell or simply ignore the prices
The owners of unquoted mortgages were right: with no quoted price there was no loss
Listed bonds should be avoided, because their prices can fall when markets panic
Both groups had lost exactly the same amount of value, so neither choice made any difference in the end
questions.why: A quoted market gives you options without forcing you to accept its price. Having no quotation does not stop value from shrinking.

questions.q: According to Graham, what three factors drive the price swings of convertible bonds and preference shares?
options: The related share price, the company’s credit standing, and general interest rates
Inflation, exchange rates and the price of oil, which together drive company profits
Index inclusion, analyst coverage and the trading volume in the related shares
Dividends, share buybacks and share splits announced by the issuing company
questions.why: Being pulled three ways, convertibles rarely deliver the hoped-for mix of bond safety and share upside.

questions.q: Zweig lists what an investor can control. Which of these is NOT on his list?
options: Whether your shares beat the market this year
Your brokerage and ownership costs
Your risk, through allocation, diversification and rebalancing
Your own behaviour
questions.why: Short-run returns are hostage to Mr Market. Costs, expectations, risk, taxes and, above all, behaviour are yours to control.

questions.q: A share rises 50% from R10 to R15. What percentage fall takes it straight back to R10?
options: About 33%
50%, the same as the rise
questions.why: A R5 fall from R15 is a third. This is why Graham speaks of a 50% rise and the “equivalent one-third” decline.

questions.q: A share falls 50%. What gain does it then need to return to its starting price?
questions.why: R100 falls to R50, and getting back to R100 means doubling. Graham notes that a 50% decline fully offsets a 100% advance.

questions.q: A company’s tangible book value is R30 a share. Following Graham’s suggestion for conservative investors, roughly what is the most you would pay?
options: About R40
About R60
About R30
About R90
questions.why: No more than one-third above tangible asset value: R30 × 1⅓ = R40. You would also check earnings, finances and stability.

questions.q: A company you analysed carefully falls 40% in a market panic, though nothing in its business has changed. What would Graham do?
options: Recheck the analysis; if the value is intact, ignore the fall or buy more
Sell, because a 40% fall shows the market knows something you don’t
Sell half to limit the damage, and keep the rest in case it recovers
Wait for the price to get back to what you paid, then sell and move on
questions.why: This is his A&P lesson. If no shrinkage in underlying value has occurred, the holder has suffered no real loss and can use the bargain if he has the funds and courage.

questions.q: A company with annual revenue of R100m and no profits is valued at R25 billion. What is its price-to-sales ratio?
options: 250 times
25 times
2.5 times
0.25 times
questions.why: R25,000m ÷ R100m = 250. Inktomi traded at about this level in 2000; two years later it was at 0.35 times sales, though its revenue had grown.

questions.q: A news anchor shouts that the market “plunged 100 points” with the index at 8,000. In proportion, how big was the fall?
options: About 1.25%
About 12.5%
About 8%
About 0.1%
questions.why: 100 ÷ 8,000 = 1.25%. Zweig compares it to a weatherman shrieking that the temperature has plunged from 27 °C to 26.7 °C.

questions.q: Interest rates rise sharply. All else equal, which high-grade bond will fall most in price?
options: A 30-year bond
A 5-year bond
A one-year bond
They all fall by the same percentage
questions.why: Long maturities swing most, because the fixed repayment at par has less moderating effect. Graham’s Northern Pacific 3s due 2047 lost two-thirds of their price as rates rose.

questions.q: You have R20,000 for shares and the market is around normal valuation levels. What does Graham’s summary suggest?
options: Invest it now; wait only if the market is far above established value standards
Wait for the next bear market before buying anything, however long it takes
Invest only after a sharp rally has confirmed that the market’s trend is up
Put it all in the share that has risen most this year, to ride its momentum
questions.why: Holding off for low levels may mean a long wait and lost income. He suggests buying whenever you have the money, except when the market is clearly too high.

questions.q: You hold shares in a JSE-listed food producer. A sector-wide sell-off takes the price down 30% in a month; its earnings outlook and balance sheet are unchanged. What does the intelligent investor do?
options: Sell now, before the sector falls further and wipes out more of your capital
Hold, and consider buying more if the price is now below your estimate of value
Hold until the price gets back to what you paid, then sell and move on
The price is an offer you may accept or ignore, not a verdict on the business
A sharp fall usually means that insiders know something the public doesn’t know yet
Volatility is the main risk an investor faces, so cut it when it rises

questions.why: Mr Market’s moods offer prices; they don’t set values. The true investor uses them, or ignores them.
miss: Selling after a fall with the business unchanged hands the gain to whoever buys from you.
That lets the price, not the value, make the decision.

questions.q: A share falls {d|0%}. What percentage rise does it then need to get back to its old price?
