work: After the fall it is worth 1 − {d|0%} = {1-d|2} of the old price

errs.why: The rise is measured from the lower price, so it must be bigger than the fall.

questions.why: Losses need bigger gains to recover, which is why avoiding a large loss matters more than catching a large gain.

questions.q: The market has risen 40% in a year, and your estimates suggest several of your shares are now well above their value. Mr Market is offering high prices. What does Graham suggest?
options: Consider selling some to him, or at least stop buying at these prices
Buy more: a strong year shows the market expects higher earnings
Do nothing at all: a long-term investor should never act on prices
Use Mr Market’s offers when they suit you; high prices are a chance to sell
Markets always fall back after a 40% year, so selling early is a safe bet
Selling is a speculator’s tool; a true investor only ever buys and holds

questions.why: The investor can take advantage of Mr Market’s mood in either direction: selling to him when he is too eager.

questions.q: Graham guesses that the average person who invested only through funds did better than the average person who bought shares directly.
options: True
False
Funds kept people away from hot new issues and speculation, despite their costs
Funds always beat the market, so the people who owned them did much better
Funds charged almost nothing in his day, so their returns were higher than now

questions.why: Even though funds matched rather than beat the market and cost more, they kept people away from hot new issues and speculative temptations.

questions.q: Graham criticises the fund industry above all for failing to beat the market as a whole over the years.
options: True
False
Professionals hold so much of the market that together they must roughly match it
He blames the managers for that failure, and calls it plain negligence on their part
He says funds did beat the market, so there was nothing there to criticise

questions.why: He says they can’t be blamed: professionals hold so much of the market that their combined results must roughly equal the market’s.

questions.q: Graham’s rule is to buy closed-end funds at a 10% to 15% discount to asset value rather than pay about a 9% premium for open-end load funds.
questions.why: If both groups perform about the same, the discount buyer gets considerably more assets for each rand invested.

questions.q: Graham found that closed-end funds sell at discounts because their investment results are much worse than those of open-end funds.
options: True
False
Results in 1961–70 were similar: the discount reflects having no salesmen
Their results were worse, which is exactly what the discount to assets reflects
Their results were better, so the discount is a mistake that soon disappears

questions.why: Their results over 1961–1970 were very similar. The discount reflects the absence of salesmen pushing them, not poorer performance.

questions.q: Graham suggests the typical investor buy his bonds directly rather than through the bond portion of a balanced fund.
questions.why: Balanced funds yielded only about 3.6% on their offer price. Government savings bonds, A-rated corporates or tax-free bonds would do better.

questions.q: Over the 20 years to 2002, only about 15% of US share funds beat a low-cost S&P 500 index fund.
questions.why: 37 of 248 funds, and that understates the index’s edge, because funds that closed down were left out of the figures.

questions.q: Zweig says funds with higher fees tend to earn higher returns, so in fund investing you get what you pay for.
options: True
False
Research shows the reverse: higher-fee funds earn less, and fees persist
He agrees that higher fees buy better managers and so lead to better returns
He says fees and returns have no relationship in either direction over time

questions.why: Decades of research show the reverse: higher-fee funds earn less over time. High returns are temporary, but high fees are nearly permanent.

questions.q: Graham concludes that smaller size seems necessary for a fund to keep producing outstanding results.
questions.why: The funds that stayed ahead were small and specialised. Large, soundly managed funds can at best do slightly better than average.

questions.q: Fund performance is no better than the market and costs are higher. Why, then, does Graham think funds still served the average person well?
options: The real alternative was poor new issues from salesmen and a brokerage account full of temptations
Funds beat the market after costs over most ten-year periods, so the extra fees paid for themselves
Fund holdings were guaranteed by the government, so the average person could not lose his capital
Funds paid no tax at all, which more than made up for their higher costs and average results
questions.why: The average person was not choosing between a fund and a well-built portfolio of his own. He was choosing between a fund salesman and wilier peddlers of second-rate offerings.

questions.q: How does Graham say an investor may sensibly use a fund’s past performance?
options: Compare at least five years, as long as the period was not one of a big rise in the whole market
Pick the fund with the best single year, since a great year shows the managers’ true skill
Ignore it completely, since past results have no bearing on what a fund will do in future
Pick the fund that gained most in the last bull market, since it is likely to lead the next one too
questions.why: Spectacular results in a big up-market may just mean the managers took undue speculative risks and got away with it for a while.

questions.q: What worried Graham about the “performance fund” managers of the late 1960s?
options: Most were young, had known only a bull market, and paid prices far out of line with assets or earnings
They held too many government bonds and too little in shares to keep up with a rising market
They refused to buy technology companies, so their funds missed the decade’s fastest growers
They charged no fees at all, which meant they had to take extra risks to keep their firms in business
questions.why: They treated a “sound investment” as one likely to rise in the next few months. The results were brilliant for a while, then calamitous.

questions.q: Most buyers look first at a fund’s past performance. In what order does Zweig say the intelligent investor should look?
options: Expenses, then risk, then the managers, then past performance
Past performance, then the managers, then risk, then expenses
Star rating, then past performance, then expenses
The managers’ fame, then the fund’s size, then expenses
questions.why: Expenses are the most predictable driver of future returns. Past performance is a pale predictor, so it comes last.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of Zweig’s reasons that winning funds rarely stay winners?
options: Regulators cap the returns of successful funds
Star managers leave for rivals
New money swells the fund and its trading costs
Successful managers become timid and copy each other
questions.why: There is no such cap. The real problems are migrating managers, “asset elephantiasis”, rising costs and herding.

questions.q: Which of these does Zweig list as a red flag that it may be time to sell a fund?
options: A sudden, sharp change in investment strategy
Lagging the index for one year while its style is out of favour
Being boring
Not appearing on financial television
questions.why: His red flags are a strategy shift, higher expenses, large tax bills from heavy trading, and suddenly erratic returns. A temporary lag is not one.

questions.q: Which of these is a trait Zweig finds in the rare funds that beat the index?
options: The managers are among the fund’s biggest shareholders
It advertises its top ranking widely to attract investors
Its holdings closely match those of the index it tracks
It takes in as much new money as it can, as fast as possible
questions.why: His other traits are low cost, daring to be different, closing to new investors before getting too big, and not advertising.

questions.q: You invest R1,000 in a load fund priced at 109% of its asset value, or R1,000 in a closed-end fund at 85% of asset value (ignore commission). About how much underlying asset value do you get in each?
options: About R917 against about R1,176
R1,000 in each
About R1,090 against about R850
About R917 against R1,000
questions.why: R1,000 ÷ 1.09 ≈ R917 and R1,000 ÷ 0.85 ≈ R1,176, about 28% more assets for the closed-end buyer if both perform alike.

questions.q: A fund charges a 5.75% sales load on a R10,000 investment. What percentage of the amount actually invested does the charge represent?
options: About 6.1%
About 5.4%
About 11.5%
questions.why: R575 goes to the seller, leaving R9,425 invested, and R575 ÷ R9,425 ≈ 6.1%. Graham calls quoting it the standard way a sales gimmick.

questions.q: Shares return 7% a year for 20 years. An index fund costs about 0.3% a year in total; a typical active fund about 3.5%. Roughly what does R10,000 become in each?
options: About R36,600 against about R19,900
About R38,700 in both
About R30,000 against about R25,000
About R19,900 against about R36,600
questions.why: 1.067²⁰ ≈ 3.66 and 1.035²⁰ ≈ 1.99. Costs that look small compound into a gap of nearly half.

questions.q: A R100m fund puts 2% of its assets into a company with a market value of R500m. If the fund grows to R10bn and still wants 2% in that company, what share of the company would it need?
questions.why: 2% of R10bn is R200m, and R200m ÷ R500m = 40%. Success forces big funds out of small companies, one of the reasons hot funds cool down.

questions.q: Your value fund has lagged the index for two years while value shares were out of favour. Its strategy, fees and managers are unchanged. What does Zweig advise?
options: Hold on: you hired it to invest this way, and selling locks you out of the recovery
Sell at once and buy last year’s best fund, which shows where the market is going
Sell half now and wait to see whether the other half recovers before deciding
Switch to a sector fund in whichever industry has risen most over those two years
questions.why: He notes that fund investors trailed their own funds by about 4.7 points a year by buying high and selling low. If you can’t stay married through lean years, don’t marry.

questions.q: A fund earned 10% a year, but its investors as a group earned only about 5%. What is the most likely explanation?
options: They bought after good years and sold after bad ones
The fund misreported its returns in its marketing
Taxes and fees always halve what fund investors keep
The index fell over the period while the fund itself rose
questions.why: Investors’ timing of money in and out, not the fund itself, cost them dearly. It is the same buy-high, sell-low behaviour Graham warns about.

questions.q: A balanced fund holds 40% in bonds and yields 3.6% on its offer price, while A-rated corporate bonds bought directly yield 7.5%. What would Graham suggest for the bond part of your portfolio?
options: Buy good bonds directly instead of through the balanced fund
Stay in the balanced fund, since its convenience outweighs the yield
Buy a second balanced fund as well, to spread the bond risk further
Avoid bonds entirely and hold the money in shares instead
questions.why: He found it more logical for the typical investor to make bond investments directly, where the income is far higher.

questions.q: R100,000 is invested for 20 years at a gross return of {g|1%} a year. Fund A charges {fa|1%} a year; an index fund charges {fi|1%}. How much more does the index fund end with?

errs.why: Fees compound: the gap grows each year with the lost returns on the fees.

questions.why: Costs compound against you just as returns compound for you. Zweig’s advice: buy funds with low costs.

questions.q: Last year’s top-performing unit trust returned 45%. Its fees are 2.5% a year. A Member wants to switch everything into it. What would Zweig say?
options: Be wary: last year’s winners rarely stay on top, and high costs keep dragging
Switch now: a 45% year shows the manager has a real skill that will carry on into next year
Switch half now and the rest next year, to spread the timing risk
Hot funds tend to cool as their style falls out of favour and new money floods in
High fees are a sign of better managers, who more than earn the cost back in returns
A fund’s past year is the best guide to its returns in the year after

questions.why: Zweig’s evidence: top funds seldom repeat, and costs are the most reliable predictor of a fund’s future returns.

questions.q: A closed-end fund (an investment trust) trades at 15% below its net asset value. An open-end fund holding similar shares charges a sales fee. Which would Graham favour?
options: The closed-end fund at a discount
The open-end fund with the sales fee
Neither: funds are never suitable
At a discount you buy R1 of assets for less than R1; with a sales fee you pay more
Open-end funds can be sold back to the manager at any time, which is worth the sales fee
Closed-end funds are run by better managers, who choose fixed capital

questions.why: Graham pointed out that buying closed-end funds at a discount gives the investor an edge over buying open-end funds with a load.

questions.q: Graham notes that businesspeople seek professional advice on parts of their business, but don’t expect to be told how to profit.
options: True
False
So asking others to earn investment profits for you has an element of naivety
He says businesspeople should expect their advisers to show them how to profit
He says business advice is useless, so investors should never pay for any of it

questions.why: That is why asking others to make investment profits for you has an element of naivety. There is no true counterpart in ordinary business.

questions.q: Graham says the well-established investment counsel firms promise their clients brilliant results.
questions.why: They are modest: careful, conservative and competent. Their aim is to conserve capital and produce an acceptable income.

questions.q: Graham thinks the chief value of good investment counsel may be shielding clients from costly mistakes.
options: True
False
Conserving capital and a fair income come first; avoiding mistakes is the core
Their chief value lies in picking the few shares that will beat the market
Their chief value lies in forecasting where the whole market will move next

questions.why: Anything beyond conserving principal and a fair income they treat as extra service. That is as much as the defensive investor can rightly expect.

questions.q: Graham regards the financial services’ stock-market forecasts as their most valuable product.
questions.why: He says they have no real significance, except for what they reveal about human nature. Their business data and forecasts are far more useful.

questions.q: Graham criticises financial services for recommending a share when its near-term prospects look good, whatever its price.
options: True
False
That habit keeps them from judging value against long-term earning power
He says near-term prospects are the best guide to a share, whatever its price
He criticises them for ignoring prospects and looking at price and nothing else

questions.why: That superficial principle keeps them from the real work: judging whether the share is over- or undervalued against its long-term earning power.

questions.q: Graham says advice from relatives and friends is usually dependable, since much good advice is given free.
options: True
False
He warns that much bad advice is given free, by friends and relatives alike
He says friends’ advice is dependable, because they have no fees of their own to earn
He says relatives’ advice is dependable, but only if they happen to work in finance

questions.why: The trap reverses his line: “Much bad advice is given free.” Choosing lay advisers is almost as hard as choosing securities unaided.

questions.q: Zweig suggests shopping for another adviser if fees would take more than about 1% of your assets a year.
questions.why: Costs are predictable and compound against you. High fees are a red flag, along with refusing to show regulatory filings.

questions.q: Graham says investors who get advice without paying for it specifically are entitled to expect better-than-average results.
options: True
False
In most cases they are not entitled to, and shouldn’t expect, better than average
He says free advice is usually better, since it carries no motive to sell
He says anyone with a paid adviser should expect to beat the market over time

questions.why: He says the reverse: in most cases they are not entitled to, and should not expect, better than average results.

questions.q: What is Graham’s basic thesis for investors who rely chiefly on others’ advice?
options: Keep to standard, conservative investments, or know the adviser unusually well
Follow whichever adviser has the best record over the most recent few years
Use several advisers at once and average their picks to spread the risk of error
Trust advisers fully, since they are trained professionals bound by rules
questions.why: In an ordinary business relationship, you can accept less conventional ideas only once you are competent to judge them yourself.

questions.q: Why does Graham think brokerage houses have found it hard to operate on a truly professional basis?
options: Wall Street lived on speculation, so acting professionally would have shrunk their own business
Brokers are not allowed to give investment advice, only to carry out the orders their clients give
Their analysts are poorly trained, and most firms can’t afford to hire better-qualified people
Commissions are fixed by law, which leaves brokers no room to charge for proper advice
questions.why: Speculators as a class lose money, yet they are the most profitable customers. A true profession would steer them away from that business.

questions.q: How should a genuine investor deal with a stockbroker, according to Graham?
options: Make clear, in word and deed, that he wants nothing resembling a market tip
Ask the broker for his best short-term ideas, then check them against the news
Let the broker trade freely on his behalf, since the broker knows the market
Avoid speaking to brokers at all and place every order through a website
questions.why: Once the broker understands he has a real investor on his hands, Graham says, he will respect that and cooperate.

questions.q: Why does Graham say brokerage analysts are greatly handicapped?
options: They are expected to be market forecasters, so “is it sound?” really means “will it rise soon?”
They lack access to company accounts, so they must rely on what management chooses to say
They are paid too little to do thorough work, so their reports are rushed and shallow
Regulations stop them from forming firm opinions about any of the shares their firms are selling
questions.why: Analysing with one eye on the ticker is not conducive to sound conclusions. Ask them value questions and you get better answers.

questions.q: When an individual buys new issues from an underwriter, where does Graham say the buyer’s protection mainly lies?
options: In the scruples and ethics of the selling firm, so he must bring his own independent judgment
In government guarantees on new issues, which refund buyers if the company fails early
In the offer price, which is set below fair value so that buyers make an early profit
In his right to return the shares to the underwriter within a year if their price falls back
questions.why: The relationship is that of salesman to buyer, and the individual is often inexperienced and hoping for a quick profit.

questions.q: Which three systems does Zweig say a good adviser should put in place with you?
options: A financial plan, an investment policy statement and an asset-allocation plan
A trading system, a stop-loss rule for every share and a list of hot tips
A market forecast, a sector-rotation plan and a sensible limit on borrowing
A tax shelter, an offshore account and a place in a private hedge fund
questions.why: These protect you from your own worst impulses. They should be built together with you, not imposed.

questions.q: How should a defensive investor, unable to judge recommendations himself, use a broker’s analyst?
options: Say clearly what kind of securities he wants, and ask the analyst to confirm the prices are conservative
Ask for the analyst’s highest-growth picks, since the analyst is paid to find the winners for him
Let the analyst choose whatever he likes, since he can’t judge the recommendations himself
Avoid analysts altogether and buy the new issues his broker offers, since the underwriters have vetted them
questions.why: High-grade bonds and leading companies at prices that are not high are easy for any reputable analyst to list and check.

questions.q: An adviser charges 1.5% a year on a R500,000 portfolio and puts you in funds charging another 1%. What is your annual cost, and how does it compare with Zweig’s guide?
options: R12,500 (2.5%): well above his 1% guide, so shop around
R7,500 (1.5%): acceptable, since fund fees don’t count
R5,000 (1%): exactly at his guide, so nothing to change
R2,500 (0.5%): cheap for a portfolio of that size and type
questions.why: 1.5% + 1% = 2.5%, which is R12,500 a year. Fees are one of the few things you can control, and they compound against you.

questions.q: An adviser says: “It’s guaranteed, there’s no downside, and you need to hurry.” What should you do?
options: Treat these as warning signs, check his record with the regulator, and walk away if anything is wrong
Act quickly so that you don’t miss out, since good opportunities rarely stay open for long
Invest a small amount first to test him, then add more once the promised returns arrive
Ask for an even higher guaranteed return in writing, since a guarantee means he carries all the risk
questions.why: “Guaranteed”, “no downside” and “hurry” are classic red-flag phrases. Con artists depend on talking you into trusting them and out of checking them.

questions.q: An adviser tells you he can reliably earn 25% a year on your money. What does Zweig’s checklist say?
options: Anything over about 8% to 10% a year is unrealistic; be very sceptical
Reasonable for a skilled adviser with a strong record and good research
Only possible in bond funds, where returns are fixed in advance each year
Fine, as long as he has a proprietary computer model behind his picks
questions.why: He asks advisers what average return they think is feasible, and treats an answer above 8% to 10% as unrealistic.

questions.q: Before hiring a financial adviser in South Africa, which step best applies Zweig’s “trust, then verify”?
options: Check the FSCA register to confirm the adviser is licensed, and look for any debarments or complaints
Rely on the testimonials on the adviser’s own website, which come from satisfied clients
Choose whichever adviser promises the highest returns, since competition keeps them honest
Ask the adviser to vouch for himself in writing, and keep his letter safely on file in case of trouble
questions.why: Zweig urges checking regulators’ records and complaints, never relying on the adviser’s word. The Financial Sector Conduct Authority keeps the South African register.

questions.q: You ask a prospective adviser, “What do you do when an investment does poorly for a whole year?” Which answer should rule them out?
options: “Sell it.”
“Re-examine whether the business has changed.”
“Check whether its style is temporarily out of favour.”
“Review it against our written plan.”
questions.why: Zweig says any adviser who simply answers “sell” is not worth hiring. That is selling low on price alone.

questions.q: A Member has learned enough to judge investments and wants to act as an enterprising investor alongside an adviser. How should they work together, according to Graham?
options: Have every recommendation explained and pass their own judgment on it
Follow all of the adviser’s advice without question, since that is what he is paid for
Ignore the adviser and trade on instinct once they feel confident enough
Act only on the tips that the adviser marks as urgent or time-sensitive
questions.why: Only where an adviser’s integrity and competence are thoroughly proven should anyone act without understanding and approving the decision.

questions.q: An adviser promises to “beat the market by 5% a year”, charges 2.5% a year and urges you to sign today. What is the intelligent response?
options: Walk away: promises to beat the market and pressure to act fast are warning signs
Sign: a 5% yearly edge more than covers a 2.5% fee, so you still come out ahead
Sign for half your money, and move the rest once the first results come in
A good adviser explains costs, starts from your goals and keeps you to your plan
Advisers who promise a return are legally bound to deliver it, so it’s low-risk
Testing an adviser with part of your money removes the risk of a bad choice

questions.why: Graham expected advisers to give sound, conservative guidance, not brilliant results. Zweig adds that a good adviser’s real value is keeping you to your plan.
questions.src: Chapter 10: The investor and his advisers

questions.q: Sort each sign: good or worrying in a financial adviser?

items.t: Explains every fee clearly, in writing
Asks about your goals and circumstances before recommending anything
Promises returns above the market
Encourages frequent trading
Is paid a fee by you, not commissions on products
Urges you to act today before it’s too late

questions.why: Look for transparency and a focus on your needs; avoid promises and pressure.

questions.q: Graham’s chief test of a corporate bond’s safety is how many times its interest has been covered by past earnings.
questions.why: Coverage is the main criterion. For preference shares, bond interest and preference dividends are combined.

questions.q: Graham’s minimum for an investment-grade industrial bond is interest covered three times before tax, on a seven-year average.
questions.why: The trap is the number. He asks for seven times on the seven-year average, or five times in the poorest year.

questions.q: Graham says asset values, rather than earning power, are the main protection for most bonds.
options: True
False
Safety lies in earning power: if that fails, the assets lose most of their value
He says assets are the main protection, and that earnings matter much less
He says neither matters much, provided the bond carries a high enough coupon rate

questions.why: Experience shows safety lies in earning power; if that fails, assets lose most of their value. Assets still matter for utilities, property companies and investment companies.

questions.q: Graham’s coverage test for preference shares counts the preference dividends twice, because they are not tax-deductible.
options: True
False
Interest is paid before tax, preference dividends after; doubling allows for it
Preference dividends are counted twice because they are paid twice a year
Counting them twice is a penalty for their weaker legal claim, not a tax matter

questions.why: Interest is deducted before tax, but preference dividends come from after-tax profits. Doubling them roughly allows for the difference.

questions.q: Graham warns that the more a valuation rests on the future rather than the past, the more exposed it is to error.
options: True
False
Analysts are most precise just where precision is least reliable, as with growth
Valuations based on the future are safer, because the past no longer applies
He says all valuations are equally reliable as long as the arithmetic is right

questions.why: His paradox: analysts become most mathematical exactly where exact treatment is least reliable, as with high-multiple growth shares.

questions.q: Graham finds forecasts for individual companies more dependable than estimates made for a whole group of companies.
options: True
False
The reverse: estimates for a group are far more dependable, so funds diversify
He finds company forecasts better, because analysts know each company in detail
He finds neither dependable, so he relies on dividend yields and nothing else

questions.why: The reverse: group estimates are much more dependable. That is why funds diversify widely.

questions.q: Graham’s simplified formula for growth shares is: value = current normal earnings × (8.5 + 2 × the expected annual growth rate).
questions.why: The growth rate should be the one expected over the next seven to ten years. He offers it as a rough guide, not a precise tool.

questions.q: Graham says good management should be added as a separate bullish factor, on top of a company’s record and prospects.
options: True
False
Good management already shows in the record; counting it again overvalues the share
He agrees: good management deserves its own premium of about a third of value
He says management makes no difference to value, in every company and every case

questions.why: Good management already shows in the record and the forecasts; counting it again leads to overvaluation. It matters most where a recent change has not yet reached the figures.

questions.q: Chemical companies the market rated highly in 1963 showed almost no earnings growth by 1970, while lower-rated oil companies did better.
questions.why: Graham’s example of market multipliers built on past performance proving “as likely to be wrong as right”.

questions.q: Why does Graham call funds’ wide diversification a “pragmatic repudiation” of Wall Street’s faith in selectivity?
options: No one can tell in advance which individual forecasts are reliable, so funds spread their bets
Diversification is required by law for funds, whatever the managers believe about selection
Selective funds charge more, so wide diversification became a way to compete on cost
Concentrated portfolios can’t be audited properly, so funds are forced to hold a great many shares
questions.why: It would be better to concentrate on the one share you know will do best, but that cannot be done dependably.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the factors Graham says shape a share’s capitalisation rate (its multiplier)?
options: Recent share-price momentum
General long-term prospects
Financial strength and capital structure
Dividend record
questions.why: His five are long-term prospects, management, financial strength and capital structure, dividend record, and the current dividend rate.

questions.q: Why does Graham say valuations of high-growth shares must build in a margin of safety?
options: Assuming growth above about 8% a year forever gives an infinite value, so the valuer must assume less
Growth companies seldom pay dividends, so the valuer has no income stream to discount at all
Accountants overstate growth companies’ earnings, so the reported figures must be cut back first
Interest rates are assumed to stay fixed for decades, so any error in the growth rate goes unnoticed
questions.why: The arithmetic breaks down at high growth rates. The buyer should still earn his target if growth falls well short of projections.

questions.q: What is Graham’s suggested two-part appraisal process?
options: First a value based on past performance continuing, then an adjustment for expected new conditions
First a forecast of the whole market, then a forecast of the industry the company belongs to
First the dividend yield compared with bonds, then the trend in the share price over a year
First interviews with management about their plans, then a price target based on what they say next
questions.why: Showing both the original and the adjusted values, with reasons, builds a record of experience, as in medicine.

questions.q: Why do higher interest rates lower the value of a given stream of future earnings?
options: Future rands are worth less today when money grows faster elsewhere, and bonds become a stronger rival
Higher rates always cut companies’ sales, because customers spend less when they borrow less
Companies must pay out all their earnings as dividends when rates rise, leaving nothing to reinvest
Rates have no real effect on share values; only the reported earnings themselves matter
questions.why: At higher rates, less money set aside today grows to the same future sum, so a fixed future stream is worth less now.

questions.q: What does Graham think of most brokerage industry studies?
options: They mostly cover facts the public already knows and the market has largely priced in
They are the most reliable guide to future profits, since analysts visit every company
They are too technical for ordinary investors to use, though professionals rely on them
They correctly predict which industries will fall, but few investors act on their warnings
questions.why: Rarely does a study show convincingly that a popular industry is heading for a fall, or an unpopular one is due to prosper.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of Zweig’s warning signs when studying a company?
options: A wide competitive “moat”
Making two or three or more acquisitions a year
Relying on borrowing or share issues for cash year after year
Depending on one customer for most revenue
questions.why: A moat (brand, scale, a unique asset or resistance to substitution) is a positive sign. The others are serial acquirers, OPM (other people’s money) addicts and one-customer firms.

questions.q: How does Zweig define Buffett’s “owner earnings”?
options: Net income plus depreciation and amortisation, minus normal capital spending
Revenue minus the cost of sales, before any overheads, interest or tax
Dividends paid plus share buybacks, the cash actually returned to owners
EBITDA before any one-off charges, adjusted upwards for the cost of share options
questions.why: It asks how much cash you would have in your pocket at year-end if you owned the whole business. Zweig also subtracts option costs, “one-off” charges and pension income.

questions.q: Using Graham’s growth formula, what is a share worth if normal earnings per share are R5 and expected growth is 6% a year?
A share trades at R150 with normal earnings of R5. By Graham’s formula, what annual growth rate is the market implying?
options: About 10.75%
About 15%
About 30%
About 6%
questions.why: Multiplier = 150 ÷ 5 = 30. Then 30 = 8.5 + 2g, so g = 10.75%. Graham ran this reverse calculation for the Dow and leading shares.

questions.q: A company earning R1 a share is expected to grow 15% a year for 15 years (to about R8.14) and trade at 35 times earnings. If growth comes in at 14% instead (about R7.14) and the market cuts the multiple to 20, roughly where does the price end up?
options: About R143, half of the R285 expected
About R250, slightly below the R285 expected
About R285, unchanged from what was expected
About R200, about a third below the R285
questions.why: R8.14 × 35 ≈ R285, but R7.14 × 20 ≈ R143. A one-point miss in growth halves the outcome: precise-looking projections are fragile.

questions.q: An industrial company’s pre-tax earnings available for fixed charges averaged R70m over seven years (R55m in the worst year). Its fixed charges are R12m. Does its bond meet Graham’s standard?
options: No: about 5.8 times on average (needs 7) and about 4.6 in the worst year (needs 5)
Yes: coverage above 5 times on average is enough for an industrial company’s bond
Yes: it passes the poorest-year test, and passing either test is enough
No: an industrial company’s bond needs 10 times coverage on average
questions.why: R70m ÷ R12m ≈ 5.8 and R55m ÷ R12m ≈ 4.6. Meeting either test would suffice, but it fails both.

questions.q: Graham’s alternative bond test for an industrial company is pre-tax earnings of at least 33% of the debt’s principal. A company with R300m of debt earns R90m before interest and tax. Does it pass?
options: No: it earns 30%, just below 33%
Yes: it earns 30%, above 25%
Yes: earnings exceed a quarter of debt
No: it would need 100%
questions.why: R90m ÷ R300m = 30%. Graham proposed this test because high interest rates made coverage ratios harder to meet. It is 20% for utilities and 25% for railways.

questions.q: A company pays out about two-thirds of its earnings. Expected earnings are R3 a share and the dividend R2. Valued at 12 times earnings, what multiple of the dividend gives the same value?
options: 18 times
12 times
8 times
24 times
questions.why: 12 × R3 = R36, and R36 ÷ R2 = 18. With a standard payout, valuing on earnings or on dividends gives about the same answer.

questions.q: A company’s cash from operations has been negative for five years, while cash from financing (new debt and shares) has been strongly positive. What is Zweig’s reading?
options: It depends on other people’s money because its business does not generate cash; be wary
It is investing heavily for growth, which is a good sign for long-term shareholders
It is a cash-rich company returning money to shareholders through dividends and buybacks
Cash flows don’t matter as long as reported earnings keep rising year after year
questions.why: Zweig’s “OPM addict”: a sick company can look as if it is growing on borrowed money. Global Crossing and WorldCom showed how that ends.

questions.q: A company has 4.5 billion shares in issue and options outstanding on another 657 million. Roughly how much would its future earnings be diluted if all options were exercised?
options: About 15%
About 1.5%
About 50%
About 6.6%
questions.why: 657m ÷ 4,500m ≈ 14.6%. Zweig’s point: factor in the “option overhang” whenever you estimate future value per share.

questions.q: A company’s long-term debt (including preference shares) is R600m out of total capital of R1,000m. How does that compare with Zweig’s guideline?
options: Too high: he suggests long-term debt below 50% of total capital
Fine: up to 75% of total capital is acceptable for most companies
Too low: companies should borrow more to raise their return on equity
Debt levels don’t matter as long as earnings are rising each year
questions.why: 60% exceeds his general guide of under 50%. He also suggests checking whether the debt is fixed- or variable-rate.

questions.q: A company’s normal earnings are {e|R2} a share and you expect {g|0}% yearly growth over the next seven to ten years. What value does Graham’s simple growth formula give?

errs.why: The growth rate counts twice: 8.5 plus 2 × g.
Add twice the expected growth rate to 8.5.

questions.why: Graham offered the formula to show what growth expectations a price implies, not as a precise valuation: the higher the growth assumed, the less reliable it is.
questions.src: Chapter 11: Capitalisation rates for growth stocks

questions.q: An analyst projects 20% yearly growth for a decade and values a share at 40 times earnings. What would Graham say?
options: Be sceptical: the more a value rests on distant growth, the more it can be wrong
Accept it: forecasting a decade is the analyst’s job, and they have the data
Raise it: shares growing 20% a year usually deserve 60 times earnings or more
High growth rarely lasts, and a price that depends on it leaves no room for error
Analysts are paid to be optimistic, so their growth figures should always be halved
The higher the growth rate, the more precise the valuation formula becomes

questions.why: Graham: the more a valuation depends on the future rather than past performance, the more it is exposed to miscalculation and serious error.
questions.src: Chapter 11: Security analysis for the lay investor

questions.q: Graham’s first piece of advice in this chapter is: don’t take a single year’s earnings seriously.
options: True
False
One year can mislead; he also warns of booby traps in the per-share figures
He says the latest year is the best guide to what a company will go on to earn
He says single years matter more than averages for the fast-growing companies

questions.why: His second, in case you ignore the first, is to watch for booby traps in the per-share figures.

questions.q: ALCOA’s 1970 annual report gave four different figures for earnings per share.
questions.why: Primary, after special charges, fully diluted before charges and fully diluted after charges: $5.20, $4.32, $5.01 and $4.19.

questions.q: Graham approved of ALCOA charging the expected costs of future closures against 1970, because it gave a cleaner picture of its earnings.
options: True
False
Losses charged in advance belong to no year, and make later years look better
He approved, because it put all of the bad news into one place for the reader
He approved of it, as long as the charges were reversed in the following years

questions.why: He calls it “neat work” but possibly misleading. Losses charged in advance belong to no year at all, and later years look better for it.

questions.q: Graham says special charges and credits should be included when averaging a company’s earnings over many years.
options: True
False
They are part of its history; an average over seven to ten years absorbs them
They should be left out completely, because they will never happen again
They should be counted twice, so that the estimate errs on the side of caution

questions.why: Most such gains and losses are part of the company’s operating history. Averaging over seven to ten years absorbs them sensibly.

questions.q: To measure growth, Graham suggests comparing the average of the last three years’ earnings with the same average ten years earlier.
questions.why: Averages at both ends smooth out a single good or bad year that could distort the growth rate.

questions.q: Graham thought a 21-cent difference in how Dow Chemical classified one 1969 item mattered greatly to its value.
questions.why: He found the fuss rather absurd: tiny differences in one year’s results have no real bearing on long-term average earnings or value.

questions.q: Graham concludes that share valuations are really dependable only in exceptional cases.
options: True
False
So most investors should simply make sure they get good value for the price
So investors should rely on analysts’ precise valuations of each company instead
So valuations are dependable in most cases, as long as there is enough data

questions.why: So, for most investors, it is best to make sure they get good value for the price they pay, and leave it there.

questions.q: Zweig recommends “pro forma” earnings as the truest picture of a company’s results.
options: True
False
Pro forma shows how it might have done had it not done as badly: ignore it
He says they are the truest picture, because they strip out one-off items
He recommends them, but only for companies that have recently made acquisitions

questions.why: He says pro forma figures show how well a company might have done if it hadn’t done as badly as it did. The only thing to do with them is ignore them.

questions.q: Zweig suggests reading a company’s annual report from the back towards the front.
questions.why: Anything the company would rather you didn’t find is buried in the back, especially in the notes to the financial statements.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the factors Graham says can distort comparisons of earnings per share?
options: The proportion of earnings paid out as dividends
Dilution from convertible securities and warrants
Lower tax charges because of past losses
Special charges kept out of the per-share figures
questions.why: His list also includes changes in depreciation method, the treatment of research costs, and FIFO versus LIFO inventory accounting.

questions.q: Why does Graham suspect so many companies piled special charges into 1970?
options: Investors had already written 1970 off, so dumping costs there made later years look better
New accounting rules took effect in 1970 that required the charges to be booked in that year
1970 was a record-profit year that could absorb the charges without any visible harm
Auditors forced every company to clean house after the scandals of the late 1960s
questions.why: Charging as much as possible to a forgotten bad year starts the next ones with a slate specially prepared to show pleasing growth.

questions.q: A big write-off lets a company earn future profits without paying tax for several years. How does Graham suggest valuing it?
options: Value it on earnings with full normal tax, then add a bonus for the temporary tax exemption
Value it on the untaxed earnings as if the exemption were permanent, since profits are real
Ignore the tax saving entirely, since it comes from past losses rather than from the business
Value it only on its assets, since the earnings are distorted until the tax credit runs out
questions.why: The exemption is real but temporary, so it deserves a one-off bonus, not a permanently higher earnings base. Watch for dilution too.

questions.q: ALCOA grew about as fast as Sears from 1958 to 1970, yet sold at about 11½ times earnings against Sears at 27. What does Graham see as the likely decisive reason?
options: ALCOA’s return on its capital had been only average or less
ALCOA paid no dividends, while Sears paid a generous one
ALCOA had far more shares in issue, which held down its price
Sears was in the Dow and ALCOA was not, so funds favoured it
questions.why: High multipliers have lasted only for companies that keep better-than-average profitability on their capital.

questions.q: Why should earnings per share be reduced (“diluted”) for convertible bonds and warrants?
options: They will be exercised whenever that pays the holders, spreading earnings over more shares
They are already counted as shares in issue, so earnings must be divided by the total
They reduce sales, because converting holders receive part of the company’s revenue
Accountants require it for banks, which issue convertibles more often than other firms
questions.why: In some cases, allowing for conversion rights and warrants can cut apparent earnings by half or more.

questions.q: Global Crossing began treating much of its network construction spending as capital assets instead of expenses. What was the effect?
options: Reported profits rose and assets grew, though cash was still pouring out
Its reported profits fell sharply because of the larger depreciation charges
It paid more tax, since the spending could no longer be deducted as an expense
Nothing changed in its reported results; only the notes to the accounts
questions.why: Capitalising normal operating costs moves them off the income statement. Zweig says to understand what a company capitalises, and why.

questions.q: According to Zweig, when should income from a company’s pension plan make you cautious?
options: When it is more than about 5% of net income, or the assumed return on plan assets is high or rising
Whenever a company has a pension plan at all, since every plan is a hidden liability for shareholders
Only if the plan is invested mainly in bonds, which can’t earn the returns that companies assume
Never: pension income is real profit that belongs to shareholders like any other income
questions.why: SBC raised its assumed return from 8.5% to 9.5%, booking $1.4 billion of pension “income” in a year when its plan actually lost money.

questions.q: Zweig notes that the biggest risk in owning growth shares is not that growth stops. What is it?
options: Merely that growth slows, which the market punishes hard
That dividends are cut to fund the next stage of growth
That the founding management team leaves the company
That the share is dropped from a major index, forcing funds to sell
questions.why: Great expectations lead to great disappointments. Over the long run, a slowdown is not just a risk but a near certainty.

questions.q: A share trades at R62. Its latest quarterly “primary” EPS is R1.58, but only R0.70 after special charges. Annualising each, what P/E ratios result?
options: About 10 times on primary earnings, about 22 times after charges
About 39 times on primary earnings, about 89 times after charges
About 10 times either way, since special charges are excluded
About 22 times on primary earnings, about 10 times after charges
questions.why: R1.58 × 4 = R6.32, and R62 ÷ R6.32 ≈ 9.8. R0.70 × 4 = R2.80, and R62 ÷ R2.80 ≈ 22. Which earnings you trust changes everything.

questions.q: A company’s average earnings over the last three years are R5.00 a share; the same average ten years earlier was R2.00. Roughly what annual compound growth rate is that?
options: About 9.6%
About 15%
About 25%
About 6%
questions.why: R5 ÷ R2 = 2.5 over ten years, and 2.5^(1/10) ≈ 1.096. That is Graham’s three-year-average method.

questions.q: A company earns R10m with 5m shares in issue. Convertible bonds would add 1m shares on conversion and save R0.5m of after-tax interest. What is fully diluted EPS?
questions.why: (R10m + R0.5m) ÷ 6m = R1.75, against R2.00 undiluted. The interest saved goes back into earnings, but the share count rises.

questions.q: A company’s net income is R7.2bn, of which R1.4bn came from its pension plan. By Zweig’s test, should this concern you?
options: Yes: pension income is about 19% of net income, far above his 5% flag
No: pension income is real profit, so its size doesn’t matter at all
No: at about 19% it is still below his limit of 25% of net income
Only if the share price falls after the next set of results is out
questions.why: R1.4bn ÷ R7.2bn ≈ 19%. Ask whether you would be comfortable with the remaining earnings if those pension gains disappeared.

questions.q: A company’s EPS over seven years was R3, R4, −R1 (a special write-off), R5, R4, R6 and R7. What is its seven-year average, treated Graham’s way?
options: About R4.83
questions.why: Include the write-off: (3 + 4 − 1 + 5 + 4 + 6 + 7) ÷ 7 = R4.00. Dropping the loss and averaging the other six (R4.83) is the trap.

questions.q: A company has booked “one-off” restructuring charges in six of the last seven years, and excludes them from its headline earnings. How should you treat them?
options: As normal, recurring costs of the business: deduct them when judging earnings
As truly one-off events, so ignore them when judging the company’s earnings
As a sign of strong management that is willing to clean up the business
As extra profit for future years, since the costs have already been written off
questions.why: Zweig’s Micron example: “non-recurring” write-downs that recur every quarter have become a chronic condition. Graham would include them in the average.

questions.q: A directory publisher starts booking a whole year’s advertising revenue on publication day, though advertisers pay monthly. What does Zweig make of a change like this?
options: Aggressive revenue recognition, often a sign of deeper problems; investigate further
Prudent accounting, since booking revenue early lowers the profit reported later
Irrelevant, since the total revenue over the year comes out the same either way
A sign of rising demand, since advertisers are now committing for a whole year in advance
questions.why: Qwest did this in 1999, adding about a fifth of that year’s profit. Later restatements showed revenues overstated by $2.2 billion.

questions.q: Net income is {ni|R0m} on {sh|0m} shares. Convertible bonds would add {cv|0m} shares and save {it|R0m} of after-tax interest. What is fully diluted EPS?

errs.why: Add back the interest saved when the bonds convert.
That is basic EPS; count the new shares.

questions.why: If the bonds convert, their interest is no longer paid, but there are more shares. Graham urges investors to look at diluted figures.

questions.q: A company reports a “one-off” restructuring charge almost every year and asks investors to ignore it. How should you treat it?
options: As a recurring cost: deduct it, averaged over the years, from earnings
Ignore it, as management asks, since it doesn’t reflect the core business
Add it back to earnings, since a restructuring charge uses no cash
Charges that recur are part of the cost of doing business, whatever they are called
Accounting standards require restructuring costs to be shown below operating profit
Restructuring always pays for itself within a few years, so it nets to zero

questions.why: Graham’s ALCOA example: special charges kept outside “earnings before special items” can make a company look far more profitable than it is.
questions.src: Chapter 12: Things to consider about per-share earnings

questions.q: Graham found that the four companies’ P/E ratios varied far more than their operating performance or financial condition did.
options: True
False
ELTRA and Emhart sold at 10–12 times earnings, Emerson and Emery at 33 and 45
The P/E ratios were all similar, while the companies’ performance varied widely
Both the P/E ratios and performance varied, and by roughly the same amount

questions.why: ELTRA and Emhart sold at about 10 and 12 times earnings; Emerson and Emery at 33 and 45, though all four performed well.

questions.q: Graham thought Emery Air Freight’s price of more than 60 times recent earnings was justified for the careful investor.
options: True
False
Perhaps for someone with deep study and firm conclusions, not the careful investor
He thought it fully justified, because air freight looked set to grow for ever
He thought it justified, because Emery carried no debt and paid a rising dividend

questions.why: Maybe for someone with an in-depth study and exceptionally firm conclusions, he says, but not for the careful investor wary of Wall Street’s overenthusiasm.

questions.q: Graham measures stability by the largest fall in EPS in any of the past ten years, compared with the average of the three years before it.
questions.why: No decline at all means 100% stability. ELTRA and Emhart each fell only about 8% in the poor year of 1970.

questions.q: Graham’s standard for a manufacturing company is at least R2 of current assets for every R1 of current liabilities.
questions.why: The three manufacturers met it. Emery, a service business with a fine record, had a lower ratio but could easily raise cash.

questions.q: ELTRA and Emhart both met Graham’s seven statistical requirements for a defensive investor’s portfolio.
questions.why: Both sold close to book value with satisfactory returns on capital, stability and growth: reasonably protected investments.

questions.q: Graham would have advised holders of Emerson and Emery to switch at once into ELTRA and Emhart, expecting them to do better within months.
options: True
False
There was no reason to expect quick gains; the switch suits those who prefer value
He promised that the switch would beat the market within a matter of months
He advised holders never to switch between shares, whatever their relative prices

questions.why: There was no reason to expect quick outperformance, since popular shares can keep their momentum. The switch makes sense only for someone who prefers value to glamour.

questions.q: Zweig argues that a 2-for-1 share split makes shareholders richer, since they now own twice as many shares.
options: True
False
A split doubles the shares and halves the price: two nickels make one dime
He says splits add value by making the shares more affordable to small investors
He says splits add value because they always come before higher dividends

questions.why: Two nickels are not worth more than one dime. A split doubles the shares and halves the price, so the value is unchanged.

questions.q: Two of Graham’s seven tests are a price of no more than 1.5 times net asset value and no more than 15 times average earnings of the past three years.
questions.why: These are his price limits for the defensive investor. The others cover size, finances, dividends, earnings stability and growth.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of Graham’s seven requirements for the defensive investor?
options: A strong share-price trend over the past year
No earnings deficit in the past ten years
Dividends paid for at least the past 20 years
Ten-year growth in EPS of at least one-third
questions.why: Price momentum is for speculators. His tests concern size, finances, dividends, earnings stability, growth and the price paid.

questions.q: Why does Graham suggest that Emery’s spectacular past growth may mean less for its future?
options: It began from a very small base, and high growth is much harder once profits are large
Its accounts were unreliable, so the reported growth may never have happened at all
It paid no dividends, so shareholders saw none of the growth in their own pockets
Air freight was a shrinking industry, so the company’s growth was bound to reverse soon
questions.why: Net earnings were only $570,000 in 1958. Size itself makes a repeat performance more difficult.

questions.q: What point does Graham make by comparing Emerson Electric with Zenith Radio?
options: High valuations carry high risks: Zenith had a brilliant record too, until its profits halved and its share slumped
Emerson would certainly fail as Zenith did, because the two companies operated in the same market for the same customers
Radio and electronics companies are poor investments, since their products go out of date so quickly
Large companies hardly ever lose much of their value, so Emerson’s size made it far safer than Zenith had been
questions.why: Zenith also reached about $1.7 billion in market value. Then its profits halved and its share fell from 89 to 22½.

questions.q: Analysts may prefer Emerson and Emery for their better “market action” and faster recent growth. How does Graham treat these two reasons?
options: Market action is not a valid reason for a conservative investor; faster growth is valid only within limits
Both are excellent reasons, since price momentum and fast growth tend to go on together for years
Both are irrelevant, since a conservative investor should look only at assets and dividends
Market action is a valid reason, since prices reflect what insiders know, but growth is never a reason
questions.why: Price momentum is “something for the speculators to play around with”. Growth counts, but not at any price.

questions.q: What did Zweig find when he removed EMC’s 1999 acquisition of Data General from its revenue?
options: Its existing business grew only about 3.6%, almost nothing
Its growth was even faster than the 24% it had reported
It had no revenue from data storage at all before the deal
Its profits doubled, even though its revenue barely moved
questions.why: Revenue appeared to jump 24%, but most came from the purchase. At 103 times earnings, the market was paying for growth that wasn’t there.

questions.q: Graham warned that today’s investor “is so concerned with anticipating the future that he is already paying handsomely for it in advance”. What follows?
options: Even if the forecast comes true, he may make no profit, and if it falls short he may suffer a serious loss
Accurate forecasts bring large profits, so the investor should spend more effort on forecasting
Forecasting is unnecessary, because the market price already tells him everything he needs
Paying for growth in advance is usually cheap, since the growth arrives sooner than people expect it to
questions.why: When the price already assumes the good future, getting the future right is not enough. This is the core risk of glamour shares.

questions.q: A share trades at R66 and its book value per share is R10.34. What is its price-to-book ratio, and does it pass Graham’s 1.5-times test?
options: About 6.4 times: it fails
About 1.5 times: it just passes
About 0.16 times: it passes
About 3 times: it fails
questions.why: R66 ÷ R10.34 ≈ 6.4. That was Emerson Electric in 1970, far above Graham’s limit.

questions.q: A company earns R2.70 a share on a book value of R27.05 a share. What is its return on book value?
options: About 10%
About 27%
About 2.7%
About 1%
questions.why: R2.70 ÷ R27.05 ≈ 10%. That was ELTRA: satisfactory, but well below Emerson’s 22% and Emery’s 34.5%.

questions.q: A share trades at R33 with net asset value of R27 a share and three-year average EPS of R2.81. Does it pass both of Graham’s price tests?
options: Yes: about 1.2 times net assets and about 11.7 times earnings
No: at about 1.2 times net assets it fails the asset test
No: at about 11.7 times earnings it fails the earnings test
No: it fails both the asset test and the earnings test
questions.why: R33 ÷ R27 ≈ 1.22 (limit 1.5) and R33 ÷ R2.81 ≈ 11.7 (limit 15). This is roughly Emhart at the end of 1970.

questions.q: A company’s average EPS is now R1.30, against R1.00 ten years ago. Does it meet Graham’s ten-year growth test?
options: No: 30% is short of the required one-third
Yes: any growth over ten years is enough
Yes: 30% is close enough to one-third
No: it needs 100% growth over ten years
questions.why: The test asks for at least a 33⅓% increase in per-share earnings over ten years, measured with three-year averages at each end.

questions.q: A company has current assets of R20.4m and current liabilities of R11.8m. How does its current ratio compare with Graham’s standard for a manufacturer?
options: About 1.7 to 1, below the 2-to-1 standard
About 2.7 to 1, comfortably above the standard
Exactly 2 to 1, which meets the standard
About 0.6 to 1, far below the standard
questions.why: R20.4m ÷ R11.8m ≈ 1.73. That was Emery Air Freight, which Graham excused as a different kind of business.

questions.q: You own 100 shares at R100 each. The company splits its shares 2-for-1. What do you own afterwards?
options: 200 shares at about R50: the same R10,000
200 shares at R100: R20,000
100 shares at R200
200 shares at R60, because splits lift prices
questions.why: A split changes the number of slices, not the size of the cake. Zweig likens it to swapping a dime for two nickels.

questions.q: A company starts the year with R156m in cash, raises R1.3bn in new financing, and ends the year with R1.0bn. Roughly how much cash did its business consume?
options: About R456m
About R1.0bn
About R156m
Nothing: cash rose
questions.why: R156m + R1,300m − R1,000m ≈ R456m. That was Exodus in 1999: rising cash can hide a business devouring money.

questions.q: Using Graham’s growth formula from Chapter 11 (multiplier = 8.5 + 2 × growth), what annual growth does a P/E of 45 imply?
options: About 18%
About 45%
About 10%
About 27%
questions.why: 45 = 8.5 + 2g gives g ≈ 18.25% a year for seven to ten years: a demanding rate to sustain from a large base.

questions.q: Two companies have grown earnings at the same rate. One trades at 40 times earnings, the other at 12. For a new buyer, which carries more risk?
options: The one at 40 times
The one at 12 times
They carry the same risk
A high price needs the growth to continue; any disappointment cuts earnings and the multiple
A cheap share is usually cheap for a good reason, so the company at 12 times is the bigger risk
Both have grown at the same rate, so the market has priced the same risk into each

questions.why: Graham’s comparison of four companies shows the market paying heavily for growth that may not last, and how far such prices can fall.
questions.src: Chapter 13: A comparison of four listed companies

questions.q: Sort each feature: does it point to a sound investment or a speculative one, in Graham’s terms?

items.t: Price close to book value
A long, unbroken dividend record
A P/E above 50
Only three years of earnings history
Modest debt relative to working capital
A price driven by a fashionable theme

questions.why: Graham looked for value backed by assets, earnings and dividends; fashionable themes and high multiples are the speculative markers.

questions.q: Graham says the simplest approach for the defensive investor is to buy equal amounts of each of the 30 shares in the Dow.
options: True
False
It gives a cross-section of leading companies; an index fund now does it better
He says equal amounts in each share guarantee that the investor beats the market
He recommends the approach only for investors over 60 who need a steady income

questions.why: That gives a true cross-section of leading companies. Zweig notes a low-cost total-market index fund now does the job even better.

questions.q: Graham’s minimum size for an industrial company in the defensive portfolio is $50 million of total assets.
questions.why: For an industrial company it is at least $100 million of annual sales. The $50 million of total assets is his minimum for a public utility.

questions.q: Besides a 2-to-1 current ratio, Graham requires that an industrial company’s long-term debt not exceed its net current assets.
questions.why: Net current assets, or working capital, are current assets minus current liabilities. Both parts make up his test of financial strength.

questions.q: Graham’s earnings-stability test allows a company to report a loss in up to three of the past ten years.
options: True
False
He asks for some earnings in each of the past ten years: no losses at all
He allows one loss in the ten years, not three, for the defensive investor
He looks only at the latest year’s earnings, rather than the past ten years

questions.why: He asks for some earnings for the ordinary shares in each of the past ten years: no deficits at all.

questions.q: Graham found the financial-strength tests the most severe of his criteria under the conditions of his time.
questions.why: Many large, formerly strong companies had weakened their current ratio, overexpanded their debt, or both.

questions.q: For public-utility shares, Graham keeps the 2-to-1 current-ratio test but drops the dividend test.
options: True
False
He drops the current-ratio test for utilities and asks for enough equity instead
He keeps both tests, because utilities are just as risky as industrial companies
He drops every test for utilities, because their prices and profits are regulated

questions.why: He drops the current-ratio test, because utilities finance growth continuously through bonds and shares. He requires adequate equity relative to debt instead.

questions.q: On selling a share that has risen too far, Graham says it is better to sell and pay the tax than not sell and repent.
options: True
False
Change holdings when they look overpriced and better value exists elsewhere
He says never to sell, because selling triggers tax and costs that eat returns
He says to sell a share only when its price falls below what the investor paid

questions.why: Even defensive portfolios should be changed from time to time when holdings look excessively priced and better-value replacements exist.

questions.q: Zweig considers the “forward” P/E, based on next year’s forecast earnings, the most reliable way to judge a share’s price.
options: True
False
Dividing a known price by unknown earnings is nonsense: use a three-year average
He agrees, because the market is always looking ahead to next year’s profits
He prefers to use the latest single year’s earnings, which are the most current

questions.why: He calls it nonsensical to divide a known price by unknown future earnings. Use price ÷ the average of the past three years’ actual earnings.

questions.q: Zweig points out that Graham’s growth test, a third more EPS over ten years, works out to less than 3% a year.
questions.why: He calls it a very low hurdle and suggests 50% over ten years (about 4% a year) as slightly less conservative.

questions.q: Graham advises the defensive investor to rely on a skilled analyst to pick the best few shares rather than diversify widely.
options: True
False
Leave the “best” shares alone and diversify: nobody picks winners unerringly
He says a few concentrated picks are safer than holding a wide spread of shares
He says analysts reliably pick the best few shares, so investors should follow them

questions.why: He says to let the choice of “best” shares alone and emphasise diversification. If anyone could pick the best unerringly, diversifying would only lose.

questions.q: What made Penn Central’s 1970 bankruptcy so shocking to the financial world?
options: It had paid dividends for over 120 years, and its share had been near its peak only a year or two earlier
It was a small, obscure company that few investors had ever heard of, so no one had studied its accounts closely
It had never paid a dividend, so its shareholders had already lost faith in it years before
It was the first railroad ever to fail, and the industry had been thought immune to bankruptcy
questions.why: Graham later shows how a competent student could have detected its weaknesses in time. More than half of US railroad mileage had been in bankruptcy at some point in 50 years.

questions.q: What is Graham’s suggestion on railroad shares?
options: There’s no compelling reason to own them; buy only when the value is too great to look elsewhere
Avoid them completely and forever, since the industry’s record of bankruptcies speaks for itself
Buy them as a whole class, since railroad shares tend to rise together when the economy recovers
Own them in place of utilities, since both are regulated and pay similar dividends
questions.why: He avoids blanket recommendations and blanket condemnations. Zweig applies the same advice to airline shares.

questions.q: What does an investor who stresses “protection” rather than “prediction” mainly seek?
options: A substantial margin of present value above the market price, able to absorb bad news
Confidence that the company’s earnings will grow fast for many years to come
The share with the strongest and most consistent upward price trend in its sector
The best management team in the industry, whatever price the market is asking for the shares
questions.why: Such an investor needn’t be enthusiastic about long-run prospects, only reasonably confident the business will get along.

questions.q: A hundred analysts are asked to choose the “best” five shares in the Dow. Why does Graham expect their lists to differ widely?
options: Prices already reflect the known facts and opinions, so any preference rests mostly on personal partialities
Most analysts are poorly trained, so their choices are close to random whatever the facts may be
The data available to each analyst differ, since companies brief some analysts more fully and more often than others
Analysts are paid to disagree with one another, so that their firms can sell more research to clients
questions.why: If all analysts agreed one share was best, its price would quickly rise until its advantages were offset.

questions.q: Graham calls the protective approach “quantitative”. What does it emphasise?
options: Measurable relationships between price and earnings, assets and dividends, as in sound bond selection
Prospects, management quality and other intangibles that numbers alone can’t capture
Charts of past price movements and trading volume, which show where prices are heading
The opinions of leading analysts, combined into a single average score for each share on the approved list
questions.why: The predictive approach is the qualitative one. Graham was always committed to getting ample value in concrete, demonstrable terms.

questions.q: As 1972 began, what did Graham see as the central appeal of utility shares for the defensive investor?
options: They sold at a moderate price relative to book value, so he could be a part owner of sound businesses
They had the fastest earnings growth of any group of shares over the previous twenty years
They paid no tax on their profits, so far more of their earnings could be paid out to shareholders as dividends
Their dividends and share prices were guaranteed by the government that regulated them
questions.why: They offered almost as much past growth as the industrials, steadier figures, lower prices relative to earnings and assets, and higher dividends.

questions.q: How does Zweig suggest a defensive investor who enjoys stock-picking should set up a portfolio?
options: Keep about 90% of the share money in an index fund and use about 10% to pick shares
Pick all of the shares personally and avoid index funds, which only match the market
Split the share money 50/50 between index funds and shares chosen personally
Put it all into the ten best-known companies, since familiar names are the safest
questions.why: The index fund is the foundation. Only after that solid core is in place should you experiment at the edges.

questions.q: Zweig suggests checking how much of a company is owned by institutions. What level hints that a share is “overowned”?
options: More than about 60%
More than about 10%
More than about 30%
Less than 60%
questions.why: When big institutions sell, they tend to move in lockstep, with disastrous results for the share, like the Rockettes toppling off the stage at once.

questions.q: By early 2003, many former high-tech darlings had plenty of cash and little or no debt. What lesson does Zweig draw?
options: The best values are often found in shares that were once hot and have since gone cold
Technology shares are safe once they have fallen, because their cash protects them
A defensive investor should buy every share in such a table at once, without analysis
Financial strength no longer matters once a share has fallen far enough in price
questions.why: A defensive investor can prosper by looking patiently through the wreckage of a bear market, using Graham’s strength tests.

questions.q: A share sells at 9 times its three-year average earnings and 2.4 times book value. Does it pass Graham’s price-to-assets test?
options: Yes: 9 × 2.4 = 21.6, within the 22.5 limit, even though book value is above 1.5 times
No: at 2.4 times book value it is well above the limit of 1.5 times, so it fails the test outright
No: the product of the P/E and price-to-book must be below 15 to pass the test
Yes, but only because the P/E is below 10, which lets any price-to-book pass
questions.why: A low earnings multiplier can justify a higher asset multiplier. Graham’s own example: 9 times earnings and 2.5 times book.

questions.q: A share sells at 12 times three-year average earnings and 2.0 times book value. What is the verdict?
options: Fails: 12 × 2.0 = 24, above 22.5
Passes: its P/E is below 15
Passes: its product is below 30
Passes: 2.0 is close enough to 1.5
questions.why: Each test looks fine on its own terms except book value, and the blended multiplier confirms it is too expensive.

questions.q: High-grade bonds yield 10%. By Graham’s rule that a share portfolio’s earnings yield should be at least the bond rate, what is the highest overall P/E it should have?
questions.why: Earnings yield = 1 ÷ P/E, so 10% means a P/E of 100 ÷ 10 = 10. Graham’s own example: 7.5% bonds gave a maximum of 13.3.

questions.q: An industrial company has current assets of R480m, current liabilities of R220m and long-term debt of R300m. How does it fare on Graham’s financial-strength tests?
options: Passes the current-ratio test (about 2.2 to 1) but fails the debt test: debt exceeds R260m working capital
Passes both tests: the current ratio is about 2.2 to 1, and debt is below total current assets of R480m
Fails both tests: the current ratio is below 2 to 1 and debt is above working capital
Fails the current-ratio test at about 1.5 to 1, but passes the debt test comfortably
questions.why: R480m ÷ R220m ≈ 2.18, and working capital is R480m − R220m = R260m, which is less than the R300m of debt.

questions.q: A utility has R900m of debt and ordinary shareholders’ equity at book value of R400m. Does it meet Graham’s test for utilities?
options: No: debt is 2.25 times equity, above the limit of twice equity
Yes: debt is below R1bn, the limit for a utility of this size
Yes: utilities have no debt limit, since their profits are regulated
No: under Graham’s rules utilities may carry no debt at all
questions.why: R900m ÷ R400m = 2.25. For utilities Graham allows debt of up to twice the stock equity at book value.

questions.q: A company’s EPS was R1.80, R2.10 and R2.10 ten years ago, and R2.50, R2.70 and R2.90 in the last three years. Does it pass Graham’s growth test?
options: Yes: the averages are R2.00 and R2.70, a 35% rise
No: per-share growth is below the required 50%
No: the latest year is only R2.90, below the target
Yes: the last year alone is up 61% on the first
questions.why: Compare three-year averages, not single years: R2.70 ÷ R2.00 = 1.35, above the one-third minimum.

questions.q: A share is R60. Analysts forecast R5 of EPS next year; the past three years averaged R3. What P/E does Graham’s method give, and does it pass?
options: 20 times: it fails the limit of 15
12 times: it passes the limit of 15
15 times: it just passes the limit
5 times: it is very cheap indeed
questions.why: R60 ÷ R3 = 20. The 12 times on forecast earnings is the forward P/E Zweig warns against: 59% of consensus forecasts miss by 15% or more.

questions.q: A share falls 99.5%, as MicroStrategy did from 2000 to 2002. What gain would it need to get back to its old price?
options: About 19,900%: it must rise 200-fold
About 99.5%, the same as the fall
About 995%: it must rise tenfold
About 200%: it must roughly triple
questions.why: What is left is 0.5% of the old price, and 1 ÷ 0.005 = 200 times. Diversification is the only reliable insurance against being wrong.

questions.q: At the end of 1970 the Dow stood at 839, with three-year average earnings of 55.5 and net asset value of 562. How did the average fare on Graham’s price tests?
options: About 15 times earnings and 1.49 times assets: just within both limits
About 10 times earnings and 1.0 times assets: comfortably cheap
About 15 times earnings but 2.5 times assets: fails the asset test
About 20 times earnings and 1.5 times assets: fails the earnings test
questions.why: 839 ÷ 55.5 ≈ 15.1 and 839 ÷ 562 ≈ 1.49. All seven criteria were met in aggregate, two of them only just.

questions.q: SableCo, a large fictional JSE industrial (well above Graham’s size test): price R30.00; three-year average earnings R2.40 a share; book value R18.00 a share; current assets 2.3 times current liabilities; long-term debt R400m against net current assets of R520m; profits in each of the past ten years; earnings per share up 45% over ten years on three-year averages; dividends paid without a break for 14 years. Does it pass the defensive investor’s screen?
options: No: the dividend record is six years short of 20
No: price-to-book is above Graham’s limit of 1.5
Yes: it passes all seven of Graham’s tests
questions.why: Price-to-book of 1.67 is allowed, because P/E of 12.5 × P/B of 1.67 = 20.8, under Graham’s 22.5. Every other test passes; only the dividend record fails.
questions.src: Chapter 14: Stock selection for the defensive investor
miss: A P/B above 1.5 is allowed when P/E × P/B stays under 22.5: here it is 20.8.
Graham requires dividends without a break for at least 20 years.

questions.q: A share trades at {pe|1x} its three-year average earnings and {pb|1x} its book value. What is the product of the two, which Graham caps at 22.5?

errs.why: Multiply the two ratios.

questions.why: Graham allows a higher price-to-book when the P/E is low, as long as the product stays at or below 22.5.

questions.q: Average earnings per share for the first three years of a decade were {a|R2}; for the last three years, {b|R2}. By what percentage did they grow (Graham requires at least a third)?

errs.why: That is the change in rand; express it as a percentage of the starting average.

questions.why: Graham measures earnings growth on three-year averages at each end of ten years, which smooths out a single good or bad year.

questions.q: Graham reads the funds’ failure to beat a broad average as strong evidence that doing so is extremely difficult.
options: True
False
They had the best research, yet a 1960–68 study found random portfolios did better
He says the funds failed only because their costs were too high, not their choices
He says the funds beat the average easily, which shows the task is a simple one
