questions.why: It only gives a better chance of profit than loss. That is why it goes hand in hand with diversification, as in insurance underwriting.

questions.q: Graham argues that a sufficiently low price can turn a security of mediocre quality into a sound investment.
options: True
False
For a diversified buyer, a low enough price creates the margin of safety
Quality alone decides: no price, however low, can make a weak security sound
Low prices are always a sign that the company will soon get into trouble

questions.why: Provided the buyer is informed and experienced and diversifies adequately. A low enough price creates the margin of safety that defines investment.

questions.q: Graham says that if the crowd disagrees with you, that is good evidence that your analysis is wrong.
options: True
False
Your data and reasoning make you right, whatever the crowd thinks
He says the crowd is usually right, so disagreeing with it should worry you
He says the crowd is always wrong, so disagreeing with it proves you right

questions.why: “You are neither right nor wrong because the crowd disagrees with you. You are right because your data and reasoning are right.”

questions.q: Graham ends: “To achieve satisfactory investment results is easier than most people realize; to achieve superior results is harder than it looks.”
questions.why: The typical investor can succeed by limiting ambition to capacity and keeping to the safe, narrow path of defensive investment.

questions.q: Peter Bernstein, drawing on Pascal’s wager, says that when deciding under uncertainty, the probabilities must dominate the consequences.
questions.why: The reverse: the consequences must dominate the probabilities, because we never know the future. You can’t control being wrong sometimes, but you can control what it costs.

questions.q: According to Graham, a true margin of safety is one that can be demonstrated by what?
options: Figures, persuasive reasoning and a body of actual experience
A strong market trend and the opinion of leading experts
Management’s forecasts and the analysts’ ratings of the share
Recent price momentum and unusually heavy trading volume
questions.why: To have a true investment there must be a true margin of safety. It is the touchstone that separates investment from speculation.

questions.q: Why does Graham doubt that speculators really enjoy a margin of safety, even when they feel the odds are in their favour?
options: Their claims rest on subjective judgment, unsupported by evidence or conclusive reasoning
Speculators seldom make money for long, so any margin they have soon disappears
Speculators nearly always use borrowed money, which wipes out any margin they might have
Their trades are too small and too short for any margin to build up in their favour
questions.why: Each feels the time is right, his skill superior or his system trustworthy. Betting on the market’s direction offers no safety margin in any useful sense.

questions.q: Why did Graham feel there were real risks in 1972, even in a diversified list of sound shares?
options: Typical earnings yields had fallen well below 9%, leaving too small an excess over bond interest
Companies had stopped raising their dividends, so share income no longer kept pace with prices
High-grade bonds were no longer available to individual investors at reasonable cost or yield
Diversification no longer worked, because all shares had begun to rise and fall together
questions.why: At 12 times earnings, the earnings yield was 8.33% against much higher bond rates than before. The old package of good profits and small risk was no longer available.

questions.q: When can an ordinary share offer a margin of safety as large as a good bond’s?
options: When a debt-free company sells for less than the bonds that could safely be issued against its assets and earnings
When it is a member of a major index, since the index funds then guarantee steady demand for it
When its dividend is higher than any bond’s coupon, so its income alone is better than a bond’s
When its price has risen for three years in a row, which shows the market is confident in the company’s future
questions.why: Many strong companies were in that position in 1932–33. The investor then gets a bond’s safety plus a share’s chances of gain.

questions.q: How does Graham link the margin of safety and diversification?
options: They work together: each holding has better odds of profit than loss, so many make an overall gain more certain
They are unrelated ideas, since one is about the price of a share and the other only about the number of shares held
Diversification replaces the need for a margin of safety, since losses on some shares are offset by others
A margin of safety makes diversification unnecessary, since each holding is safe enough on its own
questions.why: This is the simple basis of insurance underwriting. Without a margin, as in roulette, spreading bets only makes a loss more certain.

questions.q: What does the first business principle, “Know what you are doing; know your business”, mean for the investor?
options: Don’t aim for more than normal interest and dividends unless you know securities as well as a merchant knows his goods
Only buy shares in the company you work for, since that is the business you know best of all
Read the financial pages every day, so that you know what is happening in every market you are in
Always use a reputable broker, who knows the business of buying and selling securities far better than you can ever hope to
questions.why: Investment is most intelligent when it is most businesslike. Buying and selling for profit is a business venture of your own.

questions.q: What does Graham’s third business principle mean for the enterprising investor?
options: Base operations on arithmetic, not optimism, and avoid ventures with little to gain and much to lose
Act on optimism when markets are rising, and on caution only when they are falling
Trade often to capture many small gains, since small profits add up over the years
Follow the calculations of trusted experts without checking them yourself, since they know far more than you
questions.why: For every investor, if you accept a small return, as in a conventional bond, you must demand convincing evidence that you aren’t risking much of your principal.

questions.q: Which two factors does Daniel Kahneman say characterise good decisions?
options: Well-calibrated confidence and correctly anticipated regret
Speed in acting and boldness in the size of the bet
Expert advice and a strong record of recent performance
High conviction and a willingness to make concentrated bets
questions.why: Ask how well you really understand the investment, and how you will react if you are wrong. Zweig: risk is gazing back at you from the mirror.

questions.q: In the 1930s many real-estate bonds sold for under 10 cents on the dollar. What does Graham say about buying them then?
options: Many were attractive, reasonably safe investments, since true values were four or five times the price
They were pure speculation at any price, because real-estate bonds had already defaulted once and could do so again
They should have been sold, since advisers and the rating agencies had turned against them
They were safe only at par, since a low price showed that the market expected a total loss
questions.why: The same bonds had been speculative at par in the 1920s, with little value above the debt. Price turned them into investments.

questions.q: Graham says the margin of safety for bonds can be measured in two ways. Which pair is right?
options: Earnings compared with interest charges, and the value of the business compared with its debt
The coupon compared with inflation, and the bond’s price compared with its par value
The credit rating compared with peers, and the bond’s maturity compared with its yield
The dividend compared with interest, and the company’s sales compared with its total debt
questions.why: Since average share prices track average earning power, both methods usually give similar results.

questions.q: A business owes R10m and is fairly worth R30m. How far could its value fall before bondholders lose money, in theory?
options: By two-thirds
By one-third
By 10%
questions.why: R30m − R10m = R20m of cushion, which is two-thirds of R30m. That cushion is the bondholders’ margin of safety.

questions.q: A railway earns its fixed charges five times over before tax. By roughly how much could its earnings fall before the balance after interest disappears?
questions.why: If earnings are 5 and interest 1, earnings can fall to 1, a drop of 4 ÷ 5 = 80%. That is the cushion Graham’s 5-times test provides.

questions.q: A share sells at 11 times earnings and bonds yield 4%. What is the share buyer’s annual margin, and about how much might it add up to over ten years?
options: About 5 points a year, roughly 50% of the price over ten years
About 7 points a year, roughly 70% of the price over ten years
About 11 points a year, roughly 110% of the price over ten years
None: the share yields less than the bond, so there is no margin
questions.why: 1 ÷ 11 ≈ 9% earnings yield, minus 4% = about 5 points. Graham says ten years of such excess may total about 50% of the price paid.

questions.q: You buy shares at 12 times earnings with a 4% dividend yield. What is the earnings yield, and how much of your cost is reinvested for you each year?
options: 8.33%, with 4.33% reinvested
12%, with 8% reinvested
8.33%, with 4% reinvested
4%, with nothing reinvested
questions.why: 1 ÷ 12 ≈ 8.33%, and 8.33% − 4% = 4.33%. Graham found this excess over 1972 bond yields too small to be an adequate margin.

questions.q: On a wheel with 38 numbers paying R35 profit on a R1 win, you bet R1 on every number. What happens each spin, and what if the payout were R39?
options: You lose R2 each spin; at R39 you would win R2 each spin
You win R35 each spin; at R39 you would win R39 each spin
You break even each spin, whichever of the payouts applies
You lose R1 each spin; at R39 you would win R1 each spin
questions.why: You win R35 on one number and lose R1 on 37: −R2. At R39 you would net +R2. With a negative margin, diversifying guarantees a loss; with a positive one, it guarantees a gain.

questions.q: A secondary company’s shares have an indicated value of R60. What is the most Graham would suggest paying as an unconventional investment?
options: R40: two-thirds or less of indicated value
R60: the full indicated value of the shares
R54: a 10% discount to the indicated value
R30: half of the indicated value, or less
questions.why: Two-thirds of R60 is R40. The R20 gap is the margin that absorbs miscalculations or worse-than-average luck.

questions.q: A company with no debt has a total market value of R43m and pre-tax earnings of R16m. If it borrowed R43m at 7%, how well would earnings cover the interest?
options: About 5.3 times: the shares carry a bond-like margin
About 2.7 times: below Graham’s standard for bonds
About 0.4 times: the interest couldn’t be paid at all
About 16 times: far above any standard Graham set
questions.why: Interest would be R43m × 7% ≈ R3m, and R16m ÷ R3m ≈ 5.3, above Graham’s 5-times standard. That was National Presto in 1972.

questions.q: Your share falls 50% in the first year and then gains 10% a year. Roughly how long does it take just to get back to where you started?
options: About 7 years
About 5 years
About 2 years
About 16 years
questions.why: You need to double, and 1.1⁷ ≈ 1.95. Overtaking a steady 5% a year takes over 16 years: the cost of paying too much at the outset.

questions.q: A share bought at R153.42 is now R2.47. At 10% a year, roughly how long would it take to get back to the purchase price?
options: About 43 years
About 10 years
About 62 years
About 6 years
questions.why: R153.42 ÷ R2.47 ≈ 62 times, and 1.1⁴³ ≈ 60. That was JDS Uniphase, bought at its March 2000 peak.

questions.q: An investor puts 85% of his money into one fashionable sector because he is sure it will rise. By Bernstein’s reading of Pascal’s wager, what is wrong with this?
options: He has ignored the consequences of being wrong, which should dominate the probabilities
His estimate of the probability that the sector will rise is far too low, not too high
He should have used borrowed money too, since his confidence in the sector is so high
Nothing: confidence in the outcome is enough to justify any concentration of money
questions.why: Nearly a tenth of investors surveyed in 1999 held at least 85% in internet shares. Diversification and refusing to overpay keep any mistake from being catastrophic.

questions.q: You estimate a share’s value at {v|R2}; it trades at {p|R2}. What is your margin of safety, as a percentage of value?

errs.why: Express the gap as a share of value, not of price.

questions.why: The margin of safety is the gap between value and price: it absorbs errors in your estimate and bad luck.

questions.q: A share’s earnings yield is {ey|1%} on its price, and bonds yield {y|1%}. In Graham’s illustration, how much does the excess earning power add up to over ten years, as a percentage of the price paid?
work: Over ten years ≈ {ey-y|1%} × 10 = {x|0%} of the price

errs.why: That is one year’s excess; Graham adds it up over ten years.

questions.why: Graham’s point: when earnings yield comfortably exceeds the bond yield, the surplus over ten years gives the investor a cushion against a disappointing result.
questions.src: Chapter 20: The margin of safety for shares

questions.q: Graham says a margin of safety can exist even in a weak company, if the price is low enough. What does he require for that to work?
options: A diversified group of such holdings, so the odds work across many
A single large holding, so the bargain has a real effect on returns
Proof that the company’s results have started to improve again
Each has better odds of gain than loss, not certainty; many make the total dependable
Weak companies recover in most cases, once the wider market notices the low price
A low enough price guarantees a profit on every single holding, given enough time

questions.why: Graham links the two ideas: each holding has better odds of gain than loss, and many such holdings make an overall gain highly probable.

questions.q: The two partners in Graham’s Postscript averaged about 20% a year on the capital they managed.
questions.why: They kept a widely diversified portfolio of more than a hundred issues and avoided anything that looked overpriced.

questions.q: The partners bought their half-interest in a company that Wall Street was eager to finance.
options: True
False
The industry had no Wall Street appeal, and important houses had turned it down
Wall Street houses competed hard to finance it, which pushed up the price they paid
The partners financed the purchase through a public offering of new shares

questions.why: The industry had no Wall Street appeal at the time, and several important houses had turned the deal down.

questions.q: Graham says the profits from that single investment far exceeded all the others made in 20 years of wide-ranging operations.
questions.why: Its share price rose two hundred times or more the price paid for the half-interest.

questions.q: Graham promises a similarly spectacular result to every intelligent investor who stays prudent and alert.
options: True
False
He says plainly that he can’t, and promises only interesting possibilities
He promises it to anyone who sticks to his rules for at least twenty years
He promises it to enterprising investors, though not to the defensive ones

questions.why: He says plainly that he cannot. He won’t end with Raskob’s slogan “Everybody can be rich”, only with the promise of interesting possibilities.

questions.q: Zweig notes that Graham had established he could liquidate GEICO for at least what he paid for it.
questions.why: So the financial risk was small, even with about a quarter of the fund in one company. The risk he took was psychological.

questions.q: Zweig concludes that the GEICO story shows ordinary investors should put most of their money into one great company.
options: True
False
Graham called it a lucky break, so the rest of us must diversify
He concludes that concentration is the real secret of great long-term returns
He concludes that ordinary investors should copy Graham’s bet on GEICO

questions.why: The opposite. Since Graham himself called it a lucky break, the rest of us must diversify to keep investing from decaying into gambling.

questions.q: What was decisive for the partners in deciding to buy the half-interest?
options: The price was moderate in relation to current earnings and asset value
The industry was popular on Wall Street, which made a later sale easy
Other investment houses were competing to buy the same half-interest
Its share price had been rising fast, which confirmed its strong prospects
questions.why: They were impressed by its possibilities, but the deciding factor was value: the margin of safety at the price paid.

questions.q: The shares soon looked far too high by the partners’ own standards. Why did they keep a large holding?
options: They regarded the company as a sort of “family business”
They were legally barred from selling for several years
They expected a takeover bid at an even higher price
They thought it was still cheap by their own standards
questions.why: Many participants in their funds also held on and became millionaires through this one company and its later affiliates.

questions.q: What does Graham say usually lies behind the lucky break or the one supremely shrewd decision?
options: A background of preparation and disciplined capacity, plus the means, judgment and courage to act
Inside information that others don’t have, gained through close contacts with company managers
Pure chance and nothing else, since no amount of preparation can make the right opportunity appear
Following the crowd at exactly the right moment, then leaving just before everyone else does
questions.why: One must also be established enough for such opportunities to knock at one’s door. And can we tell luck and shrewdness apart?

questions.q: What does Zweig say about uncertainty and investing?
options: They are synonyms: uncertainty is permanent, and investing requires faith in a better tomorrow
Investors should wait until the uncertainty clears before committing new money to the market
Uncertainty exists only in bear markets; in bull markets the direction of prices is clear enough
Experts can remove most of the uncertainty with good forecasts, which is what investors pay them for
questions.why: No one has ever been able to see that a particular time is the best time to buy. Without faith in the future, no one would invest at all.

questions.q: Zweig says successful investing is about what?
options: Managing risk, not avoiding it
Avoiding all risk
Taking the biggest risks for the biggest gains
Predicting the market
questions.why: Graham’s large GEICO bet carried little financial risk thanks to its asset backing, though it took great courage psychologically.

questions.q: A fund puts R712,500 into one company, about 25% of its assets. Roughly how large is the fund?
options: About R2.85m
About R0.71m
About R1.78m
About R7.1m
questions.why: R712,500 ÷ 0.25 = R2.85m. Graham describes the stake as about a fifth of the fund; Zweig puts it at about 25%.

questions.q: A R11,413 holding grows to R1.66m over 24 years. Roughly what compound annual return is that?
options: About 23% a year
About 6% a year
About 14.5% a year
About 60% a year
questions.why: R1.66m ÷ R11,413 ≈ 145 times, and 145^(1/24) ≈ 1.23. That was a Graham-Newman holder who kept the GEICO shares from 1948 to 1972.

questions.q: A R712,500 half-interest later becomes worth 200 times the price paid. What is it worth?
options: About R142.5m
About R14.25m
About R71.25m
About R1.425bn
questions.why: R712,500 × 200 = R142.5m. The advance far outstripped the actual growth in profits.

questions.q: The Postscript describes one investment, GEICO, that made more money than all the partners’ other investments over twenty years. What is the lesson?
options: Preparation lets you spot a rare chance and act on it; you can’t plan the luck
Find one great company early and put everything you have into it for life
Investing is mostly luck, so success depends on staying in the game long enough
Behind such luck there is usually a background of preparation and disciplined capacity
Diversification held the partners back for years, and GEICO showed what focus could achieve
Big wins come from buying what the crowd is buying, at exactly the right moment

questions.why: One lucky break may count for more than a lifetime of journeyman effort, but only a prepared, disciplined investor can take it.

questions.q: Bankers favour enterprise value multiples partly because they are independent of capital structure.
questions.why: They are also free of differences in tax regimes and some accounting policies, which affect net income and so P/E.

questions.q: Under the treasury stock method, the proceeds from exercising options are assumed to be used to repay debt.
questions.why: They are assumed to buy back shares at the current share price. The difference between options exercised and shares bought back is the net dilution.

questions.q: If a company borrows R100m and keeps the money as cash, its enterprise value rises by R100m.
questions.why: Debt rises by R100m and so does cash, so net debt and enterprise value are unchanged. Issuing equity to repay debt is also enterprise-value neutral.

questions.q: EBITDA is not a reported (GAAP) figure; it is usually built from EBIT plus D&A taken from the cash flow statement.
questions.why: It is widely used as a proxy for operating cash flow and as an apples-to-apples comparison across capital structures and tax regimes.

questions.q: To adjust net income for a pre-tax restructuring charge, add back the full pre-tax amount.
questions.why: Add back the full amount to EBIT and EBITDA, but tax-effect it for net income: add back the charge × (1 − tax rate).

questions.q: Out-of-the-money convertible bonds are added to fully diluted shares outstanding, just like in-the-money ones.
questions.why: They stay treated as debt. Only in-the-money convertibles are converted into shares.

questions.q: In the book’s framework, which of these belongs to the financial profile rather than the business profile?
options: Return on investment
Distribution channels
Customers and end markets
Geography
questions.why: The financial profile covers size, profitability, growth, return on investment and credit. The business profile covers sector, products and services, customers and end markets, distribution channels and geography.

questions.q: Starting from scratch, where is usually the best place to begin looking for comparable companies?
options: The target’s listed competitors
Companies with the same share price
The largest companies in the market
Any company with similar EBITDA
questions.why: Competitors share key business and financial characteristics and similar opportunities and risks. Annual reports, research and industry codes then fill gaps.

questions.q: Why is the merger proxy for a recent deal in the sector a useful source of comparables?
options: Its fairness opinion excerpts list the comparable companies and multiple ranges used
It lists every listed company in the industry, along with each one’s market share
It gives the consensus estimates of the research analysts who cover the sector
It reports the credit ratings of the target and each of its main competitors
questions.why: The fairness opinion summarises the valuation work, typically comps, precedent transactions, DCF and, where relevant, LBO analysis.

questions.q: Why is EV/EBITDA generally preferred to EV/EBIT?
options: It isn’t distorted by depreciation differences from capex timing or by acquisition amortisation
EBIT is not a reported figure, so it has to be built from the notes for every company
EV/EBIT ignores the company’s debt, while EV/EBITDA takes the full capital structure into account
EV/EBITDA includes interest costs, so it reflects each company’s financing as well as its operations
questions.why: EV/EBIT can still help when D&A is unavailable, such as for divisions, or for very capital-intensive companies.

questions.q: Which of these pairings is inconsistent?
options: Enterprise value ÷ net income
Enterprise value ÷ EBITDA
Share price ÷ diluted EPS
Equity value ÷ net income
questions.why: Enterprise value belongs to debt and equity holders, so it pairs with sales, EBITDA or EBIT. Net income flows only to equity holders.

questions.q: A company trades at 55% of its 52-week high while its peers trade at 85–90% of theirs. What does this usually indicate?
options: Company-specific issues, such as missed guidance or management problems
A sector-wide downturn that has hit this company before its peers
That the company is cheap relative to its peers and should be bought
A pending share split, which has temporarily lowered its share price
questions.why: When one company is out of line with its peers, the cause is usually specific to it rather than to the sector.

questions.q: A generic drug maker is regularly sued over patent challenges. How should its legal costs be treated when scrubbing the financials?
options: Not necessarily as non-recurring: they are a normal part of its operations
As non-recurring in every case, so they are added back to EBITDA
As extraordinary gains, since the company usually wins its cases
Ignored entirely, since legal costs are not part of operating income
questions.why: What is one-off for one company can be routine for another. Bankers must use judgment, not labels alone.

questions.q: What is calendarisation for?
options: Aligning companies with different year-ends so that their multiples cover the same periods
Converting quarterly figures into monthly ones so that results can be tracked more closely
Adjusting every company’s historical figures for inflation so that the years are comparable
Removing seasonal effects from share prices so that the trading multiples are more stable
questions.why: Without it, multiples would be based on different periods and not truly comparable.

questions.q: Compared with the if-converted method, how does net share settlement treat an in-the-money convertible?
options: Face value stays as debt, settled in cash; only the excess of conversion value over par is paid in new shares
All of the bond becomes new shares at the conversion price, exactly as under the if-converted method
It is ignored until maturity, since the holder can still choose not to convert the bond at all
It is treated as preference shares, so it is added to enterprise value and never to the diluted share count
questions.why: So net share settlement issues fewer shares. As the share price rises, the excess, and so the new shares, grow.

questions.q: Which of these is a weakness of comparable companies analysis?
options: Valuations can be skewed by irrational exuberance or gloom, and pure-play peers may not exist
It relies only on management projections, which tend to be optimistic in a sale
It cannot be updated quickly, because share prices and estimates change too often
It ignores market sentiment, so it can value a company far from where it actually trades
questions.why: It may also be disconnected from the target’s cash flow and miss target-specific strengths and risks. Hence comps are used with other methods.

questions.q: A share trades at {p|R}. There are {b|0m} basic shares and {o|0m} in-the-money options with an average exercise price of {k|R}. What are fully diluted shares under the treasury stock method?

errs.why: That counts every option as a whole new share. The exercise cash buys some back, so only the net new shares count.
In-the-money options do dilute: add the net new shares to the basic count.
The bought-back shares come off the option count; they aren’t added to it.

ask.q: Why are the exercise proceeds divided by the share price?
options: The company is assumed to buy back shares at today’s price with the cash it receives
It turns the options into their fair value
Options are always settled in cash, never in shares
ask.why: The treasury stock method assumes the exercise cash buys back shares at the current price, so only the net new shares dilute.

questions.why: Only the net new shares dilute: the cash from exercise is assumed to buy shares back at today’s price.
questions.src: Step III: Calculating fully diluted shares

questions.q: A share trades at {p|R}. Tranche A: {a|1m} options at {ka|R}. Tranche B: {c|1m} options at {kc|R}. How many net new shares does the treasury stock method add?
work: Tranche B: {kc|R} is above {p|R}, so it is out of the money and ignored

errs.why: Tranche B is out of the money (its exercise price is above the share price), so it adds nothing.
The exercise cash buys back shares, so tranche A adds fewer than its full count.
Out-of-the-money options are left out, and exercise cash buys shares back.

questions.why: Only in-the-money tranches count. Out-of-the-money options would not be exercised.
questions.src: Step III: Calculating fully diluted shares

questions.q: A {face|R0m} convertible bond has a conversion price of {cp|R}, and the share trades at {p|R}. How many new shares does the if-converted method add?
work: In the money: the share price {p|R} is above the conversion price {cp|R}

errs.why: Divide by the conversion price, not the share price: the bond converts into a fixed number of shares.

questions.why: Divide the face value by the conversion price. The bond is then treated as equity, not debt.

questions.q: The same kind of bond: {face|R0m} face value, conversion price {cp|R}, share price {p|R}, but with net share settlement. How many new shares are issued?

errs.why: That is the if-converted answer. Net share settlement pays the face value in cash and issues shares only for the excess.
The excess value is settled in shares at today’s price, not at the conversion price.

ask.q: Why is only the excess settled in shares?
options: The company repays the face value in cash, like debt
The excess is taxed, so it is paid in shares
Shares are cheaper to issue than cash is to raise
ask.why: Under net share settlement the face value stays debt and is repaid in cash; only the value above it is paid in shares.

questions.why: With net share settlement the face value is paid in cash and only the excess conversion value is settled in shares.

questions.q: Equity value is {eq|R0m}. Debt is {d|R0m}, preference shares {pr|R0m}, non-controlling interest {nci|R0m} and cash {c|R0m}. What is enterprise value?

errs.why: Non-controlling interest is added: consolidated EBITDA includes all of the subsidiary, so EV must too.
Cash is subtracted. A buyer of the whole business gets the cash back.
Preference shares and non-controlling interest are claims on the business too: add them.

steps.t: Plus debt, preference shares and NCI

options: Whoever buys the whole business gets the cash too, so it offsets the price
Cash earns no return, so it is worth nothing
Cash belongs to the lenders
ask.why: Enterprise value is the price of the operations. Cash on the balance sheet comes with them, so it reduces what the business really costs.

questions.why: Add every claim on the business that isn’t ordinary equity (debt, preference shares, non-controlling interest) and take off cash.

questions.q: Sales were {S|R0m} for the last financial year. For the first nine months of this year they are {yn|R0m}, against {yp|R0m} for the same nine months last year. What are LTM sales?
work: LTM = last full year + this year to date − the same period last year

errs.why: Take off last year’s matching nine months, or they are counted twice.
Annualising nine months ignores seasonality. LTM uses actual reported figures.

steps.t: Less the same period last year

questions.why: Last twelve months: the latest full year, plus the year to date, less the matching period a year earlier.
questions.src: Step II: Calculation of LTM financial data

questions.q: A company’s year ends in March. Sales are {a|R0m} for the year to March 2026 and forecast at {b|R0m} for the year to March 2027. What are sales for calendar 2026?
work: January to March 2026 falls in the year to March 2026: 3/12 × {a|R0m} = {a*3/12|R0m}
April to December 2026 falls in the year to March 2027: 9/12 × {b|R0m} = {b*9/12|R0m}

errs.why: The weights are the wrong way round: only January to March 2026 comes from the year to March 2026.
A simple average gives each year half; the calendar year shares 3 months with one and 9 with the other.

questions.why: Weight each financial year by the months it shares with the calendar year.
questions.src: Step II: Calendarisation of financial data

questions.q: Reported net income is {ni|R0m} after a {ch|R0m} pre-tax restructuring charge you judge to be non-recurring. The tax rate is {t|0%}. What is adjusted net income?

errs.why: The charge was deductible, so it saved tax. Add back only the after-tax amount.
That adds back the tax saved, not the charge after tax.

ask.q: Why use the charge after tax?
options: The charge was tax-deductible, so profit after tax fell by less than the charge
Tax is always added back in adjustments
Net income is a pre-tax figure
ask.why: Net income is after tax. A deductible charge cut tax too, so it lowered net income by the charge less the tax it saved.

questions.why: Add back the charge after tax: it reduced taxable income, so it saved tax as well.
questions.src: Step II: Adjustments for non-recurring items

questions.q: The selected range is {m1|1x} to {m1+1|1x} EBITDA, and EBITDA is {e|R0m}. Net debt is {nd|R0m} and there are {sh|0m} fully diluted shares. What is the implied share price at the low end of the range?

errs.why: That divides enterprise value by shares. Take off net debt first: shareholders get what is left after lenders.
Net debt is subtracted to move from enterprise value to equity value, not added.

questions.why: An EV multiple gives enterprise value. Take off net debt to reach equity value, then divide by fully diluted shares.

questions.q: A P/E of {pe|1x} is applied to net income of {ni|R0m}. Net debt is {nd|R0m}. What implied enterprise value does it give?

errs.why: That is equity value. A P/E gives equity value; add net debt for enterprise value.
Going from equity value to enterprise value, net debt is added.

questions.why: P/E is an equity multiple: it gives equity value. Add net debt to get to enterprise value.

questions.q: A company has debt of {d|R0m}, cash of {c|R0m}, LTM EBITDA of {e|R0m} and interest expense of {i|R0m}. What is its net leverage (net debt to EBITDA)?

errs.why: That is total leverage. Net leverage takes cash off the debt first.
That is interest cover (EBITDA ÷ interest), a different ratio.

questions.why: Leverage compares debt with EBITDA; net leverage takes off cash first. Interest cover is a separate ratio.

questions.q: A company pays a quarterly dividend of {qd|R} a share and its share trades at {p|R}. What is the dividend yield?

errs.why: The dividend is quarterly: multiply by four for the annual figure.

questions.why: Annualise the most recent quarterly dividend, then divide by the share price.

questions.q: Diluted EPS rose from {e0|R} to {e1|R} over {n} years. What is the compound annual growth rate?

errs.why: A simple average ignores compounding. Take the n-th root of the growth multiple instead.
That is the total growth over the whole period, not the yearly rate.

questions.why: Compound growth: the n-th root of the ending value over the starting value, less one.

questions.q: Put the five steps of comparable companies analysis in order.
items: Select the universe of comparable companies
Spread the key statistics, ratios and trading multiples
questions.why: Each step feeds the next: no valuation is set until the peers are chosen, spread and benchmarked.
questions.src: Comparable Companies Analysis: the five steps

questions.q: A company borrows {x|R0m} and keeps all of it as cash. What happens to equity value, net debt and enterprise value?
questions.why: The new debt is matched by the new cash, so net debt doesn’t move, and nothing about the business has changed.

questions.q: A company issues {x|R0m} of new shares and uses all the money to repay debt. Ignoring fees, what happens to equity value, net debt and enterprise value?

mag.q: By how much does net debt fall?

questions.why: Equity value rises by the new shares and net debt falls by the same amount, so enterprise value, the value of the business, is unchanged.

questions.q: Which multiple best fits a company with heavy, lumpy capital spending that distorts depreciation from year to year?
options: EV/EBITDA
EV/EBIT
Price to book
P/E
questions.why: EBITDA sits before depreciation, so differences in capex timing and depreciation policy don’t distort the comparison.
miss: EV/EBIT is after depreciation, so the lumpy depreciation charge is still in it.
Price to book suits balance-sheet businesses such as banks, not this case.
P/E is after depreciation, interest and tax, so it carries every distortion.

questions.q: An analyst’s enterprise value bridge. Which line is wrong?

options: Plus non-controlling interest: {nci|R0m}
Plus non-controlling interest at half: {nci/2|R0m}
Leave non-controlling interest out

questions.why: Non-controlling interest is added: the EBITDA it is compared with includes all of the subsidiary.

questions.q: An analyst’s fully diluted share count, with the share at {p|R}. Which line is wrong?
lines: Tranche A: {a|1m} options at {ka|R} (in the money)
Tranche B: {c|1m} options at {kc|R}, counted in full

fix.q: What should happen to tranche B?
options: Leave it out: at {kc|R} it is out of the money
Count it with the treasury stock method
Count half of it

questions.why: Out-of-the-money options wouldn’t be exercised, so they don’t dilute.
questions.src: Step III: Calculating fully diluted shares

questions.q: An analyst’s LTM EBITDA. Which line is wrong?
lines: Plus the same six months last year: {yp|R0m}

options: Subtract the same six months last year
Add the six months twice
Leave last year’s six months out entirely

questions.why: LTM is the last full year plus the year to date, less the same period a year earlier. Adding it double counts six months.
questions.src: Step II: Calculation of LTM financial data

questions.q: Adjusting net income for a one-off charge, at a tax rate of 27%. Which line is wrong?

options: {ch*0.73|R1m}, the charge after tax
{ch|R0m}, the full charge
{ch*0.27|R1m}, the tax on it

questions.why: Net income is after tax, and the charge saved tax, so only the after-tax amount goes back.
questions.src: Step II: Adjustments for non-recurring items

questions.q: Turning a multiple into a share price. Which line is wrong?

options: ({e*m|R0m} − {nd|R0m} net debt) ÷ {sh|0m} = {(e*m-nd)/sh|R2}
({e*m|R0m} + {nd|R0m} net debt) ÷ {sh|0m} = {(e*m+nd)/sh|R2}
{e|R0m} ÷ {sh|0m} = {e/sh|R2}

questions.why: Enterprise value belongs to lenders and shareholders together; take off net debt before dividing by the share count.

questions.q: A comparables table for one peer. Which line is wrong?

options: {eq|R0m} ÷ {ni|R0m} = {eq/ni|1x}
{ev|R0m} ÷ {e|R0m} = {ev/e|1x}
{eq|R0m} ÷ {e|R0m} = {eq/e|1x}

questions.why: Match the numerator to the denominator: net income belongs to shareholders, so it pairs with equity value, not enterprise value.

questions.q: In your head: a share trades at {p|R}, with {sh|0m} shares, net debt of {nd|R0m} and EBITDA of {e|R0m}. Roughly what EV/EBITDA is it on?
questions.why: Market value of equity, plus net debt, over EBITDA: worth being able to do without a spreadsheet.

questions.q: In your head: EBITDA {e|R0m}, a peer multiple of {m|0x}, net debt {nd|R0m} and {sh|0m} shares. Roughly what share price does that imply?
questions.why: Multiple, then net debt, then shares: the order matters more than the precision.

questions.q: Before you read: someone buying the whole of a company takes on its debt and gets its cash. Which figure measures that whole price?
options: Enterprise value
Equity value (market capitalisation)
Book value of equity
questions.why: Enterprise value is the value of the business to all its funders: equity value plus net debt and other claims.

questions.q: Before you read: why might a banker value a company by looking at similar listed companies?
options: The market’s prices for similar businesses are a guide to what this one is worth
Listed companies are always correctly valued, so their prices can be copied directly
It avoids needing any of the company’s own figures, which are often hard to obtain
questions.why: Comparables use the market’s current pricing of similar businesses as a reference point.

questions.q: Before you read: a company has employee share options that are worth exercising. Which share count better reflects value per share?
options: One that adds the shares the options would create
The basic shares in issue, since options aren’t shares yet
Only the shares held by directors and senior managers
questions.why: In-the-money options would turn into shares, so a fully diluted count gives a truer value per share.

questions.q: Since IFRS 16, a JSE retailer’s EBITDA is before its store rent, which now shows up as depreciation and interest on lease liabilities. To use that EBITDA in an EV/EBITDA multiple, what must enterprise value include?
options: The lease liabilities, alongside the debt
Nothing extra: leases are operating items, so EV stays as before
Only the lease payments due in the next twelve months
questions.why: EBITDA before rent leaves the lease cost out, so the lease liabilities are a claim on that EBITDA, like debt. Leave them out of EV and the multiple looks too cheap.
miss: Then EV leaves out the very claim the higher EBITDA is paying for, and the multiple flatters the company.
All the lease liabilities fund the stores, not just the part due this year.

questions.q: A JSE retailer has equity value of {eq|R0m}, debt of {d|R0m}, cash of {c|R0m} and lease liabilities of {l|R0m}. Its EBITDA (before rent, under IFRS 16) is {e|R0m}. What is EV/EBITDA on a consistent basis?

errs.why: Add the lease liabilities: the EBITDA is before rent.
Cash is subtracted.

questions.why: EBITDA before rent goes with an enterprise value that includes the lease liabilities.

questions.q: A retailer reports EBITDA of {e|R0m} under IFRS 16 and paid {lp|R0m} on its store leases in the year. To compare it with figures from before 2019, roughly what is its EBITDA after rent?

errs.why: Under IFRS 16 the rent is already out of EBITDA’s costs: subtract the payments to get back to the old view.

questions.why: Taking the lease payments off gives the old view, EBITDA after rent. Use it only with an enterprise value that leaves the lease liabilities out.

questions.q: Peers are compared on enterprise value including leases over EBITDA before rent. A junior’s figures for one retailer. Which line is wrong?

options: EBITDA before rent: {e|R0m}, giving {ev/e|1x}
EBITDA after rent, with the leases added to EV twice
Equity value over EBITDA after rent

questions.why: Enterprise value includes the leases, so EBITDA must be before rent. Line 6 then inherits the wrong figure.

questions.q: A retailer moves to IFRS 16: its store rent of {r|R0m} a year becomes depreciation and interest on new lease liabilities. Nothing else changes. What happens to EBITDA, to debt including lease liabilities, and to the cash paid to landlords?

mag.q: By how much does EBITDA rise?

work: EBITDA no longer bears the rent of {r|R0m}, so it rises by about that much
The lease liabilities join the balance sheet as debt
The landlords are paid exactly as before
questions.why: The accounting moves the rent below EBITDA and puts the leases on the balance sheet; the cash paid is the same, so value shouldn’t change.

questions.q: Under normal market conditions, transaction comps tend to give a higher multiple range than trading comps.
questions.why: Buyers usually pay a control premium, and strategic buyers can often pay more because of expected synergies.

questions.q: With a fixed exchange ratio, the number of shares received is fixed, but their value moves with the acquirer’s share price.
questions.why: Both sides share the risk and opportunity of price moves after announcement. It is the more common structure.

questions.q: With a floating exchange ratio, the target’s shareholders bear the risk of a fall in the acquirer’s share price.
questions.why: The value per share is fixed, so the acquirer bears that risk by issuing more shares if its price falls.

questions.q: For precedent transactions, all in-the-money options are counted in fully diluted shares, whether or not they have vested.
questions.why: Unvested options typically vest on a change of control. Out-of-the-money options are still excluded.

questions.q: The share price on the day before the deal announcement is always the right base for measuring the premium.
questions.why: If there were leaks, rumours or a “strategic alternatives” announcement, that price is not unaffected. Measure from before the leak, at several intervals.

questions.q: Transaction multiples are usually shown on reported LTM figures without synergies, though synergy-adjusted ones may be added.
questions.why: Adjusted multiples add full run-rate cost synergies (excluding costs to achieve) to EBITDA or EPS to show what the buyer effectively paid.

questions.q: What are the two main reasons transaction multiples tend to exceed trading multiples?
options: A control premium, and synergies that strategic buyers expect to realise
Higher interest rates at the time of the deal, and the tax savings on debt
Lower trading volumes in the target’s shares, and accounting differences
Analyst optimism about the sector, and share buybacks by listed companies
questions.why: In return for the premium, the buyer controls the business and its cash flows. Synergies add value beyond the target’s stand-alone results.

questions.q: For which kind of deal is it hardest to find reliable deal information?
options: A private buyer acquiring a private target with non-public financing
A listed buyer acquiring a listed target, paid for with its own shares
A listed buyer issuing registered shares to pay for a private target
An LBO funded with registered high-yield bonds sold to the public
questions.why: There are no disclosure requirements, so the banker relies on press releases, news and trade journals, and some deals can’t be used at all.

questions.q: A corporation that needs cash sells a non-core division. How might this affect the price?
options: It may accept a lower value in exchange for speed and certainty of completion
It will demand the highest possible price, since it needs every rand it can get
It has no effect on the price, since buyers only look at the division’s results
The buyer must pay a higher control premium to persuade the board to sell
questions.why: Seller motivations matter. Equally, a buyer may “stretch” for an asset with big synergies or scarcity value.

questions.q: Why would a high-multiple LBO won at auction in the mid-2000s credit boom be less relevant for valuing a company in 2009?
options: Debt was abundant and cheap then, but scarce and expensive afterwards, changing what buyers could pay
LBOs never provide useful multiples, because sponsors pay less than strategic buyers do for the same assets
Auctions always produce prices below fair value, so the multiples from that time understate value
The accounting rules for LBOs were different then, so the reported EBITDA figures can’t be compared
questions.why: Market conditions directly affect the availability and cost of financing, and so the price buyers will or can pay.

questions.q: When is a floating exchange ratio typically used?
options: When the acquirer is much larger than the target
When the target is much larger than the acquirer
When the deal is all cash
When both companies are private
questions.why: A slump in a small target barely affects a big acquirer, but the reverse isn’t true, which justifies giving the target a fixed value.

questions.q: In a fixed exchange ratio deal, what does a collar do?
options: Guarantees the target’s holders a value within a set range, whatever the acquirer’s shares do
Fixes the acquirer’s share price at its level on the day the deal is announced
Caps the number of new shares the acquirer can issue to complete the transaction
Prevents rival bidders from making an offer until the shareholders have voted on the deal
questions.why: For example, an offer worth R20 a share might be guaranteed to deliver between R18 and R22 between signing and closing.

questions.q: Precedent transactions imply a valuation well below trading comps. What should the banker do?
options: Recheck both peer sets and the calculations, though it can be valid if the sector is at a cyclical high or “in play”
Use the lower figure without question, since precedent transactions reflect real prices actually paid
Discard the precedent transactions entirely, since comps are always the more reliable of the two methods
Average the two valuations and move on, since the differences between methods tend to cancel each other out
questions.why: Normally precedents sit above comps because of control premiums, so a big gap the other way is a red flag worth checking.

questions.q: In a tender offer, which document contains the target board’s recommendation to its shareholders?
options: Schedule 14D-9
Schedule TO
Form 10-Q
Schedule 13E-3
questions.why: The acquirer files the Schedule TO; the target responds with the 14D-9, typically including a fairness opinion.

questions.q: The universe’s mean is 7.5× LTM EBITDA, but the three most relevant deals were done at 8.0× to 8.5×. Which range best follows the book’s approach?
questions.why: The range leans on the best transactions while keeping the wider universe in view.

questions.q: Which of these is a weakness of precedent transactions?
options: A time lag: past deals may not reflect today’s conditions
It ignores the actual prices that buyers paid for targets
It always requires the target’s management projections
It cannot be used to value companies in M&A situations
questions.why: Other weaknesses: few truly comparable deals, limited information, and prices that rest on undisclosed projections rather than LTM figures.

questions.q: An acquirer offers {r|2} of its shares for each target share. The acquirer trades at {pa|R}, and the target has {n|0m} fully diluted shares. What equity value does the offer imply?

errs.why: That values each target share at the acquirer’s price. Multiply by the exchange ratio first.
The exchange ratio multiplies the acquirer’s price; it doesn’t divide it.

ask.q: What does the exchange ratio tell you?
options: How many acquirer shares each target share receives
The premium over the target’s share price
The share of the merged company the target will own
ask.why: A ratio of 0.6 means 0.6 of an acquirer share for every target share, so its rand value moves with the acquirer’s price.

questions.why: Value each target share at the exchange ratio times the acquirer’s price, then multiply by the fully diluted shares.

questions.q: In a fixed exchange ratio deal, each target share receives {r|2} acquirer shares, announced when the acquirer traded at {pa|R}. Before closing the acquirer’s shares fall {d|0%}, and there is no collar. What is each target share now worth?

errs.why: That is the value at announcement. With a fixed ratio and no collar, the value falls with the acquirer’s price.
Multiply the new price by the exchange ratio.

questions.why: With a fixed ratio the number of shares is locked in, so their value moves with the acquirer’s share price.

questions.q: Under a floating exchange ratio, target holders are to receive {v|R} of acquirer shares for each target share. At closing the acquirer trades at {pa|R}. How many acquirer shares does each target share receive?

errs.why: Divide the promised value by the acquirer’s price, not the other way round.

questions.why: A floating ratio fixes the value; the number of shares adjusts to the acquirer’s price at closing.
questions.hint: Acquirer shares per target share, to 3 decimal places.

questions.q: An offer gives {c|R} in cash plus {r|2} acquirer shares (trading at {pa|R}) for each of the target’s {n|0m} shares. What equity value does it imply?

errs.why: Add the value of the shares to the cash.
Value the shares at the acquirer’s price, not one rand each.

questions.why: Value the share part at the acquirer’s price and add the cash.

questions.q: A target traded at {u|R} before rumours of a sale lifted it to {pd|R} the day before the announcement. The offer is {o|R}. What premium does the offer pay over the unaffected price?

errs.why: That is the premium to the day before, which the rumours had already lifted. Use the unaffected price.
Divide the increase by the unaffected price, not by the offer.

questions.why: Measure the premium against the unaffected price, before rumours or leaks moved it.

questions.q: The offer is {o|R} a share. The target has {b|0m} basic shares and {op|1m} options with an average exercise price of {k|R}, some not yet vested. What is the equity purchase price?
work: A change of control usually makes all options vest, so count them all

errs.why: Options in the money at the offer price add shares too, vested or not.
The exercise cash buys shares back, so only the net new shares count.

questions.why: Use the offer price for the treasury stock method, and count unvested options too: a change of control usually accelerates vesting.

questions.q: The equity purchase price is {eqp|R0m}. The target has debt of {d|R0m}, cash of {c|R0m} and LTM EBITDA of {e|R0m}. What is the EV/LTM EBITDA multiple?

errs.why: That divides equity value by EBITDA. Add net debt first.
Cash is subtracted, not added.

questions.why: Transaction value is the equity purchase price plus net debt; divide by LTM EBITDA.

questions.q: A deal values the target at {ev|R0m}, on LTM EBITDA of {e|R0m}. The buyer expects {s|R0m} of annual run-rate cost synergies. What is the synergy-adjusted multiple?

errs.why: That ignores the synergies. Add them to EBITDA.
Synergies add to EBITDA; they aren’t subtracted.

questions.why: Add the expected synergies to EBITDA: the multiple the buyer is really paying is lower once they are counted.

questions.q: A buyer pays {P|R0m} for {s|0%} of a company’s shares. What equity value does that imply for the whole company?

errs.why: Divide by the stake to scale up to 100%; multiplying scales down.
That is the price of the stake, not of the whole company.

questions.why: Scale the price up from the stake bought to the whole company.

questions.q: A selected range of {m1|1x} to {m1+1|1x} LTM EBITDA is applied to a private company with LTM EBITDA of {e|R0m} and net debt of {nd|R0m}. What equity value does the low end imply?

errs.why: That is enterprise value. Take off net debt.
That is the high end of the range.

questions.why: The multiple gives enterprise value; take off net debt for equity value.

questions.q: Put the five steps of precedent transactions analysis in order.
items: Select the universe of comparable acquisitions
Locate the deal-related and financial information
Spread the key statistics, ratios and transaction multiples
questions.why: The same five-step shape as comparable companies, applied to past deals.
questions.src: Precedent Transactions Analysis: the five steps

questions.q: A deal offers {r|2} acquirer shares for each target share (a fixed ratio, no collar). Before closing the acquirer’s shares fall {d|0%} from {pa|R}. What happens to the number of acquirer shares each target holder gets, and to their value?

mag.q: What is each target share now worth?

questions.why: A fixed ratio locks in the number of shares, so the target’s holders carry the risk of the acquirer’s price falling.

questions.q: A deal promises {v|R} of acquirer shares for each target share (a floating ratio). Before closing the acquirer’s shares fall. What happens to the number of acquirer shares issued, and to the value each target holder gets?
questions.why: A floating ratio fixes the value, so the acquirer issues more shares when its price falls: the acquirer carries the price risk.

questions.q: In a takeover, which options count towards the equity purchase price?
options: All options in the money at the offer price, vested or not
Only vested options, valued at today’s share price
Only options held by directors
questions.why: A change of control usually accelerates vesting, so every in-the-money option counts, measured at the offer price.
miss: Vesting usually accelerates on a change of control, and the offer price, not today’s price, sets what is in the money.
All in-the-money options count, whoever holds them.

questions.q: An analyst’s premium calculation. Which line is wrong?

fix.q: What should the premium line say?

questions.why: A premium is measured as a percentage of the unaffected price.

questions.q: Fully diluted shares for a takeover at {o|R} a share (the target traded at {u|R} before the offer). Which line is wrong?

options: The offer price: {op*k|R1m} ÷ {o|R} = {op*k/o|2m}
The exercise price: {op*k|R1m} ÷ {k|R} = {op|2m}
No buyback at all

questions.why: In a deal, the treasury stock method runs at the offer price: that is what the options are worth when the deal closes.

questions.q: An analyst’s transaction value. Which line is wrong?

options: Less cash: {c|R0m}
Plus half the cash: {c/2|R0m}
Plus cash, less debt

questions.why: Cash is subtracted: the buyer gets it with the business.

questions.q: An analyst’s synergy-adjusted multiple. Which line is wrong?

options: {ev|R0m} ÷ {s|R0m} = {ev/s|1x}
{ev|R0m} ÷ {e|R0m} = {ev/e|1x}

questions.why: Synergies add to the EBITDA the buyer expects to own, so they lower the multiple paid.

questions.q: Valuing a whole company from a stake sale. Which line is wrong?
lines: A buyer paid {P|R0m} for {s|0%} of the shares
Plus net debt of {nd|R0m}: enterprise value {P*s+nd|R0m}

options: {P|R0m} + {s|0%} of net debt

questions.why: Scale up from the stake to the whole by dividing. Line 3’s method is right; it only inherits the wrong figure.

questions.q: Valuing a share offer. Which line is wrong?
lines: Exchange ratio: {r|2} acquirer shares per target share
questions.why: Each target share receives r acquirer shares, so it is worth r times the acquirer’s price.

questions.q: In your head: the unaffected share price was {u|R} and the offer is {o|R}. Roughly what premium is that?
questions.why: Price over unaffected price, less one: fast and worth checking against every headline.

questions.q: In your head: a buyer pays {eqp|R0m} for the shares and takes on {nd|R0m} of net debt. LTM EBITDA is {e|R0m}. Roughly what multiple is that?
questions.why: Equity price plus net debt over EBITDA.

questions.q: Before you read: why would a buyer pay more for a whole company than its shares were trading at?
options: Control lets it run the business its way and capture savings
Share prices always undervalue companies, so a premium corrects it
The law requires any buyer to pay a premium of at least 30%
questions.why: Buyers pay a control premium for the right to direct the business and capture synergies.

questions.q: Before you read: for the same company, which multiple tends to be higher?
options: The multiple paid in a takeover
The multiple it trades at day to day
They are always the same
questions.why: Deal multiples usually include a control premium and expected synergies, so they sit above trading multiples.

questions.q: Before you read: a company in the same industry can often outbid a private equity fund. Why?
options: It can save costs or grow sales by combining the two businesses
It can always borrow more cheaply than any fund is able to
Private equity funds are not allowed to pay takeover premiums
questions.why: Strategic buyers can pay for synergies a financial sponsor can’t capture.

questions.q: A JSE company has {n|0m} shares in issue, and a buyer already holds {h|1m}. How many more shares would take the buyer to 35%, the level at which South African law requires it to offer to buy out the other shareholders?

errs.why: That is the whole 35%: take off what the buyer already holds.

questions.why: Under the Companies Act and the Takeover Regulations, a buyer that goes from below 35% of a regulated company’s voting securities to 35% or more, counting anyone acting in concert with it, must make a mandatory offer to the other holders.
questions.src: South African takeover rules (beyond the book)

questions.q: Two funds, acting together, buy 20% and 16% of a JSE company in the same week. What follows?
options: Together they hold 36%, so they must offer to buy out the other shareholders
Nothing: each fund is below 35% on its own, so no rule applies to either
They must sell shares back to the market until together they hold under 35%
questions.why: The holdings of persons acting in concert are added together for the 35% test, and crossing it requires a mandatory offer, not a sale.
questions.src: South African takeover rules (beyond the book)
miss: Persons acting in concert are counted together.
The rule requires an offer to the other holders; selling down isn’t the remedy it sets.

questions.q: A shareholder that has held 40% of a JSE company for years buys another 5%. Must it now make a mandatory offer?
options: No
Yes
The offer is triggered by going from below 35% to 35% or more; buying more after that doesn’t trigger a new one
Every purchase above 35% triggers a fresh offer to all the other shareholders
Mandatory offers only apply once a buyer reaches more than half of the shares

questions.why: Section 123 looks at the acquisition that takes a holder across 35%. A holder already above it doesn’t trigger a new offer by buying more.
questions.src: South African takeover rules (beyond the book)
miss: It crossed 35% long ago; buying more doesn’t trigger a new offer.

questions.q: The value a DCF produces is called intrinsic value, as distinct from the market value at a given moment.
questions.why: That is why a DCF is a useful check on market-based methods, which can be distorted by bubbles or credit crunches.

questions.q: An increase in net working capital is a use of cash and reduces free cash flow.
questions.why: A growing company typically ties up more cash in receivables and inventory. A decrease in NWC is a source of cash.

questions.q: Depreciation and amortisation reduce reported earnings but are added back when calculating free cash flow.
questions.why: They are non-cash expenses. Capex, by contrast, is an actual cash outflow and is subtracted.

questions.q: Adding more debt to a capital structure lowers WACC without limit, because interest is tax-deductible.
questions.why: WACC falls only up to the optimal capital structure. Beyond it, the cost of possible financial distress outweighs the tax benefit, and WACC rises.

questions.q: Under CAPM, equity investors are compensated for systematic risk but not for unsystematic (company-specific) risk.
questions.why: Unsystematic risk can be diversified away, so the market pays no premium for bearing it.

questions.q: The terminal year should reflect a normalised, steady-state level of performance, not a cyclical high or low.
questions.why: Because the terminal value is such a large share of value, an unrepresentative final year would skew the whole valuation.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT deducted (or added) in moving from EBIT to unlevered free cash flow?
options: Interest expense
Taxes on EBIT
Capital expenditure
Increase in net working capital
questions.why: FCF = EBIT − taxes + D&A − capex − increase in NWC. Interest belongs to debt holders and is left out.

questions.q: When might a projection period much longer than five years be appropriate?
options: For an early-stage, fast-growing company, or one with long-term contracted revenue such as a utility
For any mature company in a stable sector, since its cash flows are easier to forecast far ahead
Whenever the WACC is high, since a longer period reduces the weight of the terminal value
When the company carries a lot of debt that will have to be repaid over more than five years
questions.why: The aim is to project until the business reaches a steady state that can support the terminal value.

questions.q: How do bankers usually estimate beta for a private company?
options: Unlever the betas of listed peers, average them, then relever at the target’s capital structure
Use a beta of 1.0, since a private company’s shares can’t be compared with the market
Use the beta of the largest listed company in the sector, as the best-known benchmark
Average the peers’ levered betas without adjustment, since they already include leverage
questions.why: Unlevering strips out each peer’s leverage; relevering applies the target’s own D/E and tax rate.

questions.q: Why do many bankers prefer a predicted beta to a historical one?
options: Past returns may not reliably show future risk, and predicted betas are meant to look forward
Historical betas can’t be used in published valuations under the regulators’ current rules
Predicted betas are always lower, which raises the valuation the seller is hoping for
Historical betas ignore the market and measure only the share’s own price movements
questions.why: Historical beta looks back over two to five years. What matters for the cost of equity is expected risk.

questions.q: Why might a banker add a size premium to the CAPM cost of equity?
options: Smaller companies appear riskier, and limited trading means beta may not fully capture that risk
Larger companies grow faster, so smaller ones need a premium to make up for slower growth
Regulators require it for any company with a market value below a set level of capitalisation
It reduces the cost of equity for smaller companies, which lifts their valuation to fair levels
questions.why: The evidence suggests smaller companies earn higher returns. The premium, tiered by market capitalisation, adds that risk.

questions.q: What target capital structure is typically used when calculating WACC for a private company?
options: The mean or median of its comparable companies
Its current capital structure, whatever it is
100% equity, since private firms rarely borrow
The structure that carries the most debt possible
questions.why: For a listed company, the existing structure is used if it is comfortably within the peer range. It is then held constant throughout the projection period.

questions.q: The perpetuity growth rate implied by your exit multiple is 7%. What does that suggest?
options: The exit multiple may be unrealistically high
The WACC is too high
The projections are too conservative
Nothing: any implied growth rate is acceptable
questions.why: Long-term growth is typically about 2–4%, roughly nominal GDP growth. Each method should sanity-check the other.

questions.q: Why do bankers often assume depreciation and capex converge by the final projection year?
options: So the asset base stays steady in perpetuity, as befits a steady-state business
To increase the valuation by lowering the capex in the terminal year
Because the tax rules require depreciation to equal capital spending
To reduce working capital needs in the final year of the projection
questions.why: Otherwise the terminal value would reflect an endlessly growing or shrinking asset base.

questions.q: Which of these is a weakness of DCF analysis?
options: Its value can rest largely on the terminal value and is very sensitive to small changes in assumptions
It ignores cash flow and relies only on accounting earnings, which can be managed by companies
It depends entirely on comparable companies, so it fails when there are no listed peers to use
It cannot model different scenarios, so it gives only a single answer for the company’s value
questions.why: It also depends on accurate forecasts and assumes a constant capital structure. Its strengths: cash-flow based, market-independent, self-sufficient and flexible.

questions.q: A company has very different business segments. What approach does the book suggest?
options: A sum-of-the-parts DCF: value each segment with its own WACC and add them up
Use the WACC of the largest segment for all of them, for consistency
Average the segments’ growth rates and value the company as one unit
Ignore the smaller segments, since they barely move the overall value
questions.why: Segments with different risks deserve different costs of capital.

questions.q: EBIT is {ebit|R0m} and the tax rate {t|0%}. D&A is {da|R0m}, capital expenditure {cx|R0m}, and net working capital rises by {dn|R0m}. What is unlevered free cash flow?

errs.why: An increase in working capital uses cash, so it is subtracted.
Tax on EBIT comes off first: free cash flow is after tax.
D&A is a non-cash charge: add it back.

ask.q: Why is tax worked out on EBIT rather than on profit after interest?
options: Unlevered free cash flow is the cash before any payments to lenders, so it is taxed as if there were no debt
Interest is never tax-deductible
Tax on EBIT is always lower, which is more prudent
ask.why: Unlevered FCF belongs to all the company’s funders. The benefit of tax-deductible interest is picked up in WACC instead, through the after-tax cost of debt.

questions.why: EBIT after tax, plus D&A (a non-cash charge), less capital spending and the increase in working capital.
questions.src: Step II: Projection of free cash flow

questions.q: Net working capital is {n0|R0m} this year and is projected at {n1|R0m} next year. What happens to next year’s free cash flow, and by how much?

mag.q: By how much does free cash flow fall?

work: Change in NWC = {n1|R0m} − {n0|R0m} = {dd|R0m}, a use of cash
questions.why: More working capital ties up more cash, so the increase is a use of cash and reduces free cash flow.

questions.q: Accounts receivable are {ar|R0m} on annual sales of {s|R0m}. What is days sales outstanding (DSO), using a 365-day year?

errs.why: That is receivables turnover (sales over receivables), not days.

questions.why: DSO measures how long customers take to pay: receivables over sales, times the days in the year.
questions.hint: In days, to the nearest day.

questions.q: Inventory is {inv|R0m} and cost of goods sold is {cogs|R0m}. How many days of inventory does the company hold (365-day year)?

errs.why: That is inventory turns, not days.

questions.why: Inventory is measured against cost of goods sold, not sales, because that is the cost it is carried at.
questions.hint: In days, to the nearest day.

questions.q: The risk-free rate is {rf|1%}, the levered beta {b|2} and the market risk premium {mrp|1%}. What is the CAPM cost of equity?

errs.why: Beta scales the market risk premium; it isn’t left out.
Only the market risk premium is multiplied by beta.
Beta multiplies the premium, not the risk-free rate.

questions.why: CAPM: the risk-free rate, plus beta times the market risk premium.

questions.q: Debt is {wd|0%} of total capitalisation, the pre-tax cost of debt {kd|1%}, the tax rate {t|0%} and the cost of equity {ke|1%}. What is WACC?

errs.why: Use the after-tax cost of debt: interest is tax-deductible.
The weights are swapped: equity is the larger share here.
Weight each cost by its share of capitalisation.

ask.q: Why is the cost of debt multiplied by (1 − tax rate)?
options: Interest is tax-deductible, so each rand of interest costs the company less than a rand after tax
Lenders are taxed on their interest, so they accept less
It converts the cost of debt to a real rate
ask.why: The interest tax shield makes debt cheaper after tax. Unlevered FCF ignores it, so WACC carries it.

questions.why: Weight the cost of equity and the after-tax cost of debt by their shares of total capitalisation.
questions.src: Step III: Weighted average cost of capital

questions.q: A peer has a levered beta of {bl|2}, a debt-to-equity ratio of {de|0%} and a tax rate of {t|0%}. What is its unlevered beta?

errs.why: Debt’s effect on beta is after tax: use (1 − t) × D/E.
That relevers. To unlever, divide.
The peer’s debt has to come out of its beta.

questions.why: Unlevering strips out the effect of the peer’s own debt, leaving the risk of the business alone.
questions.src: Step III: Unlevering and relevering beta

questions.q: The peers’ average unlevered beta is {bu|2}. Relever it at a target debt-to-equity ratio of {de|0%} and a tax rate of {t|0%}.

errs.why: Use the after-tax debt-to-equity: (1 − t) × D/E.
That unlevers. To relever, multiply.
The formula uses debt to equity, not debt to total capital.

questions.why: Relevering adds back the risk of the target’s own planned debt.
questions.src: Step III: Unlevering and relevering beta

questions.q: Terminal-year free cash flow is {f|R0m}, the perpetuity growth rate {g|1%} and WACC {w|1%}. What is the terminal value by the perpetuity growth method?

errs.why: Grow the terminal-year cash flow by one year first: the formula uses next year’s flow.
Divide by WACC less the growth rate.
Growth is subtracted from WACC, not added.

ask.q: Why is the cash flow grown by one year before dividing?
options: The formula values a stream that starts one year after the terminal year
Growth has to be counted twice to be prudent
It converts the flow into today’s money
ask.why: The Gordon growth formula gives the value at year n of cash flows from year n + 1 onwards, so it needs year n + 1’s flow.

questions.why: The perpetuity formula values the cash flow one year after the terminal year, so grow it first.

questions.q: Terminal-year EBITDA (year {n}) is {e|R0m}, the exit multiple {m|1x} and WACC {w|1%}. What is the present value of the terminal value, discounting at year-end?

errs.why: The exit-multiple value is discounted at year-end, not with the mid-year convention.
Bring the terminal value back to today.
Discount over the full {n} years.

questions.why: An exit-multiple terminal value is discounted with the full-year factor: the exit is assumed to happen at the end of the final year.
questions.src: Step V: Present value of terminal value

questions.q: A DCF gives an enterprise value of {ev|R0m}. The company has debt of {d|R0m}, cash of {c|R0m} and non-controlling interest of {nci|R0m}. What is implied equity value?

errs.why: Cash is added back on the way to equity value.
Non-controlling interest is a claim on the business: take it off.
That is the bridge the wrong way round: from enterprise value to equity, claims come off.

questions.why: Work back from enterprise value: take off the other claims (debt and non-controlling interest) and add back cash.

questions.q: The present value of the projected free cash flows is {a|R0m} and of the terminal value {b|R0m}. What share of enterprise value comes from the terminal value?

errs.why: That is the share from the projection period.
Divide by total enterprise value, not by the projection period alone.

questions.why: A share of three-quarters or more is common, which is why the terminal assumptions deserve the most scrutiny.

questions.q: At a discount rate of {w|1%}, what is the mid-year discount factor for year {n}?
work: Mid-year: the year’s cash arrives on average halfway through it, so discount over {n} − 0.5 years

errs.why: That is the year-end factor. Mid-year discounts over half a year less.
Mid-year brings the cash forward by half a year, not back.

questions.why: The mid-year convention treats each year’s cash flow as arriving in the middle of the year, which is closer to reality and slightly raises value.
questions.hint: As a factor, to 3 decimal places (for example 0.953).

questions.q: Put the five steps of a discounted cash flow analysis in order.
items: Study the target and determine its key performance drivers
Calculate present value and determine the valuation
questions.why: Understand the business, project its cash, set the discount rate, value what lies beyond the forecast, then bring it all back to today.

questions.q: WACC rises by one percentage point, with no other change. What happens to unlevered free cash flow, the present value of the terminal value and enterprise value?

measures.name: Present value of the terminal value

questions.why: WACC is the discount rate, so it changes values, not cash flows. A higher rate shrinks every present value, the terminal value most of all.

questions.q: A company pays its suppliers later, so accounts payable rise by {x|R0m}. What happens to net working capital and to free cash flow, and by how much does free cash flow change?

mag.q: By how much does free cash flow rise?

questions.why: Payables are a liability that funds the business: holding on to suppliers’ cash lowers net working capital and is a source of cash.

questions.q: Depreciation rises by {x|R0m} and the tax rate is {t|0%}. What happens to EBITDA, net income and cash?

mag.q: By how much does cash change?

work: Cash rises by the tax saved: {x|R0m} × {t|0%} = {x*t|R1m}
questions.why: EBITDA is before depreciation. Net income falls by the after-tax amount, but depreciation is not a cash cost, so cash rises by the tax it saves.

questions.q: A DCF’s terminal value by the exit multiple method implies a perpetuity growth rate of 9%, well above long-run growth in the economy. What is the best response?
options: Revisit the exit multiple: it is probably too high for a business in steady state
Raise WACC until the two methods agree
Keep it: a higher growth rate is more conservative
Drop the perpetuity growth method, since the multiple comes from the market
questions.why: Each method checks the other. An exit multiple that implies growth faster than the economy for ever is hard to defend.
questions.src: Step IV: Cross-checking the terminal value
miss: WACC is set from the market and the capital structure, not tuned to make the methods agree.
A higher growth rate raises value: it is the opposite of conservative.
The cross-check is the point: an exit multiple can embed unrealistic growth.

questions.q: Which convention gives a slightly higher DCF value, and why?
options: Mid-year, because cash is assumed to arrive through the year rather than all at its end
Year-end, because it counts a full year of cash flow before discounting each period
Neither: the timing convention only changes the terminal value, never the rest
questions.why: Mid-year discounting brings each year’s cash flow half a year closer, so each present value is a little larger.
miss: Both conventions count the same cash; year-end simply discounts it over a longer period.
It changes the discount factor on every projected year.

questions.q: A DCF uses a terminal value of {tv|R0m}, from an exit multiple. Terminal-year free cash flow is {f|R0m} and WACC is {w|1%}. What perpetuity growth rate does the terminal value imply?
work: From TV = FCF × (1 + g) ÷ (WACC − g): g = (TV × WACC − FCF) ÷ (TV + FCF)

errs.why: That is the cash yield on the terminal value, not the growth rate.
That is WACC itself; solve the formula for g.

questions.why: Rearranging the perpetuity formula turns any terminal value into the growth rate it assumes for ever: a quick sanity check.
questions.src: Step IV: Implied perpetuity growth rate

questions.q: A perpetuity growth terminal value is {tv|R0m}. Terminal-year EBITDA is {e|R0m}. What exit multiple does it imply?

errs.why: Divide the terminal value by EBITDA, not the other way round.
