questions.why: Compare it with the multiples peers trade at: a perpetuity value far above them deserves a second look at growth or WACC.

questions.q: Year {n} free cash flow is {f|R0m}. Using the mid-year convention and a WACC of {w|1%}, what is its present value?

errs.why: That is year-end discounting. Mid-year uses half a year less.

questions.why: Under the mid-year convention each year’s cash flow is discounted from the middle of that year.

questions.q: Accounts payable are {ap|R0m} and cost of goods sold {cogs|R0m}. What is days payable outstanding (DPO), using a 365-day year?

errs.why: That is payables turnover, not days.

questions.why: How long the company takes to pay its suppliers; payables are measured against cost of goods sold.
questions.hint: In days, to the nearest day.

questions.q: A junior’s terminal value. Which line is wrong?
questions.why: The perpetuity formula needs next year’s cash flow. Line 4 is the right method; it only inherits the wrong figure.

questions.q: A junior’s unlevered free cash flow. Which line is wrong?
lines: Plus D&A {da|R0m}, less capex {cx|R0m} and the increase in NWC {dn|R0m}

options: Leave it out: unlevered cash flow is before any payments to lenders
Add it back after tax
Deduct it after tax instead

questions.why: Unlevered free cash flow belongs to every funder, so interest stays out; the tax line should then be {ebit*t|R1m}, on EBIT.
questions.src: Step II: Projection of free cash flow

questions.q: A junior’s WACC, at a tax rate of {t|0%}. Which line is wrong?
lines: Cost of debt: {kd|1%} before tax, weight {wd|0%}

fix.q: What should line 3 use for debt?
options: {kd|1%} × (1 − {t|0%}) = {kd*(1-t)|2%}, the after-tax cost
{kd|1%} × {t|0%}, the tax saved
{ke|1%}, since debt and equity cost the same

questions.why: Interest is tax-deductible, so WACC uses the after-tax cost of debt.
questions.src: Step III: Weighted average cost of capital

questions.q: A junior’s cash flow bridge for one year. Which line is wrong?
lines: Plus the increase in net working capital: {dn|R0m}

options: Subtract the increase: more working capital uses cash
Leave it out: working capital isn’t cash
Add it twice, for both years

questions.why: An increase in net working capital ties up cash, so it reduces free cash flow.

questions.q: A junior relevers a beta of {bu|2} at a target debt-to-equity ratio of {de|0%} (tax {t|0%}). Which line is wrong?

options: No tax adjustment: {bu|2} × (1 + {de|2}) = {bu*(1+de)|2}

questions.why: The relevering formula uses debt to equity, not debt to total capital.
questions.src: Step III: Unlevering and relevering beta

questions.q: A junior discounts an exit-multiple terminal value with the mid-year convention switched on for the projections. Which line is wrong?

options: 1 ÷ (1 + {w|1%})^5 = {1/(1+w)^5|4}: the exit is at year-end

questions.why: An exit multiple values the business as if sold at the end of year 5, so it takes the year-end factor even when the yearly flows use mid-year.
questions.src: Step V: Present value of terminal value

questions.q: In your head: terminal-year cash flow {f|R0m}, growth {g|0%}, WACC {w|0%}. Roughly what is the perpetuity terminal value?
questions.why: Grow the flow by one year, then divide by the spread between WACC and growth.

questions.q: In your head: what is {f|R0m} received in {n} years worth today at {w|0%} (year-end)?
questions.why: Worth knowing by heart: at 10%, five years cuts value to about 0.62; at 15%, to about 0.50.

questions.q: Before you read: why is R100 received in five years worth less than R100 today?
options: Money today can be invested to earn a return, and future cash carries risk
Inflation in South Africa always runs above 10%, so prices double quickly
Cash received in the future is taxed twice, once when earned and once when paid
questions.why: The time value of money, plus risk: a DCF discounts future cash at a rate that reflects both.

questions.q: Before you read: which figure best shows the cash a business generates for all its funders?
options: Cash flow after tax, reinvestment and working capital, before any payments to lenders
Net income, which is what is left after interest, tax and every other cost
Revenue less cost of sales, which shows the cash each sale brings in for funders
questions.why: That is unlevered free cash flow, the cash a DCF discounts.

questions.q: Before you read: a DCF forecasts five years in detail. How might it value everything after that?
options: With a single “terminal value” that captures the years beyond the forecast
It ignores them, to be conservative, since no one can forecast that far
It keeps forecasting every year in detail, out to the year 2100
questions.why: The terminal value often makes up most of a DCF, so its assumptions matter a great deal.

questions.q: A DCF for a retailer adds the lease liabilities to debt in the bridge from enterprise value to equity value. How should its unlevered free cash flows treat the store lease payments?
options: Leave them out, as financing flows, like interest and debt repayments
Deduct them in full, as an operating cost of the stores
Deduct only the interest part, and leave the repayments out
questions.why: Be consistent. If leases are debt in the bridge, their payments are financing and stay out of unlevered cash flow. The other consistent route treats rent as an operating cost and leaves the leases out of the bridge.
miss: That counts the leases twice: once as cash going out, and again as debt in the bridge.
Interest on lease liabilities is financing too; only the whole payment, left out, is consistent.

questions.q: Sponsors have historically sought annual returns of 20% or more and an exit within about five years.
questions.why: The threshold can move with market conditions and the risk of the deal, but 20%+ has been the rule of thumb.

questions.q: In a traditional LBO, the sponsor’s equity makes up 60% to 70% of the financing, with debt the rest.
questions.why: Debt has typically been 60–70%, with equity 30–40%. In tight markets like 2009, equity rose towards half.

questions.q: IRR reflects the time value of money, while the cash return (multiple of money) does not.
questions.why: The same proceeds received sooner produce a higher IRR; the multiple is unchanged.

questions.q: A revolving credit facility can be drawn, repaid and drawn again, whereas a term loan cannot be reborrowed once repaid.
questions.why: The revolver provides ongoing liquidity and is usually undrawn at close; lenders earn a commitment fee on the unused part.

questions.q: Debt at the operating company is structurally senior to holding company debt, unless the operating company guarantees the latter.
questions.why: The assets sit in the operating company, whose creditors must be paid in full before anything flows up to its shareholder.

questions.q: Holding exit value fixed, more debt and a smaller equity cheque raise the sponsor’s returns, but also the company’s risk.
questions.why: Interest is tax-deductible too, but higher leverage raises the chance of financial distress and cuts flexibility.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT a typical feature of a strong LBO candidate?
options: Heavy, ongoing capital spending needs
Strong, predictable cash flow
A leading, defensible market position
A proven management team
questions.why: Low capex leaves more cash for debt service. Growth and efficiency opportunities and a strong asset base also help.

questions.q: Why does a strong asset base help an LBO?
options: It gives lenders collateral and comfort on recovery, opening up more bank debt, the cheapest kind
It raises the company’s P/E ratio, so the sponsor can sell the business for more at exit
It removes the need for covenants, since lenders can simply seize the assets if payments stop
It means little or no equity is needed, since the assets alone can secure the whole price
questions.why: Receivables and inventory are especially valued for their liquidity. Still, an asset-light company can qualify if its cash flow is strong.

questions.q: How does an institutional Term Loan B typically differ from a Term Loan A?
options: Nominal amortisation (about 1% a year), a bullet at maturity, a longer tenor and institutional lenders
Heavy amortisation and a shorter tenor, since it is held mainly by the arranging commercial banks
It is unsecured and pays a fixed rate, so it ranks behind the revolver and Term Loan A in a default
It can be repaid and drawn again during its life, like a revolver, but with a longer final maturity
questions.why: Institutional investors prefer longer, non-amortising loans with higher coupons; banks prefer the TLA to mature first.

questions.q: What does mezzanine debt typically offer investors?
options: A higher return than high yield bonds, often mixing cash and PIK interest, sometimes with warrants
First lien security over all the assets and the lowest coupon of any layer in the structure
Daily liquidity, since mezzanine debt trades on an exchange like ordinary listed bonds do
A guaranteed return of capital, since the sponsor must repay it before taking any dividends
questions.why: It sits between debt and equity and is highly negotiated. For sponsors it is cheaper than equity when other debt isn’t available.

questions.q: How does an incurrence covenant work?
options: It blocks actions such as new debt or dividends only if the issuer would then fail a ratio test and lack a basket
It requires the issuer to meet set financial ratios at the end of every single quarter, whatever actions it takes
It bans all dividends to the sponsor for as long as any of the bonds remain outstanding
It lets lenders approve the share price at which the sponsor may later sell the company
questions.why: Maintenance covenants, typical of bank debt, must be met every quarter, with leverage limits that step down over time.

questions.q: Why do sponsors usually want management to roll over or invest equity?
options: To align management’s incentives with the sponsor’s in creating value
To reduce the amount of debt needed to finance the purchase
Because lenders won’t provide the debt unless management invests
To avoid paying management salaries during the holding period
questions.why: Broad equity incentives tied to targets are often a key difference from public-company ownership.

questions.q: What does a change of control put in a bond indenture give bondholders?
options: The right to require the issuer to buy back the bonds at 101% of par if ownership changes
The right to convert their bonds into shares of the new owner at a set conversion price
A higher coupon each year until the new owner repays the bonds in full at maturity
Control of the board until the new owner has refinanced all of the existing bonds
questions.why: It protects bondholders from a new owner with a riskier plan.

questions.q: Why have sponsors traditionally preferred to sell portfolio companies to strategic buyers?
options: Strategic buyers can often pay more, thanks to synergies and a lower cost of capital
Strategic buyers never use debt, so the deal is far more certain to close on time
IPOs are prohibited for sponsor-owned companies under most stock exchange rules
Strategic buyers also take over the sponsor’s fund and its other portfolio companies
questions.why: In strong debt markets, rival sponsors can compete on price, so sales to other sponsors have grown.

questions.q: A sponsor puts in 30% of the purchase price as equity. What comfort does this give lenders?
options: The business’s value would have to fall by more than 30% before their principal is at risk
Their loans are guaranteed by the sponsor up to 30% of the purchase price if the deal fails
Interest will always be paid, since the sponsor must cover any shortfall from its own fund
They own 30% of the company’s equity, so they share in any gain the sponsor makes at exit
questions.why: Equity is wiped out before debt holders lose value. It acts as a cushion beneath the debt.

questions.q: Which company could usually support the highest leverage?
options: A subscription business with highly visible cash flows
A highly cyclical steel producer at the top of its cycle
An early-stage company with fast but volatile sales
A company in a sector that is at a cyclical peak
questions.why: Markets and rating agencies take a more conservative view of leverage in cyclical sectors, to survive the troughs.

questions.q: A sponsor invests {e0|R0m} of equity and receives {e1|R0m} after {n} years, with nothing in between. What is the IRR?

errs.why: That spreads the gain evenly and ignores compounding. Take the n-th root of the multiple.
That is the total gain over the whole period, not a yearly rate.

ask.q: Why is the IRR the multiple’s fifth root, less one, over five years?
options: IRR is the yearly rate that compounds the equity into the exit proceeds over the holding period
It spreads the total gain evenly across the five years
Fund rules require it
ask.why: A 2.5× cash return over five years means (1 + IRR)^5 = 2.5, so IRR = 2.5^(1/5) − 1. Spreading the gain evenly ignores compounding.

questions.why: The IRR is the yearly rate that compounds the equity into the exit proceeds; the cash return ignores how long that took.

questions.q: A sponsor buys a company for {p|R0m} with {d|R0m} of debt and the rest in equity. Over {n} years {rp|R0m} of debt is repaid, and the company is sold for {x|R0m}. What is the sponsor’s cash return?

errs.why: Take the debt still owed off the sale price first: that is the lenders’ share.
Only the debt still outstanding at exit comes off, not the original amount.

questions.why: Every rand of debt repaid becomes a rand of equity value, even with no growth at all.

questions.q: A company is bought for {p|R0m} with {eq|R0m} of equity and {d|R0m} of debt. By the exit, {n} years later, debt has been cut to {d2|R0m} and the company sells for {x|R0m}. What is the cash return?

errs.why: That is the return on the whole company. The sponsor’s return is on its equity.
Use the debt left at exit, not the starting debt.

questions.why: Leverage magnifies returns: the smaller the equity cheque, the more each rand of value growth and debt paydown does for it.

questions.q: A {rc|R0m} revolver charges a {cf|2%} commitment fee a year on the undrawn amount. Average usage is {u|R0m}. What is the annual commitment fee?

errs.why: The fee is on the undrawn amount, not on what is drawn.
Only the undrawn part attracts the fee.

questions.why: The commitment fee pays the banks for keeping the undrawn part available; the drawn part pays interest instead.

questions.q: An asset-based facility of {f|R0m} lends {ar|0%} against eligible receivables of {r|R0m} and {ip|0%} against eligible inventory of {i|R0m}. How much can be borrowed?
work: Available = the lower of the base ({bb|R0m}) and the facility ({f|R0m}) = {av|R0m}

errs.why: Only an advance rate on each asset can be borrowed, not its full value.
The facility is a cap: you can’t borrow more than it.

questions.why: An asset-based loan is capped by its borrowing base, and never more than the facility size.

questions.q: A term loan pays the benchmark rate plus {s|2%}, with a {fl|2%} floor on the benchmark. The benchmark is {b|2%}. What is the interest rate?
work: The benchmark used is the higher of {b|2%} and the {fl|2%} floor = {max(b, fl)|2%}

errs.why: The floor applies: the benchmark can’t count below {fl|2%}.
The floor replaces a lower benchmark; it isn’t added to it.

questions.why: A floor sets a minimum for the benchmark, protecting lenders when rates are very low.

questions.q: An {y}-year bond with a {c|2%} coupon is non-callable for {nc} years, then callable at par plus half the coupon, stepping down. At what price can it first be called (per 100 of face value)?

errs.why: That is par plus the full coupon (the equity clawback price), not the first call price.
Early on the bonds are callable only at a premium.

questions.why: Call protection rewards bondholders for being repaid early: the first call price is par plus half the coupon, stepping down to par.
questions.hint: As a price per 100 of face value, to 2 decimal places.

questions.q: A 10% high yield bond has an equity clawback. If the issuer lists within three years, how much can it redeem, and at what price?
options: Up to 35% of the bonds, at 110
All of the bonds, at par (100)
Up to 35% of the bonds, at 101
Up to 10% of the bonds, at 135
questions.why: The clawback typically allows up to 35% to be redeemed with IPO proceeds at par plus the coupon.

questions.q: A buyout uses {d|R0m} more debt at {r|1%} interest. With a {t|0%} tax rate, what is the extra after-tax interest cost in the first year?

errs.why: Interest is deductible: take off the tax it saves.
That is the tax saved, not the after-tax cost.

questions.why: Interest is tax-deductible, so its real cost to the company is lower than the coupon.
questions.src: Economics of LBOs: cost of debt

questions.q: A {f|R0m} fund charges a {mf|1%} management fee and {c|0%} carried interest. In one year it earns {pr|R0m} of profit above its required return. What do the general partners receive in total?

errs.why: Add the carried interest on profits.
Add the management fee on the fund’s size.
The rates are swapped: the fee is on the fund, the carry on profits.

questions.why: Sponsors earn a fee on the fund’s size plus a share of profits (carry) once investors’ required returns are met.

questions.q: A company with EBITDA of {e|R0m} is bought at {m|1x} EBITDA, with debt of {lv|2x} EBITDA. What share of the price is equity?

errs.why: That is the debt share. Equity is the rest.
Divide the debt by the price, not by price plus debt.

questions.why: Equity fills the gap between the price and what lenders will provide.

questions.q: Order these layers of an LBO financing from most senior (repaid first) to most junior.
items: Revolving credit facility and term loans (first lien bank debt)
questions.why: Seniority runs from secured bank debt, through unsecured and subordinated bonds and mezzanine, to equity, which is paid last and earns the most.

questions.q: A sponsor finances the same purchase with more debt and less equity. The exit value is unchanged. What happens to the equity cheque, the sponsor’s IRR and interest cover?
questions.why: Leverage magnifies returns on a smaller equity cheque, but more interest means thinner cover and more risk.

questions.q: At exit, the market multiple for the sector has fallen one turn below the entry multiple. EBITDA and debt are as planned. What happens to exit equity value, the cash return and the debt repaid?
questions.why: Multiple contraction hits equity directly; debt paydown is banked whatever the market does, which is why sponsors value it.

questions.q: Which source of LBO returns depends least on market conditions at exit?
options: Paying down debt from the company’s cash flow
Selling at a higher multiple than was paid
A hot IPO market at the time of exit
A strategic buyer bidding for synergies
questions.why: Debt paydown turns cash flow into equity value year by year; multiple expansion and exit routes depend on the market at the time.
miss: Multiple expansion depends entirely on the market at exit; prudent models assume none.
IPO windows open and close with markets.
A strategic bidder may or may not be there at exit.

questions.q: A sponsor wants the flexibility to repay debt early without penalty. Which instrument fits best?
options: Floating-rate first lien bank debt
Fixed-rate high yield notes with call protection
Senior subordinated notes
Mezzanine debt with warrants
questions.why: Bank debt is usually prepayable at par at any time; bonds and mezzanine carry call protection and premiums.
miss: Call protection is exactly what stops early repayment at par.
Subordinated notes are bonds, usually with call protection.
Mezzanine is typically non-callable early and often pays a premium.

questions.q: Lenders will provide {lv|2x} EBITDA of debt and the sponsor must put in at least {ep|0%} of the purchase price. What is the most the sponsor can pay, as a multiple of EBITDA?
work: Debt covers {1-ep|0%} of the price, so price = debt ÷ {1-ep|0%}

errs.why: Divide by the debt share of the price ({1-ep|0%}), not the equity share.
Debt is a share of the price, so divide by that share.

questions.why: Debt capacity and the minimum equity share together set the price a sponsor can afford: one way an LBO frames valuation.

questions.q: Mezzanine notes of {m|R0m} pay {r|1%} a year entirely in kind (PIK), compounding. What will be owed after {n} years?

errs.why: PIK interest compounds: interest is charged on interest already added.
The interest is added to what is owed, not paid away.

questions.why: PIK interest is added to the principal rather than paid in cash, so it compounds: cash-friendly now, expensive at exit.

questions.q: A junior’s returns for a five-year deal: equity of {e0|R0m} in, {e1|R0m} out. Which line is wrong?
questions.why: IRR compounds: dividing the total gain by the years overstates it.

questions.q: A junior’s exit equity: the company sells for {x|R0m}, with debt of {d|R0m} and cash of {c|R0m} at exit. Which line is wrong?

options: {x|R0m} − {d-c|R0m} = {x-d+c|R0m}
{x|R0m} + {d-c|R0m} = {x+d-c|R0m}
{x|R0m} − {d|R0m} − {c|R0m} = {x-d-c|R0m}

questions.why: Lenders are repaid first: equity gets the enterprise value less net debt. Line 4 then inherits the wrong figure.

questions.q: A junior’s revolver cost: a {rc|R0m} facility, {u|R0m} drawn on average, {cf|2%} commitment fee. Which line is wrong?

options: {rc|R0m} × {cf|2%} = {rc*cf|R2m}
Nothing: fees are only charged on drawn amounts

questions.why: The commitment fee is charged on the undrawn part; the drawn part pays interest.

questions.q: A junior prices a term loan: benchmark {b|2%}, floor {fl|2%}, spread {s|2%}. Which line is wrong?

options: {fl|2%} + {s|2%} = {fl+s|2%}: the floor applies
{s|2%} alone

questions.why: With the benchmark below the floor, the floor sets the base rate.

questions.q: A junior’s financing structure: price {m|1x} EBITDA of {e|R0m}, debt {lv|2x} EBITDA. Which line is wrong?

options: {e*m-e*lv|R0m} ÷ {e*lv|R0m} = {(m-lv)/lv|1%}
{e*lv|R0m} ÷ {e*m-e*lv|R0m} = {lv/(m-lv)|1%}

questions.why: Line 4 divides debt by the price, which is the debt share. The equity share is equity over the price.

questions.q: A junior’s after-tax cost of new acquisition debt ({d|R0m} at {r|1%}, tax {t|0%}). Which line is wrong?

options: {d*r*t|R1m}
{d*r|R1m}

questions.why: Tax saved reduces the cost of debt: it is subtracted.
questions.src: Economics of LBOs: cost of debt

questions.q: In your head: a {m|1x} cash return over {n} years. Roughly what IRR is that?
questions.why: Know the five-year table by heart: it turns any cash return into an IRR in seconds.

questions.q: Paper LBO: buy at {m|1x} EBITDA of {e|R0m} with {lv|1x} debt. EBITDA reaches {e5|R0m} in five years, {rp|R0m} of debt is repaid, and the exit is at {m|1x}. Roughly what IRR?
work: Cash return {mo|1x} over five years, so IRR ≈ {irr|0%}
questions.why: Price, debt, equity in; value, debt, equity out; then the multiple to an IRR. Private equity firms set this in interviews, usually with no calculator.

questions.q: Before you read: a buyer pays mostly with borrowed money and repays the debt from the company’s own cash. Why might its return on equity be high?
options: A small equity cheque captures all the value left after the debt is repaid
Interest rates are always below inflation, so the debt shrinks on its own
Lenders share part of the interest they earn with the buyer each year
questions.why: That is the leveraged buyout: leverage magnifies the return on the sponsor’s equity, and its risk.

questions.q: Before you read: which kind of business can safely carry the most debt?
options: One with steady, predictable cash flow
One with fast but erratic sales
One that needs heavy, ongoing investment
questions.why: Lenders want cash flow they can count on to pay interest and repay principal.

questions.q: Before you read: if a company fails, which investors are usually repaid first?
options: Secured lenders, such as banks
Shareholders, who own the company
Everyone equally, in proportion
questions.why: Seniority sets who is repaid first; equity is last, which is why it expects the highest return.

questions.q: In your head: a {m|1x} cash return over three years. Roughly what IRR is that?
questions.why: The shorter the hold, the higher the IRR for the same cash return: know the three-year and five-year tables.

questions.q: In your head: a sponsor buys at {m|1x} EBITDA of {e|R0m}, pays fees of {f|0%} of the price and raises debt of {lv|1x} EBITDA. Roughly how big is the equity cheque?
questions.why: Uses are the price plus fees; debt covers part, equity the rest.

questions.q: Debt financing fees are capitalised and amortised, while other deal fees are expensed and reduce the equity contributed.
questions.why: Amortisation of financing fees is a non-cash charge, added back on the cash flow statement. Under IFRS the fees are deducted from the loan’s carrying amount rather than shown as an asset, and are spread over its life through the interest charge.

questions.q: Under a 100% cash flow sweep, excess free cash flow repays prepayable bank debt, but high yield notes are left untouched.
questions.why: The notes have call protection and no amortisation, so they stay outstanding until refinanced or repaid at maturity.

questions.q: Average-balance interest creates a circular reference in the model, which needs Excel’s iteration setting.
questions.why: Interest affects net income and cash for repayment, which affects ending debt, which affects interest.

questions.q: With a fixed exit multiple, later exit years tend to show a rising cash return but a falling IRR.
questions.why: Equity value keeps growing as debt is repaid, but slower growth and the time value of money pull the annual return down.

questions.q: Banks’ credit committees require the deal team to test the target under one or more downside cases.
questions.why: Downside cases cut growth, margins and possibly cash efficiency, to check the target can still service its debt.

questions.q: Goodwill created in the deal equals the equity purchase price less the target’s net identifiable assets.
questions.why: Net identifiable assets are shareholders’ equity less existing goodwill. The book simplifies by allocating the whole premium to goodwill.

questions.q: Why is an LBO model typically projected for seven to ten years?
options: To match the maturity of the longest-dated debt in the structure
Because sponsors nearly always hold their investments for ten years
Because management projections in the CIM cover ten years
To make the IRR look higher by including more years of growth
questions.why: When a CIM gives five years, bankers often hold year-five growth and margins constant for the later years.

questions.q: Which operating case is ultimately used to set covenants and market the financing to investors?
options: The Sponsor Case
The Management Case
The Downside Case
The Upside Case
questions.why: The sponsor builds it from its own diligence. The banks check that it is feasible and that the proposed structure is marketable.

questions.q: How is cash available for debt repayment calculated in an LBO model?
options: Cash flow from operating activities plus cash flow from investing activities
EBITDA less interest expense, before any capex or working capital
Net income plus capex, since capex is added back as a non-cash item
Unlevered free cash flow from the DCF, before any interest is paid
questions.why: It is a levered free cash flow, after interest. It pays mandatory amortisation first, then optional repayments.

questions.q: In what order is excess cash usually applied to optional repayments?
options: Revolver first, then Term Loan A, then Term Loan B
Senior notes first, then the term loans, then the revolver
Term Loan B first, then Term Loan A, then the revolver
Equally across all the debt, in proportion to the balances
questions.why: Bank debt is repaid in order of seniority and prepayability; the high yield notes stay outstanding.

questions.q: In a downside case, cash available for optional repayment turns negative in one year. What does the model do?
options: Draws on the revolver or cash on hand to cover the gap, and repays it first from later surpluses
Issues new equity automatically to the sponsor, which then owns a larger share of the company
Defaults on the senior notes for that year, which the model shows as a missed coupon payment
Skips the mandatory amortisation for that year and adds it to the term loan’s final payment
questions.why: The revolver provides liquidity for exactly these periods.

questions.q: Why would a banker advising a strategic buyer run an LBO analysis?
options: To gauge what a competing sponsor could pay, and so frame the bid
Because strategic buyers usually fund deals with LBO-style financing
To calculate the synergies that the combination can be expected to deliver
To set the target’s share price before the offer is announced
questions.why: On the sell side, it also helps set price expectations for the seller.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT a primary driver of the sponsor’s IRR?
options: The target’s historical share price
The purchase price
The size of the equity contribution
The exit multiple and exit year
questions.why: IRR depends on the projections, the price, the financing structure and the exit assumptions.

questions.q: The target’s existing 8% notes must be refinanced because of a change of control, and are callable at 104. How is the cost treated?
options: As a use of funds: a 4% premium on the notes, deducted from the equity contributed
As a source of funds, since the call premium is paid by the noteholders themselves
Ignored, since the notes are repaid at par when the change of control happens
Capitalised as a financing fee and amortised over the life of the new notes
questions.why: Par plus half the coupon gives 104, so the holders receive a 4% premium. Like other deal costs, it is expensed against equity.

questions.q: How did the book derive ValueCo’s LBO valuation range?
options: From entry and exit multiples giving IRRs around 20%, with equity of 25–40%
From the highest bids received in the first round of the auction process
From the DCF terminal value, discounted back at the sponsor’s target IRR
From the target’s book value, adjusted for the market value of its assets
questions.why: The sensitivity table pointed to 7.25× to 8.25× LTM EBITDA as the range.

questions.q: A private target with LTM EBITDA of {e|R0m} is bought at {m|1x}. It has {d|R0m} of debt and {c|R0m} of cash. What is the equity purchase price?

errs.why: Cash in the business goes to the sellers: add it.
That is enterprise value. Take off net debt for the shares.
Net debt comes off on the way to equity value.

questions.why: Work back from enterprise value: the sellers of the shares get the value less the debt, plus the cash in the business.

questions.q: Uses: buy the equity for {eqp|R0m}, refinance {d|R0m} of debt and pay {f|R0m} of fees. Sources: a {tl|R0m} term loan, {nt|R0m} of notes and {c|R0m} of cash on hand. How much equity must the sponsor contribute?

errs.why: Fees are a use of funds too.
Cash on hand is a source: it reduces the equity needed.
The existing debt being refinanced is a use as well.

ask.q: Why must total sources equal total uses?
options: Every rand spent on the deal has to come from somewhere: the sponsor’s equity fills whatever the debt and cash don’t cover
It is a tax requirement
Lenders insist that sources exceed uses
ask.why: Sources and uses is a balanced table. The sponsor’s equity is the plug that makes it balance.

questions.why: Equity is the plug that balances sources and uses.

questions.q: The equity purchase price is {eqp|R0m}. The target’s shareholders’ equity is {se|R0m}, including {og|R0m} of existing goodwill. How much goodwill does the deal create?

errs.why: Existing goodwill isn’t an identifiable asset: take it out of the target’s equity first.
Only remove the existing goodwill once.

questions.why: Existing goodwill is written off and replaced: new goodwill is the price paid over the net identifiable assets.

questions.q: Fees are {a|2%} on {ba|R0m} of bank facilities, {b|2%} on {nb|R0m} of notes and {c|2%} on a {br|R0m} bridge commitment. What do these financing fees total?

errs.why: The bridge commitment fee is paid whether or not the bridge is drawn.
Apply each rate to its own facility.

questions.why: The bridge fee is paid for the commitment even if the bridge is never drawn.

questions.q: A term loan starts the year at {b0|R0m} and ends at {b1|R0m}. Its rate is {r|2%}. What interest does the average-balance method give?

errs.why: That uses the opening balance. Use the average of opening and closing.
That uses the closing balance. Use the average.
Halve the sum to get the average balance.

questions.why: Average-balance interest reflects repayments made through the year; it is why LBO models carry a circular reference.

questions.q: A {b0|R0m} Term Loan B amortises {am|0%} a year. This year’s cash available for debt repayment is {ca|R0m}, and all of it is swept to the loan. What is the ending balance?

errs.why: The sweep also applies the rest of the cash available.
The mandatory amortisation is part of the cash available, not on top of it.

questions.why: Cash available is first used for the mandatory amortisation; the sweep takes what is left. In total, all the cash available repays debt.

questions.q: At close, EBITDA is {e|R0m} and annual interest expense {i|R0m}. What is interest coverage (EBITDA ÷ interest)?

errs.why: Coverage is EBITDA over interest, not the other way round.

questions.why: Lenders watch coverage alongside leverage: how many times EBITDA covers the interest bill.

questions.q: At exit, EBITDA is {e5|R0m} and the exit multiple {m|1x}. Debt is {d|R0m} and cash nil. The sponsor invested {eq|R0m} five years earlier. What is the IRR?

errs.why: Take the debt off the exit value first.
That ignores compounding; take the fifth root.

questions.why: Exit equity is exit value less the debt; the IRR is the fifth root of the cash return, less one.

questions.q: In year 1, net income is {ni|R0m}, D&A {da|R0m}, capex {cx|R0m} and the increase in net working capital {dn|R0m}. How much cash is available for debt repayment?

errs.why: An increase in working capital uses cash.
D&A is non-cash: add it back.
Capex comes off: it is cash spent.

questions.why: Cash flow from operations plus cash flow from investing: what the business generates after reinvestment, ready to repay debt.
questions.src: Step IV: Cash available for debt repayment

questions.q: At close, the target has a {tl|R0m} term loan (secured) and {nt|R0m} of senior unsecured notes. LTM EBITDA is {e|R0m}. What is senior secured leverage?
work: Senior secured leverage = secured debt ÷ EBITDA = {tl|R0m} ÷ {e|R0m} = {ssl|2x}

errs.why: That is total leverage. Senior secured counts only the secured term loan.
The notes are unsecured: count the term loan.

questions.why: Senior secured leverage counts only secured debt; total leverage counts it all.

questions.q: Pro forma EBIT is {ebit|R0m} and net interest {i|R0m}. With a {t|0%} tax rate, what is net income?

errs.why: Interest comes off before tax.
Deduct interest before tax, not after.
That is the tax, not net income.

questions.why: Interest comes off before tax; the higher interest of an LBO cuts net income but also the tax bill.

questions.q: The sponsor contributes {sp|R0m}. Other deal fees of {df|R0m} and a {tp|R0m} tender premium are expensed at close. What shareholders’ equity appears on the pro forma balance sheet?

errs.why: Expensed fees and premiums reduce the equity on the balance sheet.
The tender premium is expensed too.

questions.why: Expensed costs reduce equity at close; the book capitalises financing fees as an asset instead. Under IFRS the fees are deducted from the loan’s carrying amount rather than shown as an asset, and are spread over its life through the interest charge.
questions.src: Step III: Pro forma balance sheet

questions.q: Put the five steps of building an LBO analysis in order.
items: Locate and analyse the necessary information
questions.why: Stand-alone model first, then the deal, then the debt schedule, then the returns and credit analysis.

questions.q: Excess cash is applied to optional repayments in a typical LBO. Order the debt from first repaid to last.
items: Senior notes (not prepayable; left until maturity)
questions.why: Prepayable bank debt is swept in order of cost and flexibility; notes are usually non-callable early and stay outstanding.

questions.q: The model switches from a 50% to a 100% cash sweep. What happens to debt at exit, total interest paid over the hold and the sponsor’s equity at exit?
questions.why: More cash goes to repaying debt sooner, which saves interest and leaves more of the exit value for equity.

questions.q: With EBITDA growing and a fixed exit multiple, the sponsor considers exiting in year 6 instead of year 5. What usually happens to the cash return and to the IRR?
questions.why: Another year of growth and paydown adds to the cash return, but spread over more years the yearly rate usually falls.

questions.q: Which deal costs are capitalised on the opening balance sheet and amortised, rather than expensed at close?
options: Debt financing fees
M&A advisory fees
Legal and accounting fees for the acquisition
A tender or call premium on refinanced notes
questions.why: Financing fees are amortised over the life of the debt; other deal costs are expensed and reduce equity at close. Under IFRS the fees are deducted from the loan’s carrying amount rather than shown as an asset, and are spread over its life through the interest charge.
miss: Advisory fees are expensed at close.
Acquisition legal and accounting costs are expensed.
Premiums to retire old debt are expensed.

questions.q: A bank’s credit committee is reviewing the LBO. Which pair of statistics will it focus on most?
options: Leverage (debt ÷ EBITDA) and interest coverage (EBITDA ÷ interest)
IRR and cash-on-cash return, which show what the sponsor makes
P/E and dividend yield, which show how the market values the shares
Revenue growth and market share against the main competitors
questions.why: Lenders care about getting repaid: how much debt the cash flow supports and how comfortably it pays the interest. Returns are the sponsor’s concern.
miss: Those are the sponsor’s measures of return, not the lender’s measure of risk.
Equity market measures; the company will be private.
Useful context, but the credit view rests on leverage and coverage.

questions.q: A {rc|R0m} revolver is drawn {u|R0m} on average at {r|2%}, with a {cf|2%} commitment fee on the undrawn part. What is its total annual cost?

errs.why: Add the commitment fee on the undrawn part.
Interest is charged on the drawn amount only.

questions.why: A revolver costs interest on what is drawn and a commitment fee on what is not.

questions.q: Debt at close is {d0|R0m}. Over five years the company repays {cum|R0m}. What share of the opening debt has been repaid?

errs.why: That is the share still outstanding.

questions.why: Cumulative paydown is a headline credit statistic: it shows how fast the structure deleverages.

questions.q: A junior’s goodwill: price {eqp|R0m}; target equity {se|R0m}, including {og|R0m} of existing goodwill. Which line is wrong?

options: {se|R0m} − {og|R0m} = {se-og|R0m}: existing goodwill isn’t identifiable
{se|R0m} + {og|R0m} = {se+og|R0m}
{eqp|R0m} − {og|R0m} = {eqp-og|R0m}

questions.why: Existing goodwill is written off in the deal, so it comes out of the net identifiable assets. Line 3 then inherits the wrong figure.

questions.q: A junior’s sources and uses. Which line is wrong?
lines: Uses: equity purchase price {eqp|R0m}, refinance debt {d|R0m}, fees {f|R0m}

options: {eqp+d+f|R0m}, including the fees
{eqp|R0m}, the shares only
{eqp+d-f|R0m}, net of fees

questions.why: Fees are a use of funds; leaving them out understates the equity the sponsor must find. Line 4 inherits the error.

questions.q: A junior’s interest on a term loan: {b0|R0m} at the start of the year, {b1|R0m} at the end, rate {r|2%}, average-balance method. Which line is wrong?
questions.why: The model uses the average balance, so repayments during the year are reflected.

questions.q: A junior’s pro forma shareholders’ equity. Which line is wrong?
lines: Less M&A advisory and other deal fees (expensed): {df|R0m}

fix.q: What should happen to the financing fees?
options: Nothing at close: they are spread over the loan’s life, not deducted from equity
Deduct them as well: every deal cost reduces equity at close
Add them back to equity, since the lenders are the ones paid

questions.why: Financing fees are spread over the life of the debt; only expensed costs reduce equity at close. Under IFRS the fees are deducted from the loan’s carrying amount rather than shown as an asset, and are spread over its life through the interest charge.
questions.src: Step III: Pro forma balance sheet

questions.q: A junior’s credit statistics: term loan {tl|R0m} (secured), notes {nt|R0m} (unsecured), EBITDA {e|R0m}. Which line is wrong?

options: {tl|R0m} ÷ {e|R0m} = {tl/e|1x}
{nt|R0m} ÷ {e|R0m} = {nt/e|1x}
{e|R0m} ÷ {tl|R0m} = {e/tl|1x}

questions.why: Senior secured leverage counts only the secured debt.

questions.q: A junior’s exit equity: exit value {ev|R0m}, debt {d|R0m}, cash {c|R0m}. Which line is wrong?

options: Add the cash: equity gets it
Leave cash out entirely
Subtract the cash twice

questions.why: At exit the sponsor sells the shares, and the cash in the business goes with them: equity is value less debt plus cash.

questions.q: In your head: exit EBITDA {e|R0m} at {m|0x}, debt {d|R0m}, equity invested {eq|R0m}. Roughly what cash return?
questions.why: Value, less debt, over what went in.

questions.q: In your head: debt of {d|R0m} against EBITDA of {e|R0m}. Roughly what is leverage?
questions.why: Debt over EBITDA, the first number any lender asks for.

questions.q: Before you read: a company borrows heavily to fund its own buyout. What will lenders most want to see in the forecast?
options: Enough cash each year to pay interest and repay debt
A rising share price and strong demand for the shares
Fast growth in headcount and new offices each year
questions.why: An LBO model exists to test exactly that: whether the cash flow can service and repay the debt.

questions.q: Before you read: a buyer pays more than the book value of a company’s net assets. Where does the extra show up on the balance sheet?
options: As goodwill
As cash
As a liability to the seller
questions.why: The excess of the price over the net identifiable assets is recorded as goodwill.

questions.q: Before you read: a private equity fund needs a 20% yearly return. Over five years, roughly how many times its money does that mean?
options: About 2.5 times
About 2 times
About 5 times
questions.why: 1.2^5 ≈ 2.49: a 20% IRR over five years is roughly a 2.5× cash return.

questions.q: Paper LBO: EBITDA of {e|R0m} grows {g|0%} a year for five years; the exit is at {m|1x}; debt at exit is {d|R0m}; the sponsor put in {eq|R0m}. Roughly what IRR?
work: EBITDA in year 5 ≈ {e|R0m} × (1 + {g|0%})^5 = {e5|R0m} (10% a year for five years is about 1.6×)
questions.why: Grow the EBITDA, apply the multiple, take off the debt, then turn the cash return into an IRR.

questions.q: In your head: EBITDA {e|R0m}, interest {i|R0m}, capex {c|R0m}, tax paid {t|R0m} and no change in working capital. Roughly how much debt can be repaid this year?
questions.why: Cash for paying down debt is what is left after interest, capex and tax: the engine of an LBO.

questions.q: A broad auction maximises competition among bidders, but is harder to keep confidential.
questions.why: More parties means more risk of leaks to customers, suppliers and competitors, and more business disruption.

questions.q: A traditional two-round auction typically takes three to six months or more from the decision to sell until signing.
questions.why: Closing then depends on regulatory approvals, third-party consents, financing and shareholder votes.

questions.q: Buyers of private companies are usually asked to bid on a cash-free, debt-free basis.
questions.why: Bids are then comparable as enterprise values; the seller keeps the cash and repays the debt from proceeds.

questions.q: For a public target, the confidentiality agreement may include a standstill that bars unsolicited offers or share purchases.
questions.why: Other common terms: use of information, permitted disclosures, return of information, non-solicitation of staff and no “clubbing” with other bidders.

questions.q: The bid with the highest headline price is always the strongest bid in an auction.
questions.why: A higher price with heavy conditions, such as financing or further diligence, may be weaker than a firmer bid at a lower price.

questions.q: The seller normally reserves the right to reject all bids, and bidders can withdraw at any time before signing.
questions.why: An auction that fails to produce a sale is called a “busted” or failed process, and can taint the asset.

questions.q: A seller prioritises speed, confidentiality and cultural fit with the buyer. Which process best suits it?
options: A targeted auction, or a negotiated sale with one party
A broad auction to as many potential buyers as possible
A public announcement inviting bids from all comers
An IPO of the whole business on the stock exchange
questions.why: A broad auction suits a seller largely indifferent to confidentiality, timing and disruption.

questions.q: What is the teaser?
options: A brief one- or two-page synopsis to spark buyers’ interest, with the bankers’ contact details
The full information memorandum, sent to buyers once they have signed the confidentiality agreement
A first draft of the purchase agreement, sent to buyers so they can mark up the main terms
The final bid procedures letter that sets out the deadline and format for binding offers
questions.why: It covers a company overview, investment highlights and summary financials. Interested parties then sign a confidentiality agreement to receive the CIM.

questions.q: Why must contact with buyers be handled carefully for a listed target?
options: The contact itself can put the company “in play” and amount to selective disclosure of material facts
Listed companies can’t be sold through an auction, so each buyer must be approached by the board
Regulators must approve every call made to a potential buyer before any information is shared
Teasers and confidentiality agreements are not allowed for listed companies under exchange rules
questions.why: Fair-disclosure rules govern what can be shared and with whom.

questions.q: Which of these belongs to the second round of an auction?
options: Management presentations, site visits and data room access
Drafting the teaser and the confidential information memo
Selecting the universe of buyers who will be approached
Signing the confidentiality agreement for the first time
questions.why: Buyers then receive the final bid procedures letter and a draft definitive agreement to mark up.

questions.q: Why does the sell-side advisor run LBO analysis and accretion/dilution analysis during the auction?
options: To estimate what sponsors and particular strategic buyers can afford to pay
To set the target’s share price ahead of the public announcement
To prepare the financing that the winning buyer will need to close
Because the regulators require both analyses for every sale process
questions.why: Sponsors frame bids on IRRs; listed strategics look at EPS effects. Running both helps judge which bids are real.

questions.q: What is the “bring-down” condition in a definitive agreement?
options: The other party’s representations must still be accurate at closing, to the agreed standard
The price falls automatically if the target’s earnings fall between signing and closing
The seller must reduce the target’s debt to an agreed level before the deal can close
The buyer must lower its bid if markets fall by more than a set amount before closing
questions.why: The standard is usually forgiving, for example inaccuracies that do not add up to a material adverse effect.

questions.q: What does a material adverse change (MAC) clause do, and how has it worked in practice?
options: It may let a buyer walk away after a significant, lasting adverse change, but that is hard to prove
It guarantees the buyer a price cut whenever profits fall, and courts have enforced it strictly
It lets the seller raise the price if the target’s results improve before the deal closes
It cancels all of the seller’s representations once the agreement has been signed by both sides
questions.why: Courts have generally read “material adverse effect” as a very significant problem likely to be lasting, not short-term.

questions.q: When would a seller typically pay a break-up fee to the buyer?
options: When it terminates the agreement to accept a better offer
When the buyer can’t obtain the financing it needs to close
When the regulators approve the deal later than expected
Whenever the deal closes, as a reward for the buyer’s costs
questions.why: If the buyer fails to obtain financing, the buyer may owe a fee to the seller instead.

questions.q: Why do some sellers hire a separate bank to give the fairness opinion?
options: The sell-side adviser may be biased, with fees contingent on closing or financing offered to the buyer
Sell-side advisers are not allowed to value the companies they are selling under exchange rules
Fairness opinions must by law come from two separate banks for any sale of a listed company
A second bank is likely to find a lower value, which helps the seller manage buyers’ expectations
questions.why: A US court found that a sell-side adviser that also offered financing to the buyer had given conflicted advice.

questions.q: Which is a disadvantage of a negotiated sale compared with an auction?
options: Less negotiating leverage and competitive tension, with the risk of leaving money on the table
It is less confidential, since every potential buyer in the sector hears about the sale
It is slower to reach signing, because every term has to be negotiated from the start
It disrupts the business more, since management must host many buyers at the same time
questions.why: Its advantages: confidentiality, less disruption, often the fastest route to signing, and less taint if talks fail.

questions.q: In a two-step tender offer, what happens if the buyer reaches the threshold (typically 90%) of tendered shares?
options: It can complete a short-form merger, squeezing out remaining holders without a shareholder vote
It must start a new auction, since the remaining holders are entitled to a competing bid
The remaining shareholders keep their shares indefinitely, as a minority in the listed company
It must still hold a shareholder meeting, though the outcome is no longer in any doubt
questions.why: If it gets only a majority, it must still hold a vote, though approval is then assured.

questions.q: A staple financing package offers debt of {lv|2x} EBITDA and requires at least {ep|0%} equity. EBITDA is {e|R0m}. What purchase price (enterprise value) does that imply?
work: Debt is {1-ep|0%} of the price, so price = {d|R0m} ÷ {1-ep|2} = {p|R0m}

errs.why: That is the debt alone; equity funds the rest of the price.
Divide the debt by its share of the price, not by the equity share.
Gross the debt up by dividing by its share of the price.

questions.why: A staple tells the seller what a sponsor can afford: the debt on offer, grossed up by the minimum equity.

questions.q: A listed acquirer with {n|0m} shares will issue {x|0m} new shares to pay for a deal. What percentage of its existing shares is that (the threshold for a shareholder vote is commonly 20%)?
work: Compare it with the common 20% threshold for a shareholder vote

errs.why: Measure the new shares against the existing shares, not the enlarged total.

questions.why: Issuing more than about 20% of existing shares usually needs the acquirer’s own shareholders to approve.

questions.q: After closing, a {L|R0m} liability emerges that the seller had represented did not exist. The indemnity has a {dd|R0m} deductible and a {cap|R0m} cap. How much can the buyer recover?

errs.why: The deductible and the cap both limit the claim.
The cap applies: the seller’s exposure is limited to {cap|R0m}.
The deductible comes off first.

questions.why: A deductible (basket) takes the first slice of loss; the cap limits the seller’s total exposure.

questions.q: Bid A is R2.0bn, but needs more diligence and is subject to financing. Bid B is R1.9bn with committed financing and a near-final contract markup. Which is usually the stronger bid?
options: Probably Bid B: firmer terms and higher certainty can outweigh a 5% lower headline price
Bid A, because the highest headline price wins in every auction, whatever the terms
Neither: both must be rejected and the process restarted to find a better offer
Bid A, because conditions such as financing don’t matter once a contract is signed
questions.why: The advisor weighs price, structure and conditionality. A conditional bid invites re-trading once the bidder is chosen.

questions.q: A buyer bids {b|R0m} on a cash-free, debt-free basis. The target has {d|R0m} of debt and {c|R0m} of cash. What do the shareholders receive?
work: Shareholders receive the bid less the debt repaid, plus the cash kept: {b|R0m} − {d|R0m} + {c|R0m} = {eq|R0m}

errs.why: The bid is for the business; the debt is repaid out of it.
The seller keeps the cash: add it.
Debt is repaid from the proceeds, so it reduces them.

questions.why: A cash-free, debt-free bid values the business; the seller repays the debt and keeps the cash out of the proceeds.

questions.q: A target earns {e|R0m} of EBITDA. A strategic buyer expects {s|R0m} of annual synergies. At {m|1x} EBITDA including synergies, what could it justify paying?

errs.why: That leaves out the synergies the strategic buyer can capture.
Capitalise the synergies at the multiple too.

questions.why: Synergies let a strategic buyer pay more than a financial buyer: knowing that is the seller’s leverage.

questions.q: A target has {n|0m} shares. In a two-step tender offer the buyer wants a short-form squeeze-out at the typical {th|0%} threshold. How many shares must be tendered?

errs.why: A simple majority isn’t enough for a short-form squeeze-out.
The threshold is below 100%: that is the point of the squeeze-out.

questions.why: Reaching the threshold lets the buyer squeeze out the remaining holders without a shareholder vote.

questions.q: Put the stages of a two-round auction in order.
items: Organisation and preparation: valuation, buyer list, teaser, CIM
First round: teaser and confidentiality agreements, then non-binding bids
Second round: management presentations, site visits, data room
Negotiations: final bids, contract mark-ups, fairness opinion
Signing and closing: approvals, financing, close
questions.why: Preparation, then two rounds that narrow the field, then negotiation and closing.

questions.q: Order these documents as a buyer typically receives them in an auction.
items: Confidential information memorandum (CIM), with the first-round bid procedures letter
Data room access and the management presentation
Final bid procedures letter, with the draft definitive agreement to mark up
questions.why: A short teaser to spark interest; the CIM only after a confidentiality agreement; detailed diligence in the second round; the draft contract comes with the final bid instructions.

questions.q: Sort each step into the round of the auction where it happens.

items.t: Buyers sign confidentiality agreements and receive the CIM
Non-binding indications of interest
Management presentations
Data room access and site visits
Final, binding bids with a contract mark-up
Initial bid procedures letter

questions.why: Round one gathers interest and indicative prices; round two lets a short list do full diligence and bid firmly.

questions.q: A family wants to sell its business quickly, keep the sale quiet and choose a buyer that will look after its staff. Which process fits?
options: A negotiated sale or a small targeted auction
A broad auction to every plausible buyer
A public announcement inviting offers
It limits who knows and lets the family pick for fit, at the risk of a lower price
It always produces the highest price
It is the only process allowed for private companies

questions.why: Each process trades value against speed, confidentiality and control. Narrowing the field gives up some competitive tension.
miss: A broad auction maximises price tension, but it is the hardest to keep quiet and the most disruptive.
A public call for offers is the least confidential option of all.

questions.q: Late in an auction, the preferred bidder replaces a “subject to financing” condition with fully committed financing at the same price. What happens to deal certainty and to the bid’s headline price?
questions.why: Value is price and terms together: the same price with fewer conditions is a stronger bid.

questions.q: Why does a sell-side adviser run LBO analysis on its own client?
options: To estimate what a financial sponsor could afford to pay, which sets a floor for bids
To decide whether the client should take on more debt before it goes to market
Because every buyer is required by law to see an LBO analysis before bidding
questions.why: Sponsors bid what their returns allow; knowing that number helps the seller judge bids and push strategic buyers higher.
questions.src: First round: valuation from buyers’ perspective
miss: The client is selling, not borrowing: the analysis frames the price, not its own debt.
It is internal work for the seller.

questions.q: A listed target agrees a deal with a break-up fee of {bf|1%} of equity value. The equity value is {eq|R0m}. If the target’s board accepts a better offer, what fee does it pay?

errs.why: Check the decimal: {bf|1%} is {bf|3}.

questions.why: A break-up fee compensates the first buyer for its time and costs if the seller walks away for a better offer.

questions.q: Bid A is {a|R0m}, all payable at closing. Bid B is {b|R0m}, but {dp|0%} of it is an earn-out that you judge has a {pr|0%} chance of paying. Ignoring the time value of money, what is Bid B worth on an expected basis?
work: Expected value = {bv|R0m}, against {a|R0m} for Bid A

errs.why: That treats the earn-out as certain. Weight it by the chance it pays.
The earn-out has some value: include it, weighted by its chance.

questions.why: A higher headline price that depends on future performance can be worth less than a lower, certain one.

questions.q: A junior’s proceeds to shareholders from a cash-free, debt-free bid of {b|R0m} (debt {d|R0m}, cash {c|R0m}). Which line is wrong?

options: Add the cash: the seller keeps it
Leave cash out
Subtract it twice

questions.why: In a cash-free, debt-free deal, the seller repays the debt and keeps the cash, so cash adds to the proceeds.

questions.q: A junior’s indemnity claim: a {L|R0m} breach, a {dd|R0m} deductible and a {cap|R0m} cap. Which line is wrong?

options: {cap|R0m}: the cap limits the claim
{L|R0m}: the whole loss
{dd|R0m}: the deductible

questions.why: The cap is the most the seller can owe under the indemnity.

questions.q: A junior’s reading of a staple: debt {lv|2x} EBITDA of {e|R0m}, minimum equity {ep|0%}. Which line is wrong?

options: {e*lv|R0m} × {ep|0%} = {e*lv*ep|R0m}
{e*lv|R0m} + {ep|0%} = {e*lv|R0m}

questions.why: Debt is the share of the price that isn’t equity, so divide by that share.

questions.q: A junior compares two bids for a seller. Which line is wrong?
lines: Bid A: {a|R0m}, subject to financing and more diligence
Bid B: {b|R0m}, committed financing, near-final contract
Recommendation: take Bid A, because the headline price is higher

options: Price and terms together: Bid B’s certainty may outweigh a {1-b/a|0%} lower price
Only the headline price
Only the speed of closing

questions.why: Value is price and terms together: conditions are risks to the seller.

questions.q: In your head: EBITDA {e|R0m}, synergies {s|R0m}, multiple {m|0x}. Roughly what could a strategic buyer justify paying?
questions.why: EBITDA plus synergies, times the multiple.

questions.q: In your head: a cash-free, debt-free bid of {b|R0m}; debt {d|R0m}, cash {c|R0m}. Roughly what do shareholders get?
questions.why: Bid less debt plus cash.

questions.q: Before you read: a company owner wants the best price for the business. Why might a banker invite several buyers at once?
options: Competition between bidders pushes the price up
The law requires at least five bidders
It makes the sale quicker and more confidential
questions.why: An auction creates competitive tension, at some cost to speed and confidentiality.

questions.q: Before you read: why might a seller ask buyers to sign a confidentiality agreement before sharing detailed information?
options: To protect sensitive business information, which competitors may be among the bidders
To make every bid legally binding as soon as it is submitted to the seller
To fix the price in advance, since the agreement sets what buyers may offer
questions.why: Bidders often include competitors, so detailed information comes only under a confidentiality agreement.

questions.q: Before you read: is the highest bid always the best one for the seller?
options: No: conditions such as financing or extra diligence can make a lower bid more certain and so more valuable
Yes: price is all that matters, since the other terms can always be negotiated away after signing
Only for listed companies, where the board must by law accept whichever offer is the highest
questions.why: Sellers weigh price, certainty, timing and terms together.

questions.q: Growing by acquisition is often cheaper, faster and less risky than building a business from scratch.
questions.why: Buying gets an established business model, infrastructure and customers. The challenge is integrating it quickly with little disruption.

questions.q: Revenue synergies are generally more reliable and easier to achieve than cost synergies.
questions.why: Cost synergies, such as headcount and facility consolidation, are easier to quantify and more often achieved. Investors and lenders give revenue synergies less credit.

questions.q: A manufacturer that buys one of its suppliers is practising backward integration.
questions.why: Moving upstream is backward integration; moving downstream towards customers, for example buying a distributor, is forward integration.

questions.q: In a stock sale, the buyer takes on all of the target’s liabilities, known and unknown.
questions.why: The target becomes a subsidiary, so its past, present and future liabilities come with it. For the seller, that makes it the cleanest structure.

questions.q: When a company sells its assets and then distributes the proceeds, its shareholders can face two layers of tax.
questions.why: The company pays tax on the gain, then shareholders pay capital gains tax on the distribution. That usually outweighs the buyer’s tax benefits.

questions.q: As a rule of thumb, in an all-share deal, buying a target on a lower P/E than your own is accretive to EPS.
questions.why: You pay less for each rand of the target’s earnings than the market pays for yours. Synergies and deal-related D&A can shift the result.

questions.q: Which of these is an example of forward integration?
options: A car manufacturer buying a distributor
A car manufacturer buying an axle maker
A car manufacturer buying a rival car maker
A car manufacturer buying a software company
questions.why: Moving downstream, closer to the end customer, is forward integration. Buying the axle maker would be backward; the rival would be horizontal.

questions.q: Why do acquirers often test a proposed deal and financing with the rating agencies first?
options: To protect their credit rating, even if that means using more equity at some cost to EPS
Because the agencies must approve every merger before it can be announced to the market
To obtain the target’s projections, which the agencies hold from their own rating work
To set the offer price, since the agencies publish the value they place on each company
questions.why: Ratings affect the cost of capital and investor perception, and some companies need a minimum rating for operations or covenants.

questions.q: Why do most corporate sellers prefer a stock sale to an asset sale?
options: It avoids double taxation and transfers all liabilities to the buyer
It gives the seller a tax step-up on the assets it sells to the buyer
It is the only structure that the competition authorities will allow
It allows the seller to keep the assets while handing over the shares
questions.why: Transferring title to individual assets can also be slow, costly and impractical; in a stock sale everything moves with the shares.

questions.q: All-debt financing usually gives the most EPS accretion. Why isn’t it always chosen?
options: It can weaken credit statistics enough to risk a ratings downgrade
Debt is always more expensive than equity once taxes are included
It is not allowed for listed companies under stock exchange rules
It reduces the synergies, since lenders limit the integration plans
questions.why: In the book’s example, all-cash funding lifted leverage to 3.6×, against 2.6× with half shares, likely costing a downgrade.

questions.q: What does contribution analysis show?
options: Each party’s share of the combined sales, EBITDA, net income and equity value
The synergies that each side brings to the combination, by type and year
The implied multiples paid at a range of offer premiums and prices
The tax that each side will pay after the deal, compared with before it
questions.why: It is mostly used in share-for-share deals. In theory, ownership of the combined company would match the contributions if both were valued alike.

questions.q: What does analysis at various prices (a valuation matrix) display?
options: The implied multiples paid at a range of offer premiums and prices
The target’s 52-week trading range, compared with its peers’ ranges
The acquirer’s historical share prices over the past five years
The financing fees that the acquirer would pay at each offer price
questions.why: It compares implied multiples with those from comps and precedents, to see whether a price is in line with the market.

questions.q: Why is a deferred tax liability created in a stock deal with asset write-ups?
options: Book D&A on the write-ups is not deductible for tax, so book tax and cash tax differ
Because the seller owes tax on its gain, which the buyer agrees to pay later on
To record the future synergies, which will be taxed only once they are realised
Because goodwill is amortised for tax purposes but not in the published accounts
questions.why: The DTL is the write-up times the tax rate. It falls each year by the tax on the write-up D&A, which is a real use of cash.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT a key driver of EPS accretion or dilution?
options: The target’s historical share price chart
The purchase price paid for the target
The financing mix and the cost of debt
The expected synergies from the deal
questions.why: Earnings projections for both companies and transaction-related D&A from write-ups also matter.

questions.q: When might an acquirer pursue a deal that is dilutive in its first year?
options: When it is a long-term strategic move, such as a fast-growing target whose earnings ramp up later
Never: dilutive deals are always rejected by the board, whatever the strategic case for them
Only if the target is a private company, since dilution matters to investors only when the target is listed
When the deal is paid entirely in cash, since cash deals can’t dilute earnings per share
questions.why: As a rule acquirers avoid deals dilutive over the foreseeable horizon, but later-year accretion can justify an exception.

questions.q: When are acquirers more inclined to pay with their own shares?
options: When their share price is high, absolutely and relative to the target’s
When their share price is at a low, so that more shares change hands
When interest rates are very low, which makes debt finance unattractive
When the target insists on certainty of value at the time of closing
questions.why: Target holders usually prefer cash, since the value of shares can move between announcement and closing; tax-sensitive holders may prefer shares.

questions.q: On the book’s football field, which method usually gives the highest value, and why?
options: DCF, because it rests on management projections, which tend to be optimistic in sale situations
Comparable companies, because their trading multiples already include a control premium
LBO analysis, because financial sponsors are willing to pay the most for any business
The 52-week trading range, because it includes the highest price the shares reached all year
questions.why: Precedents usually come next (control premium and synergies), then comps. The order varies with market conditions.

questions.q: The equity price is {eqp|R0m} and the target’s net identifiable assets {nia|R0m}. Write-ups are {tw|0%} (tangible) and {iw|0%} (intangible) of the premium over those assets. At a {t|0%} tax rate, how much goodwill is created?

errs.why: The write-ups create a deferred tax liability, which adds back to goodwill.
The write-ups take part of the premium out of goodwill.
The deferred tax liability adds to goodwill; it isn’t deducted.

questions.why: Write-ups reduce goodwill, but the deferred tax liability they create adds some back: book and tax values now differ.

questions.q: Tangible write-ups of {wt|R0m} and intangible write-ups of {wi|R0m} are written off over {n} years. With a {t|0%} tax rate, by how much does the deferred tax liability fall each year?
work: The liability unwinds by the tax on it: {dep|R1m} × {t|0%} = {fall|R1m}

errs.why: That is the extra D&A. The liability falls by the tax on it.
That is the whole liability, not one year’s fall.

questions.why: Each year, book D&A on the write-ups exceeds tax D&A; the liability unwinds by the tax effect of that gap.

questions.q: In an asset purchase, the buyer steps up the tax basis by {su|R0m}, deductible over {n} years. At a {t|0%} tax rate, what is the annual tax saving?

errs.why: That is the deduction; the saving is the tax on it.
Spread the deduction over its life first.

questions.why: A step-up turns part of the price into future tax deductions: real cash value for the buyer.

questions.q: A company with an asset and share tax basis of {b|R0m} is sold for {p|R0m}. Corporate tax is {tc|0%} and shareholders’ capital gains tax {cg|0%}. If the company sells its assets and pays out the proceeds, what do shareholders net?
work: Net to shareholders = {net|R0m}, against {stock|R0m} in a stock sale

errs.why: That is a stock sale, taxed once. The asset sale is taxed twice.
Shareholders pay tax again when the proceeds are paid out.

questions.why: An asset sale taxes the gain twice: once in the company and again when shareholders receive the proceeds.

questions.q: Stand-alone, the acquirer’s EPS is {e0|R}. Pro forma, net income is {ni|R0m} on {sh|0m} shares. By what percentage is the deal accretive (+) or dilutive (−)?

errs.why: Measure the change against the stand-alone EPS: pro forma over stand-alone, less one.
That is the change in rand per share; express it as a percentage of stand-alone EPS.

ask.q: Why is accretion measured against the acquirer’s stand-alone EPS?
options: It shows whether the deal raises or lowers earnings for each existing share
Because the target’s EPS is irrelevant
Regulators require it
ask.why: Accretion compares pro forma EPS with what the acquirer would have earned per share without the deal.

questions.why: Pro forma EPS against stand-alone EPS: above it is accretive, below it dilutive.
questions.hint: As a percentage to 1 decimal place; use − for dilution.

questions.q: An acquirer earns {na|R0m} on {sa|0m} shares trading at {pa|R}. It buys a target earning {nt|R0m} for {pp|R0m}, paid entirely in new shares at {pa|R}. What is pro forma EPS?

errs.why: Count the new shares issued to pay for the target.
Add the target’s earnings and the new shares.

questions.why: In an all-share deal, buying earnings on a lower P/E than your own is accretive; on a higher one, dilutive.

questions.q: A deal is {d|R2} a share dilutive on {sh|0m} pro forma shares. With a {t|0%} tax rate, what pre-tax synergies would make it break even?

errs.why: That is the after-tax amount; gross it up for tax.
Gross up by dividing by (1 − t), not multiplying.

questions.why: Close the gap per share across all pro forma shares, then gross it up for tax: synergies are taxed before they reach EPS.

questions.q: A buyer pays an enterprise value of {ev|R0m}, which is {m|1x} LTM EBITDA of {e|R0m}. It expects {s|R0m} of annual synergies. What is the synergy-adjusted multiple?

errs.why: That is the headline multiple; add the synergies to EBITDA.
Synergies add to EBITDA.

questions.why: Counting the synergies the buyer expects shows the multiple it is really paying.

questions.q: A target trades at {p|R} with {n|0m} fully diluted shares and net debt of {nd|R0m}. At a {pr|0%} premium, what enterprise value does the offer imply?

errs.why: That is equity value; add net debt.
Add the premium to the share price first.

questions.why: Premium on the share price, times the shares, plus net debt.

questions.q: {sp|0%} of a {eqp|R0m} equity price is paid in acquirer shares trading at {pa|R}. How many new shares are issued?

errs.why: Only {sp|0%} is paid in shares.

questions.why: Only the share part of the price is paid in new shares, at the acquirer’s price.

questions.q: Switching from part-shares to all-cash adds {d|R0m} of debt at {r|1%}. With a {t|0%} tax rate, how much does that reduce pro forma net income?

errs.why: Interest is deductible: take off the tax it saves.
That is the tax saved, not the cost.

questions.why: Interest is deductible, so net income falls by the after-tax cost; the deal issues fewer shares in return.

questions.q: Put the steps of an accretion/dilution analysis in order.
items: Set the purchase price and premium
Add the target’s earnings, synergies, new interest and extra D&A
Work out pro forma net income and shares
Compare pro forma EPS with stand-alone EPS
questions.why: Price, then how it is paid, then the combined income statement, then per share.

questions.q: An acquirer pays with more debt and fewer new shares, at the same price. What happens to the shares issued, pro forma leverage and EPS accretion (assuming the after-tax cost of debt is below its earnings yield)?
questions.why: Cheap debt usually boosts EPS, but it loads the balance sheet: the trade-off rating agencies watch.

questions.q: In a share deal for a fixed rand value, the acquirer’s share price rises before the shares are issued. What happens to the number of new shares issued and to EPS accretion?
questions.why: A higher share price means fewer new shares for the same value, so less dilution.

questions.q: Sort these synergies by type.

items.t: Closing one of the two head offices
Selling each company’s products to the other’s customers
Larger purchasing volumes and better supplier terms
Bundling products into a combined offer
Merging IT systems and back offices
Using the target’s distribution to enter new regions

questions.why: Cost synergies come from doing the same with less and are usually more reliable; revenue synergies depend on customers and are harder to achieve.

questions.q: An acquirer on a P/E of {pa|0}× buys a target on a P/E of {pt|0}×, paying entirely in new shares. Ignoring synergies, is the deal accretive or dilutive?
options: Accretive
Dilutive
Neither
The earnings bought for each new share exceed the earnings each existing share carries
Share deals are always accretive
The target’s P/E doesn’t matter in a share deal

questions.why: Paying with shares on a P/E of {pa|0} means issuing R{pa|0} of shares per R1 of earnings; buying at {pt|0}× costs only R{pt|0}, so EPS rises.
miss: Dilution happens when the target’s P/E is above the acquirer’s.
With different P/Es, EPS moves.

errs.why: Invert the P/E: earnings yield is earnings over price.

questions.why: Compare it with the after-tax cost of debt: whichever is lower is the cheaper way to fund the deal for EPS.

questions.why: Accretion is measured against the stand-alone EPS.

{eqp|R0m} ÷ ({pa|R} + {pt|R}) = {eqp/(pa+pt)|1m}

questions.q: A junior’s goodwill: premium over net assets {pr|R0m}, write-ups {wu|R0m}, tax {t|0%}. Which line is wrong?

options: {pr|R0m} − {wu|R0m} + {wu*t|R1m} deferred tax = {pr-wu+wu*t|R1m}
{pr|R0m} − {wu|R0m} − {wu*t|R1m} = {pr-wu-wu*t|R1m}
{pr|R0m} = {pr|R1m}

questions.q: A junior’s cost of funding the cash part with {d|R0m} of debt at {r|1%} (tax {t|0%}). Which line is wrong?
questions.why: Interest is deductible, so net income falls by the after-tax amount.

questions.q: A junior’s pro forma EPS for an all-share deal. Which line is wrong?

options: {sa|0m} + {nw|1m} new shares = {sa+nw|1m}
{sa|0m} − {nw|1m} = {sa-nw|1m}

questions.q: A junior’s implied enterprise value for an offer at a {pr|0%} premium to {p|R}, with {n|0m} shares and net debt of {nd|R0m}. Which line is wrong?

options: {p*(1+pr)*n|R0m} + {nd|R0m} = {p*(1+pr)*n+nd|R0m}
{p*(1+pr)*n|R0m} − {nd|R0m} = {p*(1+pr)*n-nd|R0m}
{p*n|R0m} + {nd|R0m} = {p*n+nd|R0m}

questions.why: Enterprise value adds net debt to equity value.

questions.q: In your head: enterprise value {ev|R0m}, EBITDA {e|R0m}, synergies {s|R0m}. Roughly what is the synergy-adjusted multiple?
questions.why: Price over EBITDA with the synergies added.

questions.q: In your head: {sp|0%} of a {eqp|R0m} price is paid in shares at {pa|R}. Roughly how many new shares?
questions.why: Share part of the price over the acquirer’s share price.

questions.q: Before you read: why might a company buy another rather than grow on its own?
options: It can be faster, cheaper and less risky than building the same business from scratch
Acquisitions rarely fail, so they carry less risk than any plan to grow on its own
It avoids paying any premium, since the target’s owners usually sell at market
questions.why: Speed, cost and certainty are the main reasons, along with synergies.

questions.q: Before you read: a company issues new shares to pay for a deal. What could happen to its earnings per share?
options: It can rise or fall, depending on the earnings bought against the shares issued
It always rises, because the buyer adds the target’s profits to its own
It never changes, because the new shares and the new profits cancel out
questions.why: That is the question accretion/dilution analysis answers.

questions.q: Before you read: which is usually the cheapest way for a company to pay for an acquisition?
options: Cash on hand or new debt
New shares
They all cost the same
questions.why: Debt is cheaper than equity, especially after tax; equity is more flexible but issues shares.

questions.q: A JSE-listed group with a market capitalisation of {mc|R0m} agrees to buy a business for {c|R0m} in cash. What percentage of its market capitalisation is that (the JSE’s categorisation test)?

errs.why: Compare the consideration with the acquirer’s market capitalisation alone.

options: An announcement, a circular and shareholder approval (Category 1)
An announcement only, with no shareholder vote (Category 2)
Nothing, because the price is paid in cash rather than shares
The consideration is 30% or more of the group’s market capitalisation
Every acquisition above R1bn needs shareholder approval
Deals paid in cash always need a circular to shareholders

questions.q: A JSE company declares a dividend of {dps|R2} a share. What does a South African resident individual receive per share after dividends tax?

errs.why: That uses the 27% company tax rate; dividends tax is 20%.
That is the tax withheld, not what the shareholder receives.

questions.why: Dividends tax of 20% is withheld when dividends are paid to individuals. It is not the 27% company tax, which the company has already paid on its profits.

questions.q: Which shareholder receives a dividend from a JSE company with no dividends tax withheld?
options: A South African resident company
A South African resident individual
A foreign individual without tax treaty relief
questions.why: Dividends paid to South African resident companies are exempt from dividends tax. Individuals have 20% withheld; a tax treaty can reduce the rate for foreign holders.
